Now (s − a)(s − b)(s − c) = ▲<sup>2</sup>/s and abc = 4R▲, so the product = ▲<sup>2</sup>/(s·4R▲) = ▲/(4Rs) = r/(4R). Hence r = 4R sin(α/2) sin(β/2) sin(γ/2).

questions.question: Show that r<sub>1</sub> = a cos(β/2) cos(γ/2)/cos(α/2).
questions.answer: Proof: the right-hand side simplifies to √(s(s − b)(s − c)/(s − a)) = ▲/(s − a) = r<sub>1</sub>.
questions.explanation: r<sub>1</sub> = ▲/(s − a) = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c))/(s − a) = √(s(s − b)(s − c)/(s − a)) … (1). Using cos(β/2) = √(s(s − b)/(ac)), cos(γ/2) = √(s(s − c)/(ab)) and cos(α/2) = √(s(s − a)/(bc)): a cos(β/2)cos(γ/2)/cos(α/2) = a·[s√((s − b)(s − c))/(a√(bc))]·[√(bc)/√(s(s − a))] = s√((s − b)(s − c))/√(s(s − a)) = √(s(s − b)(s − c)/(s − a)), which is (1). Hence the identity holds.

questions.question: Prove that 1/r<sup>2</sup> + 1/r<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> + 1/r<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> + 1/r<sub>3</sub><sup>2</sup> = (a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup>)/▲<sup>2</sup>.
questions.answer: Proof: 1/r = s/▲ and 1/r<sub>1</sub> = (s − a)/▲, so the sum is [s<sup>2</sup> + (s − a)<sup>2</sup> + (s − b)<sup>2</sup> + (s − c)<sup>2</sup>]/▲<sup>2</sup> = (a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup>)/▲<sup>2</sup>.
questions.explanation: 1/r = s/▲, 1/r<sub>1</sub> = (s − a)/▲, 1/r<sub>2</sub> = (s − b)/▲, 1/r<sub>3</sub> = (s − c)/▲. Put x = s − a, y = s − b, z = s − c; then s = x + y + z, a = y + z, b = z + x, c = x + y. Numerator = s<sup>2</sup> + x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> + z<sup>2</sup> = (x + y + z)<sup>2</sup> + x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> + z<sup>2</sup> = 2(x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> + z<sup>2</sup>) + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx, while a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup> = (y + z)<sup>2</sup> + (z + x)<sup>2</sup> + (x + y)<sup>2</sup> = 2(x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> + z<sup>2</sup>) + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx. The numerators are equal, so the sum equals (a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup>)/▲<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Show that 1/(2rR) = 1/(ab) + 1/(bc) + 1/(ca).
questions.explanation: r = ▲/s and R = abc/(4▲) ⇒ rR = abc/(4s), so 1/(2rR) = 2s/(abc). On the other hand 1/(ab) + 1/(bc) + 1/(ca) = (c + a + b)/(abc) = 2s/(abc). The two sides are therefore equal.

questions.question: From the top of a cliff 80 m high the angle of depression of a boat is α. If the distance between the boat and the foot of the cliff is 80√3 m, then angle α is:
questions.explanation: The angle of depression from the cliff top equals the angle of elevation of the top from the boat, so tan α = 80/(80√3) = 1/√3 ⇒ α = 30° = π/6.

questions.question: To solve an oblique triangle, we use:
questions.explanation: Every oblique triangle can be solved by the law of sines, the law of cosines or the law of tangents, depending on which three elements are given; hence all of these are used.
questions.optionsRaw: a) law of sines  b) Laws of cosines  c) Laws of tangents  d) All of these

questions.question: A circle which touches all the sides of a triangle is called ______.
questions.explanation: The circle inscribed inside a triangle, touching all three sides, is the in-circle (its centre is the in-centre and its radius the in-radius).
questions.optionsRaw: a) circum-circle  b) in-circle  c) ex-circle  d) tri-circle

questions.question: In a triangle ABC, if β = 90°, then b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup> + a<sup>2</sup> − 2ac cos β becomes:
questions.explanation: Put cos 90° = 0 in the law of cosines: b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup> + a<sup>2</sup> − 2ac(0) = a<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup>, which is the Pythagoras theorem for the right angle at B.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Law of sines  b) Law of tangents  c) Pythagoras theorem  d) None of these

questions.question: In any triangle ABC, √((s − a)(s − c)/(ac)) is equal to:
questions.explanation: The half-angle sine formula gives sin(β/2) = √((s − a)(s − c)/(ac)), because β lies opposite b and the two adjacent sides are a and c.
questions.optionsRaw: a) sin α/2  b) cos α/2  c) sin β/2  d) sin γ/2

questions.question: In any triangle ABC, cos(γ/2) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Half-angle cosine formula: cos(γ/2) = √(s(s − c)/(ab)), since γ is opposite c and the adjacent sides are a and b.
questions.optionsRaw: a) √(s(s − a)/ab)  b) √(s(s − b)/ac)  c) √(s(s − a)/bc)  d) √(s(s − c)/ab)

questions.question: In any triangle ABC, with usual notations, s is equal to:
questions.explanation: s denotes the semi-perimeter, i.e. half the sum of the sides: s = ½(a + b + c) = (a + b + c)/2.
questions.optionsRaw: a) a + b + c  b) (a + b + c)/2  c) (a + b + c)/3  d) abc/2

questions.question: √(s(s − b)/((s − a)(s − c))) = …
questions.explanation: tan(β/2) = √((s − a)(s − c)/(s(s − b))), so its reciprocal is cot(β/2) = √(s(s − b)/((s − a)(s − c))).
questions.optionsRaw: a) sin β/2  b) cos β/2  c) tan β/2  d) cot β/2

questions.question: In any triangle ABC, √((s − a)(s − b)/(s(s − c))) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Half-angle tangent formula: tan(γ/2) = √((s − a)(s − b)/(s(s − c))) = r/(s − c).
questions.optionsRaw: a) sin γ/2  b) cos γ/2  c) tan γ/2  d) cot γ/2

questions.question: We can solve an oblique triangle, if:
questions.explanation: One side with two angles (law of sines), three sides (law of cosines) or two sides with the included angle (law of cosines) each determine the triangle completely, so all of these cases can be solved.

options.text: One side and two angles are known
Two sides and their included angles are known

questions.optionsRaw: a) One side and two angles are known  b) Three sides are known  c) Two sides and their included angles are known  d) All of these

questions.question: In ΔABC, inradius = ---------
questions.explanation: The in-radius is r = ▲/s, because ▲ = rs (the area equals the in-radius times the semi-perimeter). Printed key gives (b) ▲/s — the letter is a misprint, since ▲/s is option (d).

questions.question: In any triangle ABC, Area of triangle is:
questions.explanation: The area is half the product of two sides times the sine of the included angle. Sides a and b enclose the angle γ, so ▲ = ½ab sin γ. (The angle between b and c is α and between c and a is β, so options (a) and (b) are not of the correct form.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) bc sin α  b) ½ca sin α  c) ½ab sin γ  d) ½ab sin β

questions.question: Hero's formula is:
questions.explanation: Hero’s formula: ▲ = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s = (a + b + c)/2. Option (a) omits the square root and option (d) is just s.

questions.question: The circle passing through the three vertices of a triangle is called:
questions.explanation: The circle through the three vertices is the circum-circle; its centre is the circum-centre and its radius the circum-radius.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Circum-circle  b) In-circle  c) Ex-centre  d) Escribed circle

questions.question: The point of intersection of the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle is called:
questions.explanation: The right bisectors (perpendicular bisectors) of the sides meet at the circum-centre, the centre of the circum-circle.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Circum-centre  b) In-centre  c) Escribed centre  d) Ortho-centre

questions.question: Radius of the circle which passes through all the vertices of a triangle is:
questions.explanation: The radius of the circum-circle, which passes through all three vertices, is the circum-radius R = abc/(4▲).
questions.optionsRaw: a) Circum-radius  b) In-radius  c) e-Radius  d) Diameter

questions.question: In any triangle ABC, with usual notations, abc =
questions.explanation: From R = abc/(4▲) we get abc = 4R▲.
questions.optionsRaw: a) R  b) Rs  c) 4R▲  d) ▲/s

questions.question: The point of intersection of the internal bisectors of angles of a triangle is:
questions.explanation: The internal bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent at the in-centre, the centre of the in-circle.
questions.optionsRaw: a) In-centre  b) e-centre  c) Circum-centre  d) Ex-centre

questions.question: In any equilateral triangle ABC, with usual notations, r : R : r<sub>1</sub> =
questions.explanation: For an equilateral triangle R = 2r and r<sub>1</sub> = 3r, so r : R : r<sub>1</sub> = r : 2r : 3r = 1 : 2 : 3.

questions.question: Circum radius of ΔABC is:
questions.explanation: The circum-radius is R = abc/(4▲); the options ▲/s, ▲/(s − a) and ▲/(s − b) are the in-radius and the ex-radii r<sub>1</sub>, r<sub>2</sub>.

questions.question: Prove that r<sub>2</sub> = b cos(α/2) cos(γ/2)/cos(β/2).
questions.answer: Proof: both sides equal √(s(s − a)(s − c)/(s − b)) = ▲/(s − b).
questions.explanation: r<sub>2</sub> = ▲/(s − b). Since ▲<sup>2</sup> = s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c), ▲ = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), so r<sub>2</sub> = √(s(s − a)(s − c)/(s − b)) … (1). Now cos(α/2) = √(s(s − a)/(bc)), cos(γ/2) = √(s(s − c)/(ab)) and cos(β/2) = √(s(s − b)/(ac)). Therefore b cos(α/2)cos(γ/2)/cos(β/2) = b·[s√((s − a)(s − c))/(b√(ac))]·[√(ac)/√(s(s − b))] = s√((s − a)(s − c))/√(s(s − b)) = √(s(s − a)(s − c)/(s − b)), which is (1). Hence the result.

questions.question: Prove that r<sub>1</sub>r<sub>2</sub> + r<sub>2</sub>r<sub>3</sub> + r<sub>3</sub>r<sub>1</sub> = s<sup>2</sup>.
questions.answer: Proof: the sum equals ▲<sup>2</sup>·s/[(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)] = s<sup>2</sup>.
questions.explanation: r<sub>1</sub> = ▲/(s − a), r<sub>2</sub> = ▲/(s − b), r<sub>3</sub> = ▲/(s − c), so r<sub>1</sub>r<sub>2</sub> = ▲<sup>2</sup>/[(s − a)(s − b)], r<sub>2</sub>r<sub>3</sub> = ▲<sup>2</sup>/[(s − b)(s − c)], r<sub>3</sub>r<sub>1</sub> = ▲<sup>2</sup>/[(s − c)(s − a)]. Sum = ▲<sup>2</sup>[(s − c) + (s − a) + (s − b)]/[(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)] = ▲<sup>2</sup>(3s − 2s)/[(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)] = ▲<sup>2</sup>s/[(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]. Since ▲<sup>2</sup> = s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c), this equals s·s = s<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the area of triangle ABC when a = 5.2 cm, β = 30°, γ = 40°.
questions.explanation: α = 180° − 30° − 40° = 110°. Using one side and two angles: ▲ = ½a<sup>2</sup> sin β sin γ/sin α = ½(5.2)<sup>2</sup>(sin 30°)(sin 40°)/sin 110° = 13.52(0.5)(0.64279)/0.93969 = 4.62 square units.

questions.question: Find the area of triangle ABC when a = 125 cm, b = 120 cm, γ = 150°.
questions.explanation: The included angle between a and b is γ, so ▲ = ½ab sin γ = ½(125)(120) sin 150° = 7500(0.5) = 3750 square units.

questions.question: Find R and r of ΔABC when a = 18.8 cm, b = 24.5 cm, c = 30.2 cm.
Find R and r of ΔABC when a = 13.8 cm, b = 13.8 cm, c = 10.4 cm.
Find r<sub>1</sub>, r<sub>2</sub> and r<sub>3</sub> of the escribed circles, if the measures of the sides of triangle ABC are a = 3 cm, b = 4 cm and c = 5 cm.
questions.answer: r<sub>1</sub> = 2 cm, r<sub>2</sub> = 3 cm, r<sub>3</sub> = 6 cm.
questions.explanation: a = 3, b = 4, c = 5 is right-angled at C, so s = ½(3 + 4 + 5) = 6 and ▲ = ½(3)(4) = 6 cm<sup>2</sup> (Hero’s formula: √(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 6). r<sub>1</sub> = ▲/(s − a) = 6/3 = 2 cm; r<sub>2</sub> = ▲/(s − b) = 6/2 = 3 cm; r<sub>3</sub> = ▲/(s − c) = 6/1 = 6 cm.

questions.question: A hiker walks due east at 4 km per hour and a second hiker, starting at the same point, walks 55° north-east at the rate of 5 km per hour. How far apart will they be after 3 hours?
questions.explanation: After 3 hours the first hiker has walked 4 × 3 = 12 km due east and the second 5 × 3 = 15 km in the direction 55° east of north (bearing N55°E). The angle between due east and N55°E is 90° − 55° = 35°, so by the law of cosines d<sup>2</sup> = 12<sup>2</sup> + 15<sup>2</sup> − 2(12)(15)cos 35° = 144 + 225 − 360(0.81915) = 369 − 294.89 = 74.11 ⇒ d = 8.61 km. Reading 55° from the east axis instead would give 12.75 km; the printed key 8.6 km confirms the bearing interpretation used here.

questions.question: Three points A, B, C form a triangle such that the ratio of the measures of their angles is 1 : 2 : 3. Find the ratio of the lengths of the sides.
questions.explanation: Let the angles be x, 2x, 3x. Then x + 2x + 3x = 180° ⇒ x = 30°, so the angles are 30°, 60°, 90°. By the law of sines the sides are proportional to the sines of the opposite angles: sin 30° : sin 60° : sin 90° = ½ : √3/2 : 1 = 1 : √3 : 2.

questions.question: A piece of plastic strip 1 metre long is bent to form an isosceles triangle with 95° as measure of its largest angle. Find the length of the sides.
questions.answer: Equal sides ≈ 28.78 cm each; base ≈ 42.44 cm.
questions.explanation: Let each equal side be x metres; the largest angle 95° is the vertex angle between them, so the base is b = 2x sin 47.5°. Perimeter: 2x + 2x sin 47.5° = 1 ⇒ 2x(1 + 0.73728) = 1 ⇒ x = 1/3.47456 = 0.28780 m = 28.78 cm. Base = 1 − 2(0.28780) = 0.42440 m = 42.44 cm.
questions.figure: Isosceles triangle: vertex angle 95°, base angles 42.5° each, equal sides x, base 2x sin 47.5°, perimeter 1 m.

questions.question: Two airplanes leave a field at the same time. One flies 30° East of North at 250 km/h, the other 45° East of South at 300 km/h. How far apart are they at the end of 2 hours?
questions.explanation: Distances flown: 250 × 2 = 500 km and 300 × 2 = 600 km. The first course is 30° east of north and the second 45° east of south, so the angle between the two courses is 180° − 30° − 45° = 105°. d<sup>2</sup> = 500<sup>2</sup> + 600<sup>2</sup> − 2(500)(600)cos 105° = 250,000 + 360,000 + 155,291 = 765,291 ⇒ d = 874.8 km.

questions.question: Two men are on the opposite sides of a 100 m high tower. If the measures of the angles of elevation of the top of the tower are 18° and 22° respectively, find the distance between them.
questions.explanation: Distances from the foot of the tower: x<sub>1</sub> = 100/tan 18° = 100/0.32492 = 307.77 m and x<sub>2</sub> = 100/tan 22° = 100/0.40403 = 247.51 m. Since the men are on opposite sides, distance = 307.77 + 247.51 = 555.28 ≈ 555 m.

questions.question: A man standing 60 m away from a tower notices that the angles of elevation of the top and the bottom of a flagstaff on the top of the tower are 64° and 62° respectively. Find the length of the flagstaff.
questions.explanation: Height of the top of the flagstaff = 60 tan 64° = 60(2.05030) = 123.02 m; height of the top of the tower = 60 tan 62° = 60(1.88073) = 112.84 m. Length of the flagstaff = 123.02 − 112.84 = 10.17 ≈ 10.2 m.

questions.question: The angle of elevation of the top of a 60 m high tower from a point A, on the same level as the foot of the tower, is 25°. Find the angle of elevation of the top of the tower from a point B, 20 m nearer to A from the foot of the tower.
questions.explanation: Distance of A from the foot = 60/tan 25° = 60/0.46631 = 128.67 m. B is 20 m nearer, so its distance is 128.67 − 20 = 108.67 m. tan θ = 60/108.67 = 0.55213 ⇒ θ = tan<sup>−1</sup>(0.55213) = 28.90° = 28°54′.

questions.question: Two buildings A and B are 100 m apart. The angle of elevation from the top of the building A to the top of the building B is 20°. The angle of elevation from the base of the building B to the top of the building A is 50°. Find the height of the building B.
questions.answer: Height of building B ≈ 155.6 m (key: 155.5 m).
questions.explanation: Height of building A = 100 tan 50° = 100(1.19175) = 119.18 m (angle of elevation from the base of B, 100 m away). The top of B is 100 tan 20° = 100(0.36397) = 36.40 m above the top of A. Height of B = 119.18 + 36.40 = 155.58 ≈ 155.6 m.
questions.figure: Two vertical buildings A and B, 100 m apart on level ground; height of A is 100 tan 50°, and the top of B is 100 tan 20° above the top of A.

chapters.title: Graphs of Trigonometric and Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Solution of Trigonometric Equations

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function 2 sin 3x.
questions.explanation: sin 3x is defined for every real x, so the domain is ℝ. Since −1 ≤ sin 3x ≤ 1, multiplying by 2 gives −2 ≤ 2 sin 3x ≤ 2, so the range is [−2, 2].

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function 5 cos 4x.
questions.explanation: cos 4x is defined for all x ∈ ℝ. Since −1 ≤ cos 4x ≤ 1, we get −5 ≤ 5 cos 4x ≤ 5; the range is [−5, 5].

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function 8 tan 2x.
questions.answer: Domain: ℝ − {(2n + 1)π/4 : n ∈ ℤ}; Range: ℝ.
questions.explanation: tan 2x is undefined when 2x = (2n + 1)π/2, i.e. x = (2n + 1)π/4. Hence the domain is ℝ minus these values. On its domain tan 2x assumes every real value, so the range is ℝ.

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function cosec 6x.
questions.explanation: cosec 6x = 1/sin 6x is undefined when sin 6x = 0, i.e. 6x = nπ, so x = nπ/6. Since |cosec 6x| ≥ 1, the range is (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞).

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function 5 cot 2x.
questions.answer: Domain: ℝ − {nπ/2 : n ∈ ℤ}; Range: ℝ.
questions.explanation: cot 2x = cos 2x/sin 2x is undefined when sin 2x = 0, i.e. 2x = nπ, so x = nπ/2. On its domain cot 2x takes every real value, hence the range is ℝ.

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function sin(x/3).
questions.explanation: x/3 is defined for every real x, and −1 ≤ sin(x/3) ≤ 1 for all x. Thus the domain is ℝ and the range is [−1, 1].

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function cosec(x/4).
questions.explanation: cosec(x/4) is undefined when sin(x/4) = 0, i.e. x/4 = nπ, so x = 4nπ. Since |cosec(x/4)| ≥ 1, the range is (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞).

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function tan(x/7).
questions.answer: Domain: ℝ − {7(2n + 1)π/2 : n ∈ ℤ}; Range: ℝ.
questions.explanation: tan(x/7) is undefined when x/7 = (2n + 1)π/2, i.e. x = 7(2n + 1)π/2. The tangent takes every real value on its domain, so the range is ℝ.

questions.question: Determine whether the trigonometric function f(x) = sin x cos x is even, odd or neither.
questions.explanation: f(−x) = sin(−x)cos(−x) = (−sin x)(cos x) = −sin x cos x = −f(x). Since f(−x) = −f(x) for every x, f is odd.

questions.question: Determine whether the trigonometric function g(x) = sin²x/(1 + tan x) is even, odd or neither.
questions.explanation: g(−x) = sin²(−x)/(1 + tan(−x)) = sin²x/(1 − tan x). This is neither equal to g(x) = sin²x/(1 + tan x) nor to −g(x) for all x (for example at x = π/4, g(π/4) = (1/2)/2 = 1/4 while g(−π/4) = (1/2)/0 is undefined). Hence g is neither even nor odd.

questions.question: Determine whether the trigonometric function h(x) = tan x/(x + sin x) is even, odd or neither.
questions.explanation: h(−x) = tan(−x)/(−x + sin(−x)) = (−tan x)/(−x − sin x) = tan x/(x + sin x) = h(x). Hence h is even (x = 0 is excluded from its domain).

questions.question: Determine whether the trigonometric function k(x) = x³(sin x + cos x) is even, odd or neither.
questions.explanation: k(−x) = (−x)³(sin(−x) + cos(−x)) = −x³(−sin x + cos x) = x³(sin x − cos x). This is neither k(x) = x³(sin x + cos x) nor −k(x), so k is neither even nor odd.

questions.question: Find the period of the function sin 3x.
questions.explanation: For sin kx the period is 2π/|k|. Here k = 3, so the period is 2π/3.

questions.question: Find the period of the function cos 4x.
questions.explanation: For cos kx the period is 2π/|k| = 2π/4 = π/2.

questions.question: Find the period of the function tan(x/3).
questions.explanation: For tan kx the period is π/|k|. Here k = 1/3, so the period is π/(1/3) = 3π.

questions.question: Find the period of the function sec(x/5).
questions.explanation: For sec kx the period is 2π/|k| = 2π/(1/5) = 10π.

questions.question: Find the period of the function cosec 8x.
questions.explanation: For cosec kx the period is 2π/|k| = 2π/8 = π/4.

questions.question: Find the period of the function cot(x/6).
questions.explanation: For cot kx the period is π/|k| = π/(1/6) = 6π.

questions.question: Find the period of the function √5 cos(3x/2).
questions.explanation: The constant factor √5 does not affect the period. For cos(3x/2), the period is 2π/(3/2) = 4π/3.

questions.question: Find the period of the function cot(√2 x).
questions.explanation: For cot kx the period is π/|k| = π/√2.

questions.question: Find the period of the function sin(x/3).
questions.explanation: For sin kx the period is 2π/|k| = 2π/(1/3) = 6π.

questions.question: Find the period of the function cos(x/4).
questions.explanation: For cos kx the period is 2π/|k| = 2π/(1/4) = 8π.

questions.question: Find the period of the function (7/2) cot(2πx/3).
questions.explanation: The factor 7/2 does not change the period. For cot(2πx/3), the period is π/(2π/3) = (π·3)/(2π) = 3/2.

questions.question: Find the period of the function −(2/5) sec(3x/π).
questions.explanation: The factor −2/5 does not change the period. For sec(3x/π), the period is 2π/(3/π) = 2π²/3.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of y = 4 + 3 sin θ.
questions.explanation: Write y = a + b sin θ with a = 4, b = 3. Maximum = a + |b| = 4 + 3 = 7; minimum = a − |b| = 4 − 3 = 1.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of y = 2/3 − 4 cos θ.
Find the maximum and minimum values of y = 6 − (1/3) sin(3θ + 2).
questions.explanation: Here a = 6 and b = −1/3. Maximum = 6 + 1/3 = 19/3; minimum = 6 − 1/3 = 17/3.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of y = 8 + 5 cos(θ − 25).
questions.explanation: Here a = 8 and b = 5. Maximum = 8 + 5 = 13; minimum = 8 − 5 = 3.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of y = 1/(25 − 12 sin(3θ − 2)).
questions.explanation: The denominator d = 25 − 12 sin(3θ − 2) has maximum 25 + 12 = 37 and minimum 25 − 12 = 13. Both are positive, so 1/d is largest when d is smallest and smallest when d is largest: maximum = 1/13, minimum = 1/37.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of y = 1/(1 + 6 cos(5θ − 4)).
questions.explanation: The denominator d = 1 + 6 cos(5θ − 4) runs over [−5, 7] and can also be zero (when cos(5θ − 4) = −1/6). Therefore 1/d is unbounded above and below: on d ∈ (0, 7], 1/d ∈ [1/7, ∞); on d ∈ [−5, 0), 1/d ∈ (−∞, −1/5]. The function has vertical asymptotes where d = 0. The printed key gives “Max: 1/7; Min: −1/5”, but these are only the extreme values of the two separate branches, not global extrema.

questions.question: Draw the graph of y = −sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
questions.answer: Period 2π, amplitude 1, domain [0, 2π], range [−1, 1]. The graph is the sine curve reflected in the x-axis: it starts at (0, 0), falls to (π/2, −1), returns to (π, 0), rises to (3π/2, 1) and ends at (2π, 0).
questions.explanation: The factor −1 reflects y = sin x about the x-axis. Key points of y = sin x on [0, 2π] are (0,0), (π/2,1), (π,0), (3π/2,−1), (2π,0); changing the sign of y gives (0,0), (π/2,−1), (π,0), (3π/2,1), (2π,0). Join these by a smooth sinusoidal curve. The printed key tabulates the same values.
questions.figure: Graph of y = −sin x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

questions.question: Draw the graph of y = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
questions.answer: Period 2π, amplitude 1, domain [0, 2π], range [−1, 1]. It starts at (0, 1), crosses (π/2, 0), reaches (π, −1), crosses (3π/2, 0) and returns to (2π, 1).
questions.explanation: Plot the standard cosine points (0,1), (π/2,0), (π,−1), (3π/2,0), (2π,1) and join them by a smooth wave. The maximum value 1 occurs at x = 0 and x = 2π; the minimum −1 at x = π. The printed key notes that students should draw this graph themselves.
questions.figure: Graph of y = cos x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

questions.question: Draw the graph of y = sin(x/2) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
questions.answer: Period 4π, amplitude 1. On the given interval only half a cycle is drawn: (0, 0) rises to (π, 1) and falls to (2π, 0). Range on this interval is [0, 1].
questions.explanation: Since x/2 runs from 0 to π as x runs from 0 to 2π, sin(x/2) increases from 0 to 1 at x = π and decreases to 0 at x = 2π. The full period is 2π/(1/2) = 4π, so the graph on [0, 2π] is one half of a complete sine wave.
questions.figure: Graph of y = sin(x/2), 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

questions.question: Draw the graph of y = tan 2x for −π ≤ x ≤ 2π.
questions.answer: Period π/2; range ℝ. Zeros at x = nπ/2. Vertical asymptotes at x = (2n + 1)π/4, namely x = −3π/4, −π/4, π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4 in the given interval. Each branch rises from −∞ to +∞.
questions.explanation: tan 2x is undefined when 2x = (2n + 1)π/2, giving x = (2n + 1)π/4. Between consecutive asymptotes tan 2x increases monotonically from −∞ to +∞ and crosses the x-axis at x = nπ/2. On [−π, 2π] the branches lie between the listed asymptotes; mark the zeros (−π, 0), (−π/2, 0), (0, 0), (π/2, 0), (π, 0), (3π/2, 0), (2π, 0) and the points where tan 2x = ±1 as aids.
questions.figure: Graph of y = tan 2x, −π ≤ x ≤ 2π

questions.question: Draw the graph of y = 5 sec(x/3) for −2π ≤ x ≤ 2π.
questions.answer: Period 6π; range (−∞, −5] ∪ [5, ∞); no zeros. Asymptotes at x = ±3π/2. Minimum of the positive branch is 5 at x = 0; the graph passes through (−2π, −10) and (2π, −10).
questions.explanation: sec(x/3) is undefined when cos(x/3) = 0, i.e. x/3 = (2n + 1)π/2, so x = 3(2n + 1)π/2. In [−2π, 2π] these are x = −3π/2 and x = 3π/2. At x = 0, y = 5; at x = ±2π, cos(±2π/3) = −1/2 gives y = −10. The middle branch between the asymptotes opens upward with vertex (0, 5); the left outer piece falls from −10 to −∞ as x approaches −3π/2, and the right outer piece rises from −∞ to −10 as x goes from 3π/2 to 2π.
questions.figure: Graph of y = 5 sec(x/3), −2π ≤ x ≤ 2π

questions.question: Draw the graph of y = −4 cot x for −π ≤ x ≤ 2π.
questions.answer: Period π; range ℝ. Vertical asymptotes at x = −π, 0, π, 2π; zeros at x = −π/2, π/2, 3π/2. On each interval between asymptotes the graph increases from −∞ to +∞.
questions.explanation: cot x is undefined where sin x = 0 (x = nπ) and is zero where cos x = 0 (x = π/2 + nπ). The factor −4 reflects and stretches the cotangent graph: y = −4 cot x increases on each branch, passing through (−3π/4, −4), (−π/2, 0), (−π/4, 4), (π/4, −4), (π/2, 0), (3π/4, 4), (5π/4, −4), (3π/2, 0), (7π/4, 4).
questions.figure: Graph of y = −4 cot x, −π ≤ x ≤ 2π

questions.question: Without using a table of values, guess and draw the graph of y = cos 4θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. State its period, number of cycles and amplitude.
questions.answer: Period π/2; 4 cycles in [0, 2π]; amplitude 1. Maxima 1 at θ = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π; minima −1 at θ = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4; zeros at θ = π/8 + kπ/4.
questions.explanation: The coefficient 4 compresses cos θ horizontally by a factor 4, so the period is 2π/4 = π/2 and there are 4 complete waves in [0, 2π]. Each wave has the cosine shape: maximum 1 at the start, zero a quarter-period later, minimum −1 at the half-period, zero again, and maximum at the end.
questions.figure: Graph of y = cos 4θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π

questions.question: Without using a table of values, guess and draw the graph of y = 2 sin(θ/2) for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. State its period, number of cycles and amplitude.
questions.answer: Period 4π; half a cycle in [0, 2π]; amplitude 2. The graph rises from (0, 0) to (π, 2) and falls to (2π, 0).
questions.explanation: The factor 2 doubles the amplitude, while θ/2 stretches the graph horizontally by a factor 2, giving period 4π. On [0, 2π], θ/2 goes from 0 to π, so only the positive half of a sine wave is drawn.
questions.figure: Graph of y = 2 sin(θ/2), 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π

questions.question: Without using a table of values, guess and draw the graph of y = 3 cos(θ/2) for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. State its period, number of cycles and amplitude.
questions.answer: Period 4π; half a cycle in [0, 2π]; amplitude 3. The graph starts at (0, 3), crosses (π, 0) and ends at (2π, −3).
questions.explanation: The coefficient 3 gives amplitude 3 and θ/2 gives period 4π. As θ goes from 0 to 2π, θ/2 goes from 0 to π, so the cosine falls from its maximum 3 at θ = 0 through 0 at θ = π to its minimum −3 at θ = 2π.
questions.figure: Graph of y = 3 cos(θ/2), 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π

questions.question: Without using a table of values, guess and draw the graph of y = 2 sin 3θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. State its period, number of cycles and amplitude.
questions.answer: Period 2π/3; 3 cycles in [0, 2π]; amplitude 2. Zeros at θ = kπ/3; maxima 2 at θ = π/6 + 2kπ/3; minima −2 at θ = π/2 + 2kπ/3.
questions.explanation: The coefficient 3 compresses the sine wave to period 2π/3 (3 cycles in 0 to 2π), and the factor 2 doubles its height. Each cycle has the usual sine shape with maximum 2, zero, minimum −2, zero.
questions.figure: Graph of y = 2 sin 3θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π

questions.question: Without using a table of values, guess and draw the graph of y = cos(θ/3) for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. State its period, number of cycles and amplitude.
questions.answer: Period 6π; one third of a cycle in [0, 2π]; amplitude 1. The graph starts at (0, 1), crosses the axis at θ = 3π/2 and ends at (2π, −1/2).
questions.explanation: For cos(θ/3) the period is 2π/(1/3) = 6π, so the interval [0, 2π] contains one third of a cycle. It begins at the maximum 1, decreases to 0 when θ/3 = π/2 (θ = 3π/2), and reaches cos(2π/3) = −1/2 at θ = 2π.
questions.figure: Graph of y = cos(θ/3), 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π

questions.question: Without using a table of values, guess and draw the graph of y = sin 2θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. State its period, number of cycles and amplitude.
questions.answer: Period π; 2 cycles in [0, 2π]; amplitude 1. Zeros at θ = kπ/2; maxima 1 at θ = π/4 + kπ; minima −1 at θ = 3π/4 + kπ.
questions.explanation: The coefficient 2 compresses sin θ to period 2π/2 = π, so exactly two complete sine waves occur in [0, 2π]. The amplitude remains 1.
questions.figure: Graph of y = sin 2θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π

questions.question: Using the properties of the graph of sine, cosine and tangent, show that cos(π/2 + θ) = −sin θ.
questions.explanation: Using cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B with A = π/2, B = θ: cos(π/2 + θ) = cos(π/2)cos θ − sin(π/2)sin θ = 0·cos θ − 1·sin θ = −sin θ.

questions.question: Using the properties of the graph of sine, cosine and tangent, show that sin(3π/2 + θ) = cos θ.
questions.answer: As printed the identity is false. The correct identity is sin(3π/2 + θ) = −cos θ.
questions.explanation: Using sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B with A = 3π/2: sin(3π/2 + θ) = sin(3π/2)cos θ + cos(3π/2)sin θ = (−1)cos θ + 0·sin θ = −cos θ. A graph translation confirms it: shifting y = sin θ left by 3π/2 gives the graph of y = −cos θ, not y = cos θ. Hence the printed right-hand side omits a minus sign.

questions.question: Using the properties of the graph of sine, cosine and tangent, show that cos(π − θ) = −cos θ.
questions.explanation: Using cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B with A = π: cos(π − θ) = cos π cos θ + sin π sin θ = (−1)cos θ + 0 = −cos θ.

questions.question: Using the properties of the graph of sine, cosine and tangent, show that tan(π + θ) = tan θ.
questions.explanation: tan(π + θ) = sin(π + θ)/cos(π + θ) = (−sin θ)/(−cos θ) = tan θ, provided cos θ ≠ 0. This is simply the periodicity of tan with period π.

questions.question: Using the properties of the graph of sine, cosine and tangent, show that sin(3π/2 − θ) = −cos θ.
questions.explanation: Using sin(A − B) = sin A cos B − cos A sin B with A = 3π/2: sin(3π/2 − θ) = sin(3π/2)cos θ − cos(3π/2)sin θ = (−1)cos θ − 0 = −cos θ.

questions.question: Using the properties of the graph of sine, cosine and tangent, show that cos(2π + θ) = cos θ.
questions.explanation: cos(2π + θ) = cos 2π cos θ − sin 2π sin θ = 1·cos θ − 0·sin θ = cos θ. This expresses the periodic property of cosine with period 2π.

questions.question: For any integer k, deduce that cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ.
questions.answer: cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ for every integer k.
questions.explanation: cosine is periodic with period 2π, so adding any integer multiple of 2π leaves its value unchanged. Formally, cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ cos 2kπ − sin θ sin 2kπ = cos θ·1 − sin θ·0 = cos θ, since cos 2kπ = 1 and sin 2kπ = 0 for k ∈ ℤ.

questions.question: For any integer k, deduce that cosec(θ + 2kπ) = cosec θ.
questions.answer: cosec(θ + 2kπ) = cosec θ for every integer k (with sin θ ≠ 0).
questions.explanation: cosec(θ + 2kπ) = 1/sin(θ + 2kπ). By the periodic property of sine, sin(θ + 2kπ) = sin θ, hence cosec(θ + 2kπ) = 1/sin θ = cosec θ. Both sides are undefined at the same points sin θ = 0.

questions.question: For any integer k, deduce that tan(θ + 2kπ) = tan θ.
questions.answer: tan(θ + 2kπ) = tan θ for every integer k.
questions.explanation: tan(θ + 2kπ) = sin(θ + 2kπ)/cos(θ + 2kπ) = sin θ/cos θ = tan θ, using the 2π-periodicity of sine and cosine. (Since 2kπ is also a multiple of π, this is consistent with the period π of tan.)

questions.question: For any integer k, deduce that cot(θ + 2kπ) = cot θ.
questions.answer: cot(θ + 2kπ) = cot θ for every integer k.
questions.explanation: cot(θ + 2kπ) = cos(θ + 2kπ)/sin(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ/sin θ = cot θ, provided sin θ ≠ 0. This follows from the 2π-periodicity of sine and cosine (cot in fact has period π).

questions.question: Find the solution of sin x − 1/2 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = π/6.
questions.explanation: sin x = 1/2. The reference angle is π/6, and sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, giving x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = π − π/6 = 5π/6 + 2nπ. Of these, only π/6 lies in the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]. (The printed key lists the two general families.)

questions.question: Find the solution of cos x − 1/2 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = π/3 + 2nπ or x = 5π/3 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = ±π/3.
questions.explanation: cos x = 1/2. The reference angle is π/3; cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so x = π/3 + 2nπ or x = −π/3 + 2nπ (the key writes the second family as 5π/3 + 2nπ). Both π/3 and −π/3 lie in [−π/2, π/2].

questions.question: Find the solution of cos x + 1/√2 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = 3π/4 + 2nπ or x = 5π/4 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: no solution.
questions.explanation: cos x = −1/√2. The reference angle is π/4, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants: x = π − π/4 = 3π/4 + 2nπ or x = π + π/4 = 5π/4 + 2nπ. Since cos x ≥ 0 on [−π/2, π/2], neither value (nor any equivalent one) lies in the printed interval, so the restricted equation has no solution. The printed key gives the two general families.

questions.question: Find the solution of sin x + 1/√2 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = 5π/4 + 2nπ or x = 7π/4 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = −π/4.
questions.explanation: sin x = −1/√2. The reference angle is π/4 and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants: x = π + π/4 = 5π/4 + 2nπ or x = 2π − π/4 = 7π/4 + 2nπ. The representative 7π/4 is equivalent to −π/4, which is the only solution in [−π/2, π/2].

questions.question: Find the solution of tan x − 1/√3 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = π/6 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = π/6.
questions.explanation: tan x = 1/√3. The reference angle is π/6 and tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants, so x = π/6 + nπ. The only value in [−π/2, π/2] is π/6.

questions.question: Find the solution of tan x − √3 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = π/3 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = π/3.
questions.explanation: tan x = √3. Since tan(π/3) = √3 and tan has period π, x = π/3 + nπ. Only π/3 lies in [−π/2, π/2].

questions.question: Find the solution of sin x + √3/2 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = 4π/3 + 2nπ or x = 5π/3 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = −π/3.
questions.explanation: sin x = −√3/2. The reference angle is π/3 and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants: x = π + π/3 = 4π/3 + 2nπ or x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3 + 2nπ. The latter is equivalent to −π/3 + 2nπ, so the only value in [−π/2, π/2] is −π/3.

questions.question: Find the solution of cos x − 1 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = 0.
questions.explanation: cos x = 1. Cosine equals 1 only at integer multiples of 2π, so x = 2nπ. The only such value in [−π/2, π/2] is 0.

questions.question: Find the solution of Tan x + 1/√3 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = 5π/6 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = −π/6.
questions.explanation: Tan x = −1/√3. The reference angle is π/6 and tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, so x = π − π/6 = 5π/6 + nπ (equivalently −π/6 + nπ). In [−π/2, π/2] the solution is −π/6.

questions.question: Find the solution of tan x − 1 = 0 by using properties, when −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
questions.answer: General solution: x = π/4 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ. In the printed interval [−π/2, π/2]: x = π/4.
questions.explanation: tan x = 1. Since tan(π/4) = 1 and the period of tan is π, x = π/4 + nπ; the only value in [−π/2, π/2] is π/4.

questions.question: By using the graph, find the solution of Sin x − 2x/π = 0, where Sin x is the principal sine function.
questions.explanation: The equation is Sin x = 2x/π. Its solutions are the intersections of y = Sin x with the straight line y = 2x/π. At the endpoints x = ±π/2 both sides equal ±1, and at x = 0 both are 0, so (−π/2, −1), (0, 0) and (π/2, 1) are common points. Between 0 and π/2 the sine curve is concave and lies above the chord joining (0,0) and (π/2,1), so there is no further intersection; by symmetry there is none between −π/2 and 0 either. The printed key lists only 0 and π/2.
questions.figure: Intersections of y = Sin x and y = 2x/π on [−π/2, π/2]

questions.question: By using the graph, find the solution of Cos x + x/π = 0, where Cos x is the principal cosine function.
questions.answer: x ≈ 2.481 and x = π (principal domain 0 ≤ x ≤ π).
questions.explanation: Rewrite as Cos x = −x/π; the roots are the intersections of y = Cos x with the line y = −x/π. On 0 ≤ x ≤ π the cosine falls from 1 to −1 while the line falls from 0 to −1. Besides the endpoint intersection at x = π, the line crosses the cosine curve once more between 2.4 and 2.6; solving Cos x + x/π = 0 numerically gives x ≈ 2.481. The printed key records only x = π, the obvious endpoint intersection.
questions.figure: Intersections of y = Cos x and y = −x/π on [0, π]

questions.question: By using the graph, find the solution of Tan x − 4x/π = 0, where Tan x is the principal tangent function.
questions.explanation: Rewrite as Tan x = 4x/π. Both sides are odd, so it is enough to study 0 ≤ x < π/2. At x = 0 both are 0 and at x = π/4 both are 1. Near 0, tan x ≈ x is smaller than 4x/π (whose slope is 4/π > 1), so the line lies above the tangent curve until they meet at π/4; beyond π/4 the tangent curve rises above the line. Hence the intersections are x = 0, ±π/4. The printed key gives x = π, but tan π − 4π/π = 0 − 4 ≠ 0, so x = π is not a solution (it also lies outside the principal tangent domain).
questions.figure: Intersections of y = Tan x and y = 4x/π

questions.question: By using the graph, find the solution of Sin x − 3x/π = 0, where Sin x is the principal sine function.
questions.explanation: Rewrite as Sin x = 3x/π. At x = 0 and x = π/6 both sides equal 0 and 1/2 respectively; the line has slope 3/π < 1 while the sine curve starts with slope 1, so the sine curve is above the line just after 0 and crosses it at π/6, after which the line stays above the bounded sine curve on [0, π/2]. By odd symmetry the intersections are x = 0, ±π/6. The printed key lists only π/6.
questions.figure: Intersections of y = Sin x and y = 3x/π

questions.question: By using the graph, find the solution of Cos x − 3x/(2π) = 0, where Cos x is the principal cosine function.
questions.explanation: Rewrite as Cos x = 3x/(2π). At x = 0, 1 > 0; at x = π/3, cos(π/3) = 1/2 = 3(π/3)/(2π). For x > π/3 the cosine continues to decrease while the line increases, so there is no further intersection. Hence x = π/3.
questions.figure: Intersections of y = Cos x and y = 3x/(2π)

questions.question: By using the graph, find the solution of Tan x + x = 0, where Tan x is the principal tangent function.
questions.explanation: Rewrite as Tan x = −x. On (0, π/2), tan x > 0 while −x < 0, so there is no positive intersection; on (−π/2, 0), tan x < 0 while −x > 0, so there is no negative intersection. At x = 0 both sides are 0. Hence x = 0 is the only solution.
questions.figure: Intersections of y = Tan x and y = −x

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Sin⁻¹(1).
questions.explanation: The principal value y satisfies sin y = 1 with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2. The only such angle is y = π/2.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Sin⁻¹(−1).
questions.explanation: We need sin y = −1 with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2. Hence y = −π/2.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cos⁻¹(√3/2).
questions.explanation: We need cos y = √3/2 with 0 ≤ y ≤ π. The angle in this range is y = π/6.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cot⁻¹(−1).
questions.explanation: We need cot y = −1 with 0 < y < π. Since cot(3π/4) = cos(3π/4)/sin(3π/4) = (−√2/2)/(√2/2) = −1, the principal value is 3π/4. The printed key gives −π/4, following the book worked example that used the range −π/2 < y < π/2; that contradicts the stated principal range 0 < y < π of Cot⁻¹ (and the key itself gives Cot⁻¹(−1) = 3π/4 in part (xi)).

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cos⁻¹(1/2).
questions.explanation: cos y = 1/2 with 0 ≤ y ≤ π gives y = π/3.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Tan⁻¹(−1/√3).
questions.explanation: tan y = −1/√3 with −π/2 < y < π/2 gives y = −π/6.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Tan⁻¹(1/√3).
questions.explanation: tan y = 1/√3 with −π/2 < y < π/2 gives y = π/6.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cosec⁻¹(−2/√3).
questions.explanation: Let y = Cosec⁻¹(−2/√3). Then cosec y = −2/√3, so sin y = −√3/2 with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, y ≠ 0. Hence y = −π/3.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Sin⁻¹(−1/√2).
questions.explanation: sin y = −1/√2 with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2 gives y = −π/4.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cot⁻¹(1/√3).
questions.explanation: cot y = 1/√3 with 0 < y < π. Since tan y = √3, y = π/3.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cot⁻¹(−1).
questions.explanation: cot y = −1 with 0 < y < π. In the second quadrant, cot(3π/4) = −1, so y = 3π/4. This agrees with the printed key for part (xi).

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Sec⁻¹(2).
questions.explanation: Let y = Sec⁻¹(2). Then sec y = 2, so cos y = 1/2 with 0 ≤ y ≤ π, y ≠ π/2. Hence y = π/3.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Sec⁻¹(1).
questions.explanation: sec y = 1 means cos y = 1 with 0 ≤ y ≤ π, y ≠ π/2. Hence y = 0.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cosec⁻¹(2/√3).
questions.explanation: cosec y = 2/√3 gives sin y = √3/2 with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, y ≠ 0. Hence y = π/3.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, find the value of Cosec⁻¹(1).
questions.explanation: cosec y = 1 gives sin y = 1 with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, y ≠ 0. Hence y = π/2.

questions.question: Find the value of Cos(Sin⁻¹(√3/2)).
questions.explanation: Let y = Sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3 (principal value). Then Cos(Sin⁻¹(√3/2)) = cos(π/3) = 1/2.

questions.question: Find the value of Cosec(Cos⁻¹(1/2)).
questions.explanation: Cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3 (principal value). Therefore cosec(π/3) = 1/sin(π/3) = 1/(√3/2) = 2/√3.

questions.question: Find the value of Tan(Cos⁻¹(−1)).
questions.explanation: Cos⁻¹(−1) = π (principal value). Then tan π = 0.

questions.question: Find the value of Sec(Tan⁻¹(1)).
questions.explanation: Tan⁻¹(1) = π/4 (principal value). Then sec(π/4) = 1/cos(π/4) = 1/(1/√2) = √2.

questions.question: Find the value of Cot(Tan⁻¹(−√3)).
questions.explanation: Tan⁻¹(−√3) = −π/3 (principal value). Then cot(−π/3) = 1/tan(−π/3) = 1/(−√3) = −1/√3.

questions.question: Find the value of Sin(Sec⁻¹√2).
questions.explanation: Let y = Sec⁻¹(√2). Then sec y = √2, cos y = 1/√2, and the principal value is y = π/4. Thus sin(Sec⁻¹√2) = sin(π/4) = 1/√2. (The printed key labels the six answers of question 2 as “3. (i)-(vi)”; the values themselves agree.)

questions.question: Show that Tan⁻¹(12/5) = Cot⁻¹(5/12).
questions.explanation: Let α = Tan⁻¹(12/5). Then tan α = 12/5 and α ∈ (0, π/2) because 12/5 > 0. Hence cot α = 5/12. Since α also lies in the principal range (0, π) of Cot⁻¹, it follows that α = Cot⁻¹(5/12).

questions.question: Show that Tan⁻¹(√3) = Sin⁻¹(√3/2).
questions.explanation: Tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3 because tan(π/3) = √3 and π/3 ∈ (−π/2, π/2). Also Sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3 because sin(π/3) = √3/2 and π/3 ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. Hence the two principal values are equal.

questions.question: Show that Cosec⁻¹(2/√3) = Cos⁻¹(1/2).
questions.explanation: Cosec⁻¹(2/√3) = π/3 since cosec(π/3) = 2/√3 and π/3 ∈ [−π/2, π/2], π/3 ≠ 0. Also Cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3 since cos(π/3) = 1/2 and π/3 ∈ [0, π]. Hence the two are equal.

questions.question: Show that Cos⁻¹(4/9) = Cot⁻¹(4/√65).
questions.explanation: Let α = Cos⁻¹(4/9). Then cos α = 4/9 and sin α = √(1 − 16/81) = √65/9, with α ∈ (0, π/2). Therefore cot α = cos α/sin α = (4/9)/(√65/9) = 4/√65. Since α ∈ (0, π), it is the principal value Cot⁻¹(4/√65).

questions.question: Show that Sin⁻¹(77/85) + Sin⁻¹(3/5) = Cos⁻¹(87/425).
questions.answer: As printed the identity is false. The correct identity is Sin⁻¹(77/85) + Sin⁻¹(3/5) = Cos⁻¹(−87/425).
questions.explanation: Let A = Sin⁻¹(77/85) and B = Sin⁻¹(3/5). Then sin A = 77/85, cos A = √(1 − 77²/85²) = 36/85; sin B = 3/5, cos B = 4/5. Now sin(A+B) = (77/85)(4/5) + (36/85)(3/5) = 416/425, and cos(A+B) = (36/85)(4/5) − (77/85)(3/5) = (144 − 231)/425 = −87/425. Since 0 < A+B < π, A+B = Cos⁻¹(−87/425). The printed right-hand side has the wrong sign (it would give an acute angle, whereas A+B ≈ 101.8°).

questions.question: Show that Cos⁻¹(2/√5) + Tan⁻¹(1/3) = π/4.
questions.explanation: Let A = Cos⁻¹(2/√5). Then cos A = 2/√5, sin A = 1/√5, so tan A = 1/2. Let B = Tan⁻¹(1/3), so tan B = 1/3. Then tan(A+B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) = (1/2 + 1/3)/(1 − 1/6) = (5/6)/(5/6) = 1. Both A and B are acute, so 0 < A+B < π/2; hence A+B = π/4.

questions.question: Show that Cos⁻¹(63/65) + 2Tan⁻¹(1/5) = Cos⁻¹(4/5).
Show that Cos⁻¹(3/5) − Cos⁻¹(8/17) = Cos⁻¹(84/85).
questions.answer: As printed the identity has the wrong sign. The correct identity is Cos⁻¹(3/5) − Cos⁻¹(8/17) = −Cos⁻¹(84/85).
questions.explanation: Let A = Cos⁻¹(3/5) and B = Cos⁻¹(8/17). Then sin A = 4/5 and sin B = 15/17. Thus cos(A−B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B = (3/5)(8/17) + (4/5)(15/17) = 24/85 + 60/85 = 84/85. But A ≈ 53.13° and B ≈ 61.93°, so A−B ≈ −8.8° is negative, while Cos⁻¹(84/85) is the positive angle ≈ 8.8°. Hence A−B = −Cos⁻¹(84/85); the printed positive sign is an error (the order of the two angles should be reversed).

questions.question: Show that 2Tan⁻¹(2/3) = Cos⁻¹(5/13).
Show that Sec⁻¹(√5/2) + Cot⁻¹(3) = π/4.
questions.explanation: Let A = Sec⁻¹(√5/2). Then sec A = √5/2, cos A = 2/√5, sin A = 1/√5, so tan A = 1/2. Let B = Cot⁻¹(3), so tan B = 1/3. Then tan(A+B) = (1/2 + 1/3)/(1 − (1/2)(1/3)) = (5/6)/(5/6) = 1. Both A and B are acute, so A+B = π/4.

questions.question: Show that Tan⁻¹(3/4) + Tan⁻¹(3/5) − Tan⁻¹(8/19) = π/4.
Show that Tan⁻¹(1/3) + Tan⁻¹(1/2) = Tan⁻¹(1/11) + Tan⁻¹(5/6).
questions.explanation: For the left side, tan(A+B) = (1/3 + 1/2)/(1 − (1/3)(1/2)) = (5/6)/(5/6) = 1, and A+B is acute, so the left side is π/4. For the right side, tan(C+D) = (1/11 + 5/6)/(1 − (1/11)(5/6)) = (61/66)/(61/66) = 1, and C+D is acute, so the right side is also π/4. Hence the two sums are equal.

questions.question: Prove that sin(Cos⁻¹ y) = √(1 − y²).
questions.explanation: Let θ = Cos⁻¹ y. Then cos θ = y with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, so sin θ ≥ 0. Using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, sin θ = √(1 − cos²θ) = √(1 − y²). Hence sin(Cos⁻¹ y) = √(1 − y²).

questions.question: Prove that Tan⁻¹(y) + Tan⁻¹(−y) = 0.
questions.answer: Tan⁻¹(y) + Tan⁻¹(−y) = 0 for every y ∈ ℝ.
questions.explanation: Tan⁻¹ is an odd function: tan(−θ) = −tan θ, and the principal range (−π/2, π/2) is symmetric about 0. Hence Tan⁻¹(−y) = −Tan⁻¹(y), so Tan⁻¹(y) + Tan⁻¹(−y) = 0.

questions.question: Prove that Cos⁻¹ y + Cos⁻¹(−y) = π.
questions.answer: Cos⁻¹ y + Cos⁻¹(−y) = π for −1 ≤ y ≤ 1.
questions.explanation: Let θ = Cos⁻¹ y, so 0 ≤ θ ≤ π and cos θ = y. Then π − θ also lies in [0, π], and cos(π − θ) = −cos θ = −y. By the definition of the principal inverse cosine, Cos⁻¹(−y) = π − θ. Adding gives Cos⁻¹ y + Cos⁻¹(−y) = θ + (π − θ) = π.

questions.question: Prove that sin(2Cos⁻¹ y) = 2y√(1 − y²).
questions.explanation: Let θ = Cos⁻¹ y, so cos θ = y and sin θ = √(1 − y²) (non-negative on [0, π]). Then sin(2θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ = 2√(1 − y²)·y = 2y√(1 − y²).

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation cos x + 1/2 = 0.
questions.explanation: cos x = −1/2. The reference angle is π/3; cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants. Thus x = π − π/3 = 2π/3 + 2nπ or x = π + π/3 = 4π/3 + 2nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation tan x + 1/√3 = 0.
questions.explanation: tan x = −1/√3. The reference angle is π/6 and tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants. Since the period of tan is π, x = −π/6 + nπ, which is the same set as x = 5π/6 + nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation cosec(3x/2) + 2 = 0.
questions.explanation: cosec(3x/2) = −2 gives sin(3x/2) = −1/2. The reference angle is π/6, so 3x/2 = 7π/6 + 2nπ or 3x/2 = 11π/6 + 2nπ. Multiplying by 2/3 gives x = 7π/9 + 4nπ/3 or x = 11π/9 + 4nπ/3. The period in x is 4π/3, not 2π; the printed key’s “2nπ” is incorrect because sin(3x/2) has period 4π/3.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation sec²θ − 4/3 = 0.
questions.answer: θ = π/6 + nπ or θ = 5π/6 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: sec²θ = 4/3 gives cos²θ = 3/4, so cos θ = ±√3/2. For cos θ = √3/2, θ = ±π/6 + 2nπ; for cos θ = −√3/2, θ = 5π/6 + 2nπ or 7π/6 + 2nπ. These four families combine into θ = π/6 + nπ or θ = 5π/6 + nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation 4 sin²x = 1.
questions.answer: x = π/6 + nπ or x = 5π/6 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: sin²x = 1/4, so sin x = ±1/2. For sin x = 1/2, x = π/6 + 2nπ or 5π/6 + 2nπ; for sin x = −1/2, x = 7π/6 + 2nπ or 11π/6 + 2nπ. Combining the families gives x = π/6 + nπ or x = 5π/6 + nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation sec²x = 4.
questions.answer: x = π/3 + nπ or x = 2π/3 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: sec²x = 4 means cos²x = 1/4, so cos x = ±1/2. For cos x = 1/2, x = ±π/3 + 2nπ; for cos x = −1/2, x = 2π/3 + 2nπ or 4π/3 + 2nπ. These combine into x = π/3 + nπ or x = 2π/3 + nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation 2 cos x + sin²x = 1.
questions.explanation: Replace sin²x by 1 − cos²x: 2cos x + 1 − cos²x = 1, so 2cos x − cos²x = 0, i.e. cos x(2 − cos x) = 0. Since cos x = 2 is impossible, cos x = 0, giving x = π/2 + nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation 4 cos²x − 8 sin x + 1 = 0.
questions.answer: x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: Using cos²x = 1 − sin²x: 4(1 − sin²x) − 8sin x + 1 = 0, i.e. 4sin²x + 8sin x − 5 = 0. Factor: (2sin x − 1)(2sin x + 5) = 0. Thus sin x = 1/2 (the value sin x = −5/2 is rejected), so x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation 3 tan²x + 2√3 tan x + 1 = 0.
questions.explanation: The left side is a perfect square: (√3 tan x + 1)² = 0, so tan x = −1/√3. The reference angle is π/6; since tan has period π, x = −π/6 + nπ, equivalently x = 5π/6 + nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation (cosec x + 2)(2 cos x − 1) = 0.
questions.explanation: Either cosec x = −2, i.e. sin x = −1/2, giving x = 7π/6 + 2nπ or 11π/6 + 2nπ; or 2cos x − 1 = 0, i.e. cos x = 1/2, giving x = π/3 + 2nπ or 5π/3 + 2nπ. All four families satisfy the original equation.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation tan θ = 2 sin θ.
questions.answer: θ = nπ, θ = π/3 + 2nπ or θ = 5π/3 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: Write tan θ = sin θ/cos θ with cos θ ≠ 0. Then sin θ/cos θ = 2sin θ, so sin θ(1 − 2cos θ) = 0. Hence sin θ = 0, giving θ = nπ, or cos θ = 1/2, giving θ = ±π/3 + 2nπ, i.e. θ = π/3 + 2nπ or 5π/3 + 2nπ. At θ = nπ, cos θ = ±1 ≠ 0, so these values are valid.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation 4 sin²(x/2) − 3 = 0.
questions.explanation: sin²(x/2) = 3/4, so sin(x/2) = ±√3/2. Hence x/2 = π/3, 2π/3, 4π/3 or 5π/3 (mod 2π), giving x = 2π/3, 4π/3, 8π/3 or 10π/3 (mod 4π). Because 8π/3 = 2π/3 + 2π and 10π/3 = 4π/3 + 2π, the solution set is x = 2π/3 + 2nπ or x = 4π/3 + 2nπ. The printed key’s {π + nπ} = {nπ} does not satisfy the equation (for example x = π gives 4sin²(π/2) − 3 = 1 ≠ 0).

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation cos 2x = cos x.
questions.answer: x = 2nπ, x = 2π/3 + 2nπ or x = 4π/3 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1, so 2cos²x − 1 = cos x, i.e. 2cos²x − cos x − 1 = 0. Factor: (2cos x + 1)(cos x − 1) = 0. Thus cos x = 1, giving x = 2nπ, or cos x = −1/2, giving x = 2π/3 + 2nπ or 4π/3 + 2nπ.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation sin 4θ − sin 2θ = cos 3θ.
questions.explanation: sin 4θ − sin 2θ = 2cos 3θ sin θ, so the equation becomes 2cos 3θ sin θ = cos 3θ, i.e. cos 3θ(2sin θ − 1) = 0. If cos 3θ = 0, then 3θ = π/2 + nπ, so θ = π/6 + nπ/3. If sin θ = 1/2, then θ = π/6 + 2nπ or 5π/6 + 2nπ, and both are already included in θ = π/6 + nπ/3 (take n = 0 and n = 2). Hence the full solution set is θ = π/6 + nπ/3. The printed key lists only π/6, π/2 and 5π/6 with period 2π, omitting 7π/6, 3π/2 and 11π/6.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation cos θ + cos 3θ + cos 5θ = 0.
questions.answer: θ = π/6 + nπ/3, θ = π/3 + nπ or θ = 2π/3 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation: cos θ + cos 5θ = 2cos 3θ cos 2θ, so the equation is cos 3θ(2cos 2θ + 1) = 0. If cos 3θ = 0, θ = π/6 + nπ/3. If 2cos 2θ + 1 = 0, then cos 2θ = −1/2, so 2θ = 2π/3 + 2nπ or 4π/3 + 2nπ, giving θ = π/3 + nπ or 2π/3 + nπ. The printed key gives only the representatives π/6, π/2, 5π/6, π/3 and 2π/3 with period 2π and therefore omits the remaining solutions.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation sin x + sin 3x + sin 5x + sin 7x = 0.
questions.explanation: Group the terms: (sin x + sin 7x) + (sin 3x + sin 5x) = 2sin 4x cos 3x + 2sin 4x cos x = 2sin 4x(cos 3x + cos x) = 2sin 4x(2cos 2x cos x) = 4sin 4x cos 2x cos x. Setting each factor to zero: sin 4x = 0 gives x = nπ/4; cos 2x = 0 gives x = π/4 + nπ/2; cos x = 0 gives x = π/2 + nπ. Both latter families are contained in x = nπ/4, so the complete solution is x = nπ/4. The printed key lists only a few representatives (nπ, π/4, π/2, 3π/4, 3π/2 with period 2π) and is incomplete.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation cosec θ = √3 + cot θ.
questions.explanation: The equation requires sin θ ≠ 0. Multiply by sin θ: 1 = √3 sin θ + cos θ. Since √3 sin θ + cos θ = 2sin(θ + π/6), we get sin(θ + π/6) = 1/2. Hence θ + π/6 = π/6 + 2nπ or 5π/6 + 2nπ, so θ = 2nπ or θ = 2π/3 + 2nπ. The family θ = 2nπ makes sin θ = 0, so cosec θ and cot θ are undefined; it must be discarded as extraneous. Thus only θ = 2π/3 + 2nπ remains. The printed key includes nπ, but all multiples of π are undefined in the original equation.

questions.question: Find the general solution of the trigonometric equation 2 cos x + sin²x − 1 = 0.
questions.explanation: Using sin²x = 1 − cos²x: 2cos x + 1 − cos²x − 1 = 0, so 2cos x − cos²x = 0, i.e. cos x(2 − cos x) = 0. Since cos x = 2 is impossible, cos x = 0 and hence x = π/2 + nπ.

questions.question: If y = Sin x, then domain is:
questions.explanation: Sin x is the principal sine function, whose domain is the restricted interval [−π/2, π/2].
questions.optionsRaw: a) −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2  b) 0 ≤ x ≤ π  c) [0, x], x ≠ π/2  d) None of these

questions.question: If y = Cos x, then range is:
questions.explanation: For the principal cosine function y = Cos x with domain [0, π], the values run from −1 to 1, so the range is [−1, 1]. (Options (c) and (d) are printed identically.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) −1 ≤ y ≤ 1  b) R  c) y ≤ −1 or y ≥ 1  d) y ≤ −1 or y ≥ 1

questions.question: If y = Tan⁻¹x, then domain is:
questions.explanation: The tangent function assumes every real value on (−π/2, π/2), so its inverse Tan⁻¹ has domain ℝ.
questions.optionsRaw: a) −1 ≤ x ≤ 1  b) R  c) x ≥ −1 or x ≤ 1  d) x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 1

questions.question: If y = Sec⁻¹x, then range is:
questions.explanation: For Sec⁻¹ the principal range is [0, π] with y ≠ π/2 (where sec is undefined).
questions.optionsRaw: a) 0 ≤ y ≤ π, y ≠ π/2  b) −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, y ≠ 0  c) 0 < y < π  d) −π/2 < y < π/2

questions.question: Inverse function exists if and only if the function is:
questions.explanation: An inverse exists exactly when the function is both one-to-one and onto, i.e. bijective.
questions.optionsRaw: a) bijective  b) (1-1) function  c) onto function  d) into function

questions.question: Cot⁻¹x = …………
questions.explanation: Since tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2 for all x, we have Cot⁻¹x = π/2 − tan⁻¹x.
questions.optionsRaw: a) π/2 − tan⁻¹x  b) π/2 − cot⁻¹x  c) π/2 + tan⁻¹x  d) π/2 + cot⁻¹x

questions.question: Cos(Sin⁻¹ 1/√2) = ……
cos⁻¹A + cos⁻¹B = ………
questions.explanation: Using cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β with A = cos α, B = cos β gives cos(α+β) = AB − √((1−A²)(1−B²)); hence the addition formula in option (a).
questions.optionsRaw: a) cos⁻¹(AB − √((1 − A²)(1 − B²)))  b) cos⁻¹(AB + √((1 − A²)(1 − B²)))  c) cos⁻¹(AB + √((1 + A²)(1 + B²)))  d) cos⁻¹(AB − √((1 + A²)(1 + B²)))

questions.question: tan⁻¹(−x) = …
questions.explanation: tan is an odd function and Tan⁻¹ has the symmetric principal range (−π/2, π/2), so Tan⁻¹(−x) = −Tan⁻¹x.
questions.optionsRaw: a) −tan⁻¹x  b) π − tan⁻¹x  c) cot⁻¹x  d) tan⁻¹x

questions.question: Tan⁻¹(−1) = ----------
questions.explanation: The principal angle whose tangent is −1 is −π/4.

questions.question: If tan 2x = −1, then solution in the interval [−π/2, π/2] is:
questions.explanation: tan 2x = −1 gives 2x = −π/4 + nπ, so x = −π/8 + nπ/2. In [−π/2, π/2] this gives x = −π/8 (n = 0) and x = 3π/8 (n = 1). Thus option (c) is also a valid solution; the printed key selects only (a), so the question has two correct options.

questions.question: General solution of 4 sin x − 8 = 0 is:
questions.explanation: 4 sin x − 8 = 0 would require sin x = 2, which is impossible because −1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1. Hence there is no solution.
questions.optionsRaw: a) {π + 2nπ}, n ∈ ℤ  b) {π + nπ}, n ∈ ℤ  c) {−π + nπ}, n ∈ ℤ  d) Not possible

questions.question: Solution of equation 2 Sin x + √3 = 0 in 4th quadrant is:
questions.explanation: Sin x = −√3/2. In the fourth quadrant the principal angle is x = −π/3.

questions.question: All trigonometric functions are …………… function:
questions.explanation: Every trigonometric function repeats its values at regular intervals, so all are periodic (not all are even, injective or bijective).
questions.optionsRaw: a) periodic  b) even  c) injective  d) bijective

questions.question: General solution of every trigonometric equation consists of:
questions.explanation: Because trigonometric functions are periodic, a general solution repeats with the period and therefore contains infinitely many solutions (when a solution exists).
questions.optionsRaw: a) one solution only  b) two solution  c) infinitely many solutions  d) no real solution

questions.question: The period of cos θ is:
questions.explanation: cos(θ + 2π) = cos θ, and 2π is the smallest positive period of cosine.
questions.optionsRaw: a) π/2  b) π  c) 2π  d) 4π

questions.question: One solution of Sec x = −2 is:
questions.explanation: Sec x = −2 means cos x = −1/2. In [0, π] the solution is x = 2π/3.

questions.question: If cos θ = −1/2 and sin θ = −√3/2, then θ is:
questions.explanation: Both cosine and sine are negative, so θ lies in the third quadrant. The angle with reference angle π/3 in QIII is θ = π + π/3 = 4π/3.

questions.question: The period of sin(x/2) is
questions.explanation: The period of sin kx is 2π/|k|; here k = 1/2, so the period is 2π/(1/2) = 4π.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 4π  b) π  c) 2π  d) 3π

questions.question: The value of cos 5π is
questions.explanation: cos 5π = cos(4π + π) = cos π = −1.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 0  b) 1  c) −1  d) None of these

questions.question: The period of 3 sec(x/3) is
questions.explanation: The factor 3 does not affect the period. For sec(x/3), the period is 2π/(1/3) = 6π.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 5π  b) π  c) 2π  d) 6π

questions.question: The period of 7 tan(7x) is
questions.explanation: For tan kx the period is π/|k|; here k = 7, so the period is π/7 (the factor 7 does not affect it).
questions.optionsRaw: a) 7π/3  b) 7π  c) π/7  d) π

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of the function y = 5 − 7 cos θ.
questions.explanation: Here a = 5 and b = −7. Maximum = a + |b| = 5 + 7 = 12; minimum = a − |b| = 5 − 7 = −2.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of the function y = 4 + 3 sin(2θ − 5).
questions.explanation: Here a = 4 and b = 3. Maximum = 4 + 3 = 7; minimum = 4 − 3 = 1.

questions.question: By using a graph, find the solution of the equation 2 cos θ − θ = 0.
questions.answer: θ ≈ 1.03 rad (≈ 59°); the printed key gives π/3 approximately.
questions.explanation: Rewrite the equation as 2cos θ = θ and draw y = 2cos θ together with the line y = θ. The line starts below the cosine curve at θ = 0 (0 < 2) and ends above it at θ = 2 (2 > 2cos 2 ≈ −0.83), so there is exactly one intersection. Solving 2cos θ − θ = 0 numerically gives θ ≈ 1.0299 rad ≈ 59.0°, which is close to π/3 ≈ 1.047 rad (60°); hence the printed answer π/3 (approx).
questions.figure: Intersection of y = 2 cos θ and y = θ

questions.question: Without using a calculator, show that cosec⁻¹(13/12) = tan⁻¹(12/15).
questions.answer: As printed the right-hand side is wrong. The correct identity is cosec⁻¹(13/12) = tan⁻¹(12/5).
questions.explanation: Let y = cosec⁻¹(13/12). Then cosec y = 13/12, so sin y = 12/13 with y ∈ (0, π/2]. Using sin²y + cos²y = 1, cos y = √(1 − 144/169) = 5/13. Hence tan y = sin y/cos y = (12/13)/(5/13) = 12/5, so y = tan⁻¹(12/5). The printed denominator 15 is a typographical error; 12/15 would correspond to an angle with sine 4/√41, not 12/13.

questions.question: Without using a calculator, show that cos⁻¹(√3/2) = tan⁻¹(1/√3).
questions.explanation: cos⁻¹(√3/2) = π/6 because cos(π/6) = √3/2 and π/6 ∈ [0, π]. Also tan⁻¹(1/√3) = π/6 because tan(π/6) = 1/√3 and π/6 ∈ (−π/2, π/2). Hence the two principal values are equal.

questions.question: Show that cos⁻¹(7/25) − cos⁻¹(5/13) = cos⁻¹(323/325).
Find the solution sets of the equation sec 3x = sec x.
questions.explanation: sec 3x = sec x means 1/cos 3x = 1/cos x, so cos 3x = cos x with cos x ≠ 0 and cos 3x ≠ 0. Then cos 3x − cos x = −2 sin 2x sin x = 0. Hence sin 2x = 0, giving x = nπ/2, or sin x = 0, giving x = nπ (already contained in x = nπ/2). Now exclude the values where cos x = 0, namely x = π/2 + nπ, i.e. the odd multiples of π/2. The remaining values are the even multiples of π/2, that is x = nπ. Check: sec(3nπ) = sec(nπ) = (−1)ⁿ, so all these satisfy the equation.

questions.question: Evaluate: i<sup>10</sup> · (−i<sup>12</sup>).
questions.explanation:
i4 = 1, so i10 = i8·i² = 1·(−1) = −1 and i12 = (i4)³ = 1.
Hence −i12 = −1 and the product is (−1)(−1) = 1.

questions.question: Evaluate: (−i)<sup>16</sup> · (−i)<sup>6</sup>.
Evaluate: i<sup>11</sup> · (−i)<sup>14</sup>.
questions.explanation:
i11 = i8·i³ = 1·(−i) = −i. Also (−i)14 = ((−i)²)7 = (−1)7 = −1.
Product = (−i)(−1) = i.

questions.question: For what values of n is i<sup>n</sup> equal to 1, i, −1 or −i, where 1 ≤ n ≤ 4?
questions.answer: i<sup>n</sup> = 1 for n = 4; i<sup>n</sup> = i for n = 1; i<sup>n</sup> = −1 for n = 2; i<sup>n</sup> = −i for n = 3.
questions.explanation:
Compute the first four powers: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = i²·i = −i, i⁴ = (i²)² = 1.
Matching with 1, i, −1, −i gives n = 4, 1, 2, 3 respectively.

questions.question: Show that i<sup>n</sup> + i<sup>n+1</sup> + i<sup>n+2</sup> + i<sup>n+3</sup> = 0 for all n ∈ ℤ.
questions.explanation:
Take in common: in(1 + i + i² + i³).
Since i² = −1 and i³ = −i, the bracket is 1 + i − 1 − i = 0.
Therefore the sum is in·0 = 0 for every integer n (the powers repeat with period 4).

questions.question: Simplify: (8, −4) ÷ (−2, 2).
questions.explanation:
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of −2 + 2i, namely −2 − 2i.
Numerator (8 − 4i)(−2 − 2i) = −16 − 16i + 8i + 8i² = −24 − 8i; denominator (−2)² + 2² = 8.
= −3 − i, i.e. (−3, −1).

questions.question: Simplify: (6 + 5i) − (4 + 3i).
questions.explanation: Subtract real parts and imaginary parts separately: (6 − 4) + (5 − 3)i = 2 + 2i.

questions.question: Simplify: (5 − 6i) + (3 + 4i) − (5i − 7).
questions.explanation:
Real parts: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15. Imaginary parts: −6 + 4 − 5 = −7.
Result = 15 − 7i.

questions.question: Simplify: (4 + 5i)(6 + 7i).
Simplify: (7 + 4i) ÷ (8 + 5i).
Simplify: (5, −6) + (4, 8) − (3, −2).
questions.explanation: Add and subtract componentwise: (5 + 4 − 3, −6 + 8 + 2) = (6, 4).

questions.question: Simplify: (2 − i)<sup>4</sup>.
Simplify: (−1 − i√3)².
Simplify: (−1 + i√3)².
Simplify: (1 + i)³.
Simplify: (√2 + i)/(√2 − i).
questions.explanation:
Multiply numerator and denominator by √2 + i.
Numerator: (√2 + i)² = 2 + 2√2 i + i² = 1 + 2√2 i; denominator: 2 + 1 = 3.
Result = 1/3 + (2√2/3)i.

questions.question: Simplify: (2 + i)²/(3 − 4i).
Simplify: 1/(2 − i)².
Show that z = 1 ± i satisfies the equation z² − 2z + 2 = 0.
questions.answer: Proof shown; both z = 1 + i and z = 1 − i satisfy the equation.
questions.explanation:
For z = 1 + i: z² = 1 + 2i + i² = 2i, so z² − 2z + 2 = 2i − 2(1 + i) + 2 = 2i − 2 − 2i + 2 = 0.
For z = 1 − i: z² = −2i, so z² − 2z + 2 = −2i − 2(1 − i) + 2 = −2i − 2 + 2i + 2 = 0.
Hence z = 1 ± i are the two roots.

questions.question: Find the conjugate and absolute value of 4 + 5i.
questions.explanation:
Change the sign of the imaginary part: conjugate = 4 − 5i.
|a + bi| = √(a² + b²) = √(16 + 25) = √41.

questions.question: Find the conjugate and absolute value of −1 + 7i.
Find the conjugate and absolute value of √3 i.
questions.explanation:
Write √3 i = 0 + √3 i, so the conjugate is 0 − √3 i = −√3 i.
|√3 i| = √(0² + (√3)²) = √3.

questions.question: Find the conjugate and absolute value of √7 − 3i.
Find the conjugate and absolute value of −3 − 4i.
Find the conjugate and absolute value of (5 − 4i)².
Find the conjugate and absolute value of 2/3 − √(−9/16).
Find the conjugate and absolute value of (1 + i)(1 + 2i)/(3 + i).
Find the real and imaginary parts of 2i(3 − 5i).
questions.explanation:
2i(3 − 5i) = 6i − 10i² = 10 + 6i.
Hence the real part is 10 and the imaginary part is 6.

questions.question: Find the real and imaginary parts of (√5 + i)/(√5 − i).
questions.explanation:
Multiply by (√5 + i)/(√5 + i): numerator (√5 + i)² = 5 + 2√5 i − 1 = 4 + 2√5 i; denominator 5 + 1 = 6.
= 2/3 + (√5/3)i, so Re = 2/3 and Im = √5/3.
Note: the printed answer key also lists 7(iii) = −1, but Exercise 1.1 prints only 7(i) and 7(ii) (PDF p. 12); that key entry is an orphan and no 7(iii) item exists.

questions.question: If z = x + iy where Re(z) = 0 and |z| = 2, find z.
questions.explanation:
Re(z) = 0 gives x = 0, so z = iy.
Then |z| = |y| = 2, hence y = ±2.
Therefore z = 0 + 2i = 2i or z = −2i.

questions.question: Solve the complex equation (x, y)(2, 3) = (−4, 7) for real x and y.
questions.explanation:
(x + iy)(2 + 3i) = (2x − 3y) + (3x + 2y)i = −4 + 7i.
Equate parts: 2x − 3y = −4 and 3x + 2y = 7.
Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 6x − 9y = −12, 6x + 4y = 14. Subtracting gives −13y = −26, so y = 2; then 2x − 6 = −4, so x = 1.

questions.question: Solve the complex equation (x + 3i)² = 2yi for real x and y.
questions.explanation:
(x + 3i)² = x² + 6xi + 9i² = (x² − 9) + 6xi.
Equate to 0 + 2yi: x² − 9 = 0 and 6x = 2y, i.e. x = ±3 and y = 3x.
So (x, y) = (3, 9) or (−3, −9).

questions.question: Solve the complex equation (x + 2yi)² = xi for real x and y.
questions.explanation:
(x + 2yi)² = x² + 4xyi + 4y²i² = (x² − 4y²) + 4xyi = 0 + xi.
Real part: x² − 4y² = 0. Imaginary part: 4xy = x, i.e. x(4y − 1) = 0.
If x = 0 then −4y² = 0, so y = 0. If y = 1/4 then x² = 1/4, so x = ±1/2.

questions.question: Represent the complex number (2, −3) on the complex plane.
questions.answer: Point 2 units to the right of the origin and 3 units down (quadrant IV).
questions.explanation: The number is 2 − 3i: plot 2 on the real (horizontal) axis and −3 on the imaginary (vertical) axis. The point lies in the fourth quadrant.

questions.question: Represent the complex number (3, 4) on the complex plane.
questions.answer: Point 3 units right and 4 units up (quadrant I).
questions.explanation: The number is 3 + 4i, so plot the point (3, 4): first quadrant.

questions.question: Represent the complex number (−5, 7) on the complex plane.
questions.answer: Point 5 units left and 7 units up (quadrant II).
questions.explanation: The number is −5 + 7i, so plot the point (−5, 7): second quadrant.

questions.question: Represent the complex number (−6, −2) on the complex plane.
questions.answer: Point 6 units left and 2 units down (quadrant III).
questions.explanation: The number is −6 − 2i, so plot the point (−6, −2): third quadrant.

questions.question: Represent the complex number (0, 6) on the complex plane.
questions.answer: Point 6 units up on the imaginary axis.
questions.explanation: The number is 0 + 6i; since the real part is 0, the point lies on the positive imaginary axis.

questions.question: Represent the complex number (−5, 0) on the complex plane.
questions.answer: Point 5 units left on the real axis.
questions.explanation: The number is −5 + 0i; since the imaginary part is 0, the point lies on the negative real axis.

questions.question: Find the length of the vector representing −5 + 2i.
questions.explanation: The length of the vector is the modulus: |−5 + 2i| = √((−5)² + 2²) = √(25 + 4) = √29.

questions.question: Find the length of the vector representing 7/3 + (8/3)i.
Find the length of the vector representing (1 + i)/√2.
Find the length of the vector representing (1 + √3 i)/2.
Let z₁ = 3 − 4i, z₂ = 4 + 5i and z₃ = −5 + 6i. Verify that addition of complex numbers is commutative.
questions.answer: Verified: z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁ = 7 + i
questions.explanation:
z₁ + z₂ = (3 − 4i) + (4 + 5i) = (3 + 4) + (−4 + 5)i = 7 + i.
z₂ + z₁ = (4 + 5i) + (3 − 4i) = 7 + i.
The two results are equal, so addition is commutative.

questions.question: Let z₁ = 3 − 4i, z₂ = 4 + 5i and z₃ = −5 + 6i. Verify that multiplication of complex numbers is commutative.
questions.explanation:
z₁z₂ = (3 − 4i)(4 + 5i) = 12 + 15i − 16i − 20i² = 32 − i.
z₂z₁ = (4 + 5i)(3 − 4i) = 12 − 16i + 15i − 20i² = 32 − i.
The products agree, so multiplication is commutative.

questions.question: Let z₁ = 3 − 4i, z₂ = 4 + 5i and z₃ = −5 + 6i. Verify that addition of complex numbers is associative.
questions.explanation:
z₁ + z₂ = 7 + i, so (z₁ + z₂) + z₃ = (7 + i) + (−5 + 6i) = 2 + 7i.
z₂ + z₃ = (4 + 5i) + (−5 + 6i) = −1 + 11i, so z₁ + (z₂ + z₃) = (3 − 4i) + (−1 + 11i) = 2 + 7i.
Both sides are equal.

questions.question: Let z₁ = 3 − 4i, z₂ = 4 + 5i and z₃ = −5 + 6i. Verify that multiplication of complex numbers is associative.
Let z₁ = 3 − 4i, z₂ = 4 + 5i and z₃ = −5 + 6i. Verify that multiplication of complex numbers is distributive over addition.
questions.explanation:
z₂ + z₃ = −1 + 11i, so z₁(z₂ + z₃) = (3 − 4i)(−1 + 11i) = −3 + 33i + 4i − 44i² = 41 + 37i.
z₁z₂ = 32 − i and z₁z₃ = (3 − 4i)(−5 + 6i) = −15 + 18i + 20i − 24i² = 9 + 38i.
Their sum is (32 − i) + (9 + 38i) = 41 + 37i, which equals the left side.

questions.question: If z is a complex number, prove that z + z̄ is real.
questions.answer: Proof shown; z + z̄ = 2a, which is real.
questions.explanation:
Let z = a + bi with a, b ∈ ℝ. Then z̄ = a − bi.
z + z̄ = (a + bi) + (a − bi) = 2a.
Since 2a is a real number (imaginary part 0), z + z̄ is real.

questions.question: If z is a complex number, prove that z − z̄ is imaginary.
questions.answer: Proof shown; z − z̄ = 2bi, which is purely imaginary.
questions.explanation:
With z = a + bi and z̄ = a − bi,
z − z̄ = (a + bi) − (a − bi) = 2bi.
This has real part 0, so it is imaginary (zero when b = 0).

questions.question: If z₁ and z₂ are complex numbers, prove that |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.
questions.explanation:
Let z₁ = a + bi and z₂ = c + di. Then z₁z₂ = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.
|z₁z₂|² = (ac − bd)² + (ad + bc)² = a²c² + b²d² + a²d² + b²c².
Also |z₁|²|z₂|² = (a² + b²)(c² + d²) = a²c² + a²d² + b²c² + b²d², the same expression.
Since moduli are non-negative, taking square roots gives |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.

questions.question: If z₁ and z₂ are complex numbers, prove that |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|, where z₂ ≠ (0, 0).
questions.explanation:
For z₂ ≠ 0, z₁/z₂ = z₁z̄₂/(z₂z̄₂) = z₁z̄₂/|z₂|².
Taking moduli and using |z̄₂| = |z₂|:
|z₁/z₂| = |z₁||z₂|/|z₂|² = |z₁|/|z₂|.

questions.question: Find the additive inverse of 3 + 5i.
questions.explanation:
The additive inverse of z is −z, obtained by changing the signs of both parts: −(3 + 5i) = −3 − 5i.
Check: (3 + 5i) + (−3 − 5i) = 0.

questions.question: Find the additive inverse of 6 − 5i.
Find the additive inverse of (11, 0).
questions.explanation: (11, 0) represents 11; its additive inverse is −11 = (−11, 0).

questions.question: Find the additive inverse of (2/3, 6).
questions.explanation: Negate both components: −(2/3 + 6i) = −2/3 − 6i = (−2/3, −6).

questions.question: Find the additive inverse of (8/9, −4/5).
Find the additive inverse of (0, 3/8).
Find the multiplicative inverse of 3 + 5i.
Find the multiplicative inverse of 8i.
Find the multiplicative inverse of (10, 4).
Find the multiplicative inverse of (12, −7).
Find the multiplicative inverse of (−8, 0).
questions.explanation: (−8, 0) represents −8, whose reciprocal is −1/8 = (−1/8, 0).

questions.question: Find the multiplicative inverse of (0, −3/4).
questions.explanation:
z = −(3/4)i. Then 1/z = −4/(3i) = −4i/(3i²) = 4i/3.
So the inverse is (0, 4/3).

questions.question: Find the additive and multiplicative inverses of (2, 3) by definition.
questions.explanation:
By definition z + (−z) = 0, so the additive inverse of 2 + 3i is −2 − 3i = (−2, −3).
For the multiplicative inverse use z⁻¹ = z̄/|z|² = (2 − 3i)/(4 + 9) = (2 − 3i)/13.
So z⁻¹ = (2/13, −3/13).

questions.question: Find the additive and multiplicative inverses of (−4, 5) by definition.
questions.explanation:
The additive inverse of −4 + 5i is 4 − 5i = (4, −5).
The multiplicative inverse is z̄/|z|² = (−4 − 5i)/(16 + 25) = (−4 − 5i)/41.
So z⁻¹ = (−4/41, −5/41).

questions.question: Verify |z| = |−z| = |z̄| = |−z̄| for z = 4 − 3i.
Verify that the conjugate of the conjugate of z equals z, for z = 4 − 3i.
questions.explanation:
z = 4 − 3i, so z̄ = 4 + 3i.
Taking the conjugate again changes the sign of 3i: conj(z̄) = 4 − 3i = z.

questions.question: Verify z z̄ = |z|² for z = 4 − 3i.
Verify that the conjugate of (z₁ + z₂) equals z̄₁ + z̄₂ for z₁ = 3 − 2i and z₂ = 2 + 3i.
questions.explanation:
z₁ + z₂ = (3 + 2) + (−2 + 3)i = 5 + i, whose conjugate is 5 − i.
z̄₁ + z̄₂ = (3 + 2i) + (2 − 3i) = 5 − i.
Hence the two sides agree.

questions.question: Verify that the conjugate of (z₁z₂) equals z̄₁ · z̄₂ for z₁ = 3 − 2i and z₂ = 2 + 3i.
questions.explanation:
z₁z₂ = (3 − 2i)(2 + 3i) = 6 + 9i − 4i − 6i² = 12 + 5i, so its conjugate is 12 − 5i.
z̄₁z̄₂ = (3 + 2i)(2 − 3i) = 6 − 9i + 4i − 6i² = 12 − 5i.

questions.question: Verify that the conjugate of (z₁/z₂) equals z̄₁/z̄₂ for z₁ = 3 − 2i and z₂ = 2 + 3i.
If z₁ = 3 − 2i and z₂ = 2 − 3i, express z₁z̄₂/z̄₁ in the form a + ib and verify the triangle inequality.
questions.explanation:
z̄₂ = 2 + 3i and z̄₁ = 3 + 2i.
z₁z̄₂ = (3 − 2i)(2 + 3i) = 6 + 9i − 4i − 6i² = 12 + 5i.
(12 + 5i)/(3 + 2i) = (12 + 5i)(3 − 2i)/13 = (36 − 24i + 15i − 10i²)/13 = (46 − 9i)/13.
Triangle inequality: z₁ + z₂ = 5 − 5i, so |z₁ + z₂| = 5√2, while |z₁| + |z₂| = 2√13. Since 50 < 52, the inequality holds.

questions.question: If z₁ = 3 − 2i and z₂ = 2 − 3i, express z̄₁z₂/z̄₂ in the form a + ib and verify the triangle inequality.
If z₁ = 3 − 2i and z₂ = 2 − 3i, express z̄₁z̄₂/z₁ in the form a + ib and verify the triangle inequality.
questions.explanation:
z̄₁z̄₂ = (3 + 2i)(2 + 3i) = 6 + 9i + 4i + 6i² = 13i.
Divide by z₁ = 3 − 2i: 13i/(3 − 2i) = 13i(3 + 2i)/13 = 3i + 2i² = −2 + 3i.
Triangle inequality: |z₁ + z₂| = |5 − 5i| = 5√2 = √50 and |z₁| + |z₂| = 2√13 = √52, so the inequality holds.

questions.question: Find the real and imaginary parts of (√2 + i)⁻².
Find the real and imaginary parts of (1 − √5 i)⁻¹.
Find the real and imaginary parts of (√3 − i)⁻².
Find the real and imaginary parts of (2i − √3)⁻¹.
Find the real and imaginary parts of (1/(4i − 5))⁻¹.
questions.explanation:
The inverse of the reciprocal is the number itself: (1/(4i − 5))⁻¹ = 4i − 5 = −5 + 4i.
So Re = −5 and Im = 4.

questions.question: Find the real and imaginary parts of ((3 + 4i)/(5i − 4))⁻².
Find the real and imaginary parts of ((3i − 2)/(2 − 3i))⁻².
questions.explanation:
Since 3i − 2 = −(2 − 3i), the fraction equals −1.
(−1)⁻² = 1/(−1)² = 1.
Hence Re = 1 and Im = 0.

questions.question: If x = 1 − 5i, show that x² − 2x + 26 = 0.
questions.explanation:
x² = (1 − 5i)² = 1 − 10i + 25i² = 1 − 10i − 25 = −24 − 10i.
−2x = −2 + 10i, and adding 26:
(−24 − 10i) + (−2 + 10i) + 26 = 0.
Hence x = 1 − 5i satisfies the equation.

questions.question: If x = 2 + √3 i, find the value of x⁴ − 4x² + 8x + 55.
Solve the simultaneous equations for w and z: 3z + (2 + i)w = 11 − i and (2 − i)z − w = −1 + i.
questions.explanation:
From the second equation w = (2 − i)z + 1 − i.
Substitute in the first: 3z + (2 + i)[(2 − i)z + 1 − i] = 11 − i.
Since (2 + i)(2 − i) = 5 and (2 + i)(1 − i) = 3 − i, this becomes 8z + 3 − i = 11 − i, so 8z = 8 and z = 1.
Then w = (2 − i)(1) + 1 − i = 3 − 2i.

questions.question: Solve the simultaneous equations for w and z: 2z + (3 + i)w = 9 − i and (3 − i)z − iw = −1 + i.
questions.explanation:
From the first equation z = [9 − i − (3 + i)w]/2.
Substitute in the second: (3 − i)(9 − i)/2 − [(3 − i)(3 + i)/2]w − iw = −1 + i.
(3 − i)(9 − i) = 26 − 12i and (3 − i)(3 + i) = 10, so 13 − 6i − 5w − iw = −1 + i.
Thus (5 + i)w = 14 − 7i and w = (14 − 7i)(5 − i)/26 = (63 − 49i)/26.
Back-substitute: z = [9 − i − (3 + i)w]/2 = (−2 + 29i)/26.

questions.question: Write z² + 81b² as the product of linear factors.
questions.explanation:
Since (9ib)² = 81i²b² = −81b², we can write z² + 81b² = z² − (9ib)².
This is a difference of squares: z² − (9ib)² = (z − 9ib)(z + 9ib).

questions.question: Write z³ + 3z² + z − 5 as the product of linear factors.
questions.explanation:
Let P(z) = z³ + 3z² + z − 5. P(1) = 1 + 3 + 1 − 5 = 0, so z − 1 is a factor.
Division gives z³ + 3z² + z − 5 = (z − 1)(z² + 4z + 5).
Complete the square: z² + 4z + 5 = (z + 2)² + 1 = (z + 2)² − i² = (z + 2 + i)(z + 2 − i).

questions.question: Write 4z² + 9b² as the product of linear factors.
questions.explanation:
4z² + 9b² = (2z)² + (3b)². Since (3ib)² = −9b², this is (2z)² − (3ib)².
Difference of squares: (2z − 3ib)(2z + 3ib).

questions.question: Write z³ + 3z² + 4z + 2 as the product of linear factors.
questions.explanation:
