questions.explanation: |a × b| = |a||b| sinθ, which is exactly the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b (base × height).
questions.optionsRaw: a) opposite sides  b) diagonal  c) area  d) volume

questions.question: The volume of a tetrahedron determined by vectors a, b and c is:
questions.explanation: The parallelepiped on a, b, c has volume |[a b c]|, and a tetrahedron is one sixth of that parallelepiped: V = (1/6)|[a b c]|.

questions.question: a·(b × c) = ______.
questions.explanation: The scalar triple product is unchanged under cyclic permutation: a·(b × c) = (a × b)·c. Option (a) is meaningless (dot product of a scalar with c), and (b) is not a scalar triple product.
questions.optionsRaw: a) a·b·c  b) a × b × c  c) b·(a × c)  d) (a × b)·c

questions.question: If a and b are parallel then a·b = ______.
questions.explanation: For parallel vectors in the same direction, θ = 0°, so a·b = |a||b| cos0° = ab. (For antiparallel vectors the value would be −ab, but the intended answer here is ab.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) 1  b) −1  c) 0  d) ab

questions.question: If three vectors a, b and c are coplanar, then [a b c] = ______.
questions.explanation: Coplanar vectors have zero scalar triple product, because the parallelepiped they determine is flat and has zero volume.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 1  b) 0  c) c  d) a

questions.question: Direction cosines of the vector i + j − k are:
questions.explanation: |i + j − k| = √3, so the direction cosines are 1/√3, 1/√3 and −1/√3.

questions.question: a × b is ______ to the plane of a and b.
questions.explanation: By definition, the cross product a × b is perpendicular to both a and b, hence normal to the plane containing them.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Parallel  b) Perpendicular  c) Opposite  d) None of these

questions.question: If a = P₁P₂, where P₁(0,0,1) and P₂(−3,1,2), then |a| =
If p = 4i + 6k and q = 6i − 4j, then |p − q| is:
For non-zero vectors a and b, a × b is a unit vector and |a| = |b| = √2; then the angle θ between a and b is:
questions.explanation: |a × b| = |a||b| sinθ = (√2)(√2) sinθ = 2 sinθ. Since a × b is a unit vector, 2 sinθ = 1, so sinθ = 1/2 and θ = π/6 (θ lies between 0 and π). Printed key gives (b) π/3, but that would give |a × b| = 2 sin(π/3) = √3, not 1.

questions.question: Magnitude of a = 3i − j + 2k is:
The position vector of the point (1, 0, 2) is:
questions.explanation: The position vector of (x,y,z) is xi + yj + zk. With y = 0 this gives i + 2k.
questions.optionsRaw: a) i + j + 2k  b) i + 2j  c) 2i + 3k  d) i + 2k

questions.question: If O is the origin and OP = 2i + 3j − 4k and OQ = 5i + 4j − 3k, then PQ is equal to:
questions.optionsRaw: a) 7i + 7j − 7k  b) −3i + j − k  c) 3i + j + k  d) −7i − 7j + 7k

questions.question: k × j = ______.
questions.explanation: For the right-handed unit vectors, j × k = i, k × i = j and i × j = k. Reversing the order changes the sign, so k × j = −(j × k) = −i.
questions.optionsRaw: a) i  b) k  c) j  d) −i

questions.question: If |a × b| = |a·b| then the angle between a and b is:
questions.explanation: |a × b| = |a||b| sinθ and |a·b| = |a||b||cosθ|. Equality gives sinθ = |cosθ|, so tanθ = 1 when cosθ > 0 and θ = π/4. (θ = 3π/4 also satisfies sinθ = |cosθ|, but it is not among the options.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) 0  b) π/2  c) π/4  d) π

questions.question: The distance of the point (−3,4,5) from the origin is:
questions.optionsRaw: a) 50  b) 5√2  c) 6  d) None of these

questions.question: The vector having initial and terminal points as (2,5,0) and (−3,7,4) respectively is:
questions.explanation: Vector = terminal − initial = (−3−2)i + (7−5)j + (4−0)k = −5i + 2j + 4k.

questions.question: If |a| = 10, |b| = 2 and a·b = 0, then the value of |a × b| is:
questions.explanation: a·b = 0 means a and b are perpendicular (θ = 90°). Hence |a × b| = |a||b| sin90° = 10 × 2 × 1 = 20.

questions.question: The number of unit vectors of unit length perpendicular to the plane of the vectors a = 2i + j + 2k and b = j + k is:
questions.explanation: A normal to the plane is a × b. The unit normals are ±(a × b)/|a × b|; there are exactly two, pointing to the two sides of the plane.
questions.optionsRaw: a) One  b) Two  c) Three  d) Infinite

questions.question: Write PQ in the form xi + yj for P(4,6) and Q(−4,5).
Write PQ in the form xi + yj for P(−5/2, 9) and Q(10, 8).
Find the vector PQ joining the points P(3,4,2) and Q(−2,3,4), and also find the direction cosines of PQ.
questions.explanation: PQ = (−2−3)i + (3−4)j + (4−2)k = −5i − j + 2k. Its magnitude is √(25+1+4) = √30, so the direction cosines are −5/√30, −1/√30 and 2/√30.

questions.question: Show that P(2,3,6), Q(3,7,4) and R(4,11,−2) are collinear.
questions.answer: As printed the points are not collinear: PQ = (1,4,−2) and QR = (1,4,−6) are not parallel. If R is (4,11,2), then QR = PQ and the points are collinear.
questions.explanation: PQ = Q − P = (1,4,−2) and QR = R − Q = (1,4,−6). For collinearity these must be parallel, but (1,4,−6) is not a scalar multiple of (1,4,−2); equivalently PQ × PR = (1,4,−2) × (2,8,−8) = (−16,4,0) ≠ 0. Hence the printed coordinates do not give collinear points. Replacing R by (4,11,2) gives QR = (1,4,−2) = PQ, so P, Q, R would then be collinear.

questions.question: Show that the vectors (1/7)i + j + k, 2i − 3j + 3k and 4i + j − 5k are mutually perpendicular.
questions.answer: They are not mutually perpendicular as printed: a·b = 2/7, a·c = −24/7 and b·c = −10.
questions.explanation: Let a = (1/7)i + j + k, b = 2i − 3j + 3k, c = 4i + j − 5k. Then a·b = (1/7)(2) + (1)(−3) + (1)(3) = 2/7; a·c = (1/7)(4) + (1)(1) + (1)(−5) = 4/7 − 4 = −24/7; b·c = (2)(4) + (−3)(1) + (3)(−5) = 8 − 3 − 15 = −10. Since none of the dot products is zero, the printed vectors are not mutually perpendicular; the statement appears to contain a misprint. In fact b·c = −10 ≠ 0, so b and c themselves are not perpendicular, and no change to the first vector alone can make all three mutually perpendicular.

questions.question: Find the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are 3i − 5j + 6k and i + 3j − 4k. Also find a unit vector parallel to its diagonal through the common initial point.
questions.answer: Area = 2√131 square units; unit vector = (1/√6)(2i − j + k).
questions.explanation: Let a = 3i − 5j + 6k and b = i + 3j − 4k. Then a × b = |i j k; 3 −5 6; 1 3 −4| = i(20−18) − j(−12−6) + k(9+5) = 2i + 18j + 14k. Area = |a × b| = √(4+324+196) = √524 = 2√131. The diagonal through the common initial point is a + b = 4i − 2j + 2k, whose length is √24 = 2√6. Its unit vector is (4i − 2j + 2k)/(2√6) = (2i − j + k)/√6.

questions.question: Prove that [p + q, q + r, r + p] = 2[p q r].
questions.explanation: Using linearity of the scalar triple product: [p+q, q+r, r+p] = [p, q+r, r+p] + [q, q+r, r+p]. In the first term, [p, q+r, r+p] = [p,q,r] + [p,q,p] + [p,r,r] + [p,r,p] = [p,q,r] (the other three have a repeated vector). In the second, [q,q,r] = [q,q,p] = [q,r,r] = 0, leaving [q,r,p], which equals [p,q,r] by cyclic permutation. Hence the sum is 2[p q r].

questions.question: For the vectors a = i + 2j + k, b = 3i − j − k and c = i + 8j + k, verify the distributive property of the cross product.
Find the nth term (rule of formation) of the sequence: 2, 4, 6, ...
questions.explanation: The terms are 2(1), 2(2), 2(3), ... — an A.P. with first term a = 2 and common difference d = 2. Hence a<sub>n</sub> = a + (n − 1)d = 2 + (n − 1)2 = 2n.

questions.question: Find the nth term (rule of formation) of the sequence: 1², 2², 3², ...
questions.explanation: Each term is the square of its position: 1², 2², 3². Hence the nth term is a<sub>n</sub> = n².

questions.question: Find the nth term (rule of formation) of the sequence: 3, 9, 27, ...
questions.explanation: The terms are 3¹, 3², 3³ — a G.P. with a = 3 and r = 3. Hence a<sub>n</sub> = ar<sup>n−1</sup> = 3·3<sup>n−1</sup> = 3<sup>n</sup>.

questions.question: Find the nth term (rule of formation) of the sequence: 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, ...
questions.explanation: The numerator of each term equals its position n and the denominator is one more than the numerator: 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, ... Hence a<sub>n</sub> = n/(n + 1).

questions.question: Find the nth term (rule of formation) of the sequence: 1, −1/3, 1/9, −1/27, ...
questions.explanation: Each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by r = −1/3, so it is a G.P. with a = 1, r = −1/3. Hence a<sub>n</sub> = ar<sup>n−1</sup> = (−1/3)<sup>n−1</sup>, which is the same as (−1)<sup>n−1</sup>/3<sup>n−1</sup>.

questions.question: Find the nth term (rule of formation) of the sequence: 1, 8, 27, 64, ...
questions.explanation: The terms are 1³, 2³, 3³, 4³, i.e. the cubes of the natural numbers, so a<sub>n</sub> = n³.

questions.question: Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = (2n/3)(n + 1).
Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = (−1)<sup>n+1</sup> · 3<sup>n−1</sup>.
Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = (1/4)n²(n + 1)².
Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = n/(3n + 1).
Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = (1/6)n(n + 1)(n + 2).
Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = (1/6)n(n + 1)(2n + 7).
Find the first five terms of the sequence defined by a<sub>n+1</sub> = 6 + a<sub>n</sub>, where a<sub>1</sub> = 2.
questions.explanation: The rule adds 6 each time. a<sub>1</sub> = 2; a<sub>2</sub> = 6 + 2 = 8; a<sub>3</sub> = 6 + 8 = 14; a<sub>4</sub> = 6 + 14 = 20; a<sub>5</sub> = 6 + 20 = 26. It is an A.P. with a = 2, d = 6.

questions.question: Find the first five terms of the sequence defined by a<sub>n</sub> = (n/2)a<sub>n+1</sub>, where a<sub>1</sub> = 1.
questions.explanation: Rewrite the rule as a<sub>n+1</sub> = (2/n)a<sub>n</sub>. Then a<sub>2</sub> = (2/1)(1) = 2; a<sub>3</sub> = (2/2)(2) = 2; a<sub>4</sub> = (2/3)(2) = 4/3; a<sub>5</sub> = (2/4)(4/3) = 2/3.

questions.question: Find the sequence by using T<sub>n+1</sub> = (n + 1)T<sub>n</sub>, where T<sub>1</sub> = 2.
questions.explanation: T<sub>2</sub> = (2)T<sub>1</sub> = 2·2 = 4; T<sub>3</sub> = (3)T<sub>2</sub> = 3·4 = 12; T<sub>4</sub> = (4)T<sub>3</sub> = 4·12 = 48; T<sub>5</sub> = (5)T<sub>4</sub> = 5·48 = 240. In general T<sub>n</sub> = n!·T<sub>1</sub> = 2·n!, so the sequence is 2, 4, 12, 48, 240, ...

questions.question: Find the values of the nth term of the triangular sequence when n = 7, 9, 12 and 16.
questions.explanation: The nth triangular number is T<sub>n</sub> = n(n + 1)/2. Hence T<sub>7</sub> = 7·8/2 = 28; T<sub>9</sub> = 9·10/2 = 45; T<sub>12</sub> = 12·13/2 = 78; T<sub>16</sub> = 16·17/2 = 136.

questions.question: Find the first five terms of the sequence with general term a<sub>n</sub> = (n + 1)!/2!.
Find the Pascal sequence when n = 5, 6, 7 and 8 (using the formula n!/(r!(n − r)!) for r = 0, 1, ..., n).
questions.explanation: Each entry of row n is <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> = n!/(r!(n − r)!). For n = 5 these are 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1; for n = 6 they are 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1 (each inner entry is the sum of the two above it); for n = 7, 1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, 7, 1; and for n = 8, 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the A.P. 1, 5, 9, ... ; find a<sub>12</sub>.
questions.explanation: Here a = 1 and d = 5 − 1 = 4. Using a<sub>n</sub> = a + (n − 1)d: a<sub>12</sub> = 1 + (12 − 1)4 = 1 + 44 = 45.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the A.P. −15, −9, −3, ... ; find a<sub>10</sub>.
Find the indicated term of the A.P. 2, 6, 10, 14, ... ; find a<sub>7</sub>.
Find the indicated term of the A.P. −5, 4, 13, ... ; find a<sub>30</sub>.
Find the indicated term of the A.P. 23, 26, 29, ... ; find a<sub>14</sub>.
Find the indicated term of the A.P. 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, ... ; find a<sub>6</sub>.
Find the first five terms of the arithmetic sequence for which a<sub>n</sub> = 2n − 3.
questions.explanation: a<sub>1</sub> = 2(1) − 3 = −1; a<sub>2</sub> = 1; a<sub>3</sub> = 3; a<sub>4</sub> = 5; a<sub>5</sub> = 7 (an A.P. with d = 2).

questions.question: Find the first five terms of the arithmetic sequence for which a<sub>n−2</sub> = 3n − 5.
questions.explanation: Take n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 to obtain a<sub>1</sub>, a<sub>2</sub>, ..., a<sub>5</sub>: a<sub>1</sub> = 3(3) − 5 = 4; a<sub>2</sub> = 3(4) − 5 = 7; a<sub>3</sub> = 10; a<sub>4</sub> = 13; a<sub>5</sub> = 16. The common difference is 3.

questions.question: Find the first five terms of the sequence for which a<sub>n</sub> = n/(2n + 1).
Find the first five terms of the sequence for which a<sub>n</sub> = (n + 1)a<sub>n−1</sub> and a<sub>1</sub> = 1.
Find the first five terms of the sequence for which a<sub>n</sub> − a<sub>n−1</sub> = n + 2 and a<sub>1</sub> = 2.
Find the first five terms of the arithmetic sequence whose first term is a = 5 and which contains the three consecutive terms 23, 26, 29.
questions.explanation: The consecutive terms 23, 26, 29 show that d = 26 − 23 = 3. With a = 5 the first five terms are 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 (indeed 23 is the 7th, 26 the 8th and 29 the 9th term).

questions.question: If a<sub>n−3</sub> = 2n − 5, find the nth term of the sequence.
questions.explanation: Replace n by n + 3 in the given relation: a<sub>(n+3)−3</sub> = 2(n + 3) − 5, i.e. a<sub>n</sub> = 2n + 6 − 5 = 2n + 1. (Check: n = 4 gives a<sub>1</sub> = 3 = 2(4) − 5.)

questions.question: Find the 20th term of the sequence 1, 2 − x, 3 − 2x, ...
Find the 21st term of the A.P. whose 6th term is 11 and whose 15th term is 47.
questions.explanation: a<sub>6</sub> = a + 5d = 11 and a<sub>15</sub> = a + 14d = 47. Subtracting gives 9d = 36, so d = 4 and a = 11 − 5(4) = −9. Then a<sub>21</sub> = −9 + 20(4) = 71.

questions.question: Which term of the sequence −15, −9, −3, ... is 75?
Which term of the sequence 5, 2, −1, ... is −85?
Which term of the sequence −2, 4, 10, ... is 148?
Find the nth term of the sequence (6/7)², (11/7)², (16/7)², ...
questions.explanation: The bases 6/7, 11/7, 16/7 form an A.P. with a = 6/7 and d = 5/7. Their nth term is 6/7 + (n − 1)(5/7) = (5n + 1)/7. Squaring gives a<sub>n</sub> = ((5n + 1)/7)².

questions.question: If a, b, c are the lth, mth and nth terms of an A.P., show that a(m − n) + b(n − l) + c(l − m) = 0.
questions.answer: a(m − n) + b(n − l) + c(l − m) = 0
questions.explanation: Let A be the first term and d the common difference of the A.P. Then a = A + (l − 1)d, b = A + (m − 1)d, c = A + (n − 1)d. Hence a(m − n) + b(n − l) + c(l − m) = A[(m − n) + (n − l) + (l − m)] + d[(l − 1)(m − n) + (m − 1)(n − l) + (n − 1)(l − m)]. The first bracket is 0. Expanding the second: (lm − ln − m + n) + (mn − ml − n + l) + (nl − nm − l + m) = 0, since every term cancels. Thus the whole expression equals 0.

questions.question: If a, b, c are the lth, mth and nth terms of an A.P., show that l(b − c) + m(c − a) + n(a − b) = 0.
questions.answer: l(b − c) + m(c − a) + n(a − b) = 0
questions.explanation: With a = A + (l − 1)d, b = A + (m − 1)d, c = A + (n − 1)d we get b − c = (m − n)d, c − a = (n − l)d and a − b = (l − m)d. Hence l(b − c) + m(c − a) + n(a − b) = d[l(m − n) + m(n − l) + n(l − m)] = d[lm − ln + mn − ml + nl − nm] = 0.

questions.question: If 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in A.P., show that b = 2ac/(a + c).
questions.explanation: Since 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in A.P., the middle term is the average of the other two: 2/b = 1/a + 1/c = (a + c)/(ac). Taking reciprocals, b = 2ac/(a + c).

questions.question: If 1/(a − b), 1/(b − c), 1/(c − a) are in A.P., then show that (a + c)/(a − b) = (a + b)/(c − a).
questions.answer: The hypothesis is equivalent to (a − b)² + (c − a)² = 2(b − c)²; the printed identity does not follow in general (it is equivalent to b² + c² = 2a², an extra condition).
questions.explanation: Put x = a − b, y = b − c, z = c − a, so that x + y + z = 0. The A.P. condition 2/(b − c) = 1/(a − b) + 1/(c − a) gives 2/y = (x + z)/(xz) = −y/(xz), i.e. 2xz = −y². Then x² + 2xz + z² = x² + z² − y², so (x + z)² = x² + z² − y²; but x + z = −y, hence y² = x² + z² − y², that is x² + z² = 2y², i.e. (a − b)² + (c − a)² = 2(b − c)² — the squares of the three differences are in A.P. On the other hand (a + c)/(a − b) = (a + b)/(c − a) is equivalent to (a + c)(c − a) = (a + b)(a − b), i.e. to b² + c² = 2a². This is an additional condition, not a consequence of the hypothesis: for a = 3, b = 4 − √3, c = 2 − √3 the reciprocals (√3 + 1)/2, 1/2, −(√3 − 1)/2 do form an A.P. (common difference −√3/2), yet (a + c)/(a − b) ≈ 4.46 while (a + b)/(c − a) ≈ −1.93. So the identity as printed is not valid in general.

questions.question: An object falling from rest falls 12 metres during the first second, 24 metres during the next second, 36 metres during the third second and so on. How much will it fall during the 8th second?
questions.explanation: The distances 12, 24, 36, ... form an A.P. with a = 12 and d = 12. For the 8th second, n = 8: a<sub>8</sub> = 12 + (8 − 1)12 = 12 + 84 = 96 metres.

questions.question: A man deposits Rs. 13,000 in a bank in the first month, Rs. 14,500 in the second month, Rs. 16,000 in the third month and so on. Find how much he has to deposit in the bank at the end of a year (i.e. in the 12th month).
A boy saves Rs. 200 at the end of the first week and goes on increasing his saving by Rs. 25 weekly. After how many weeks will his weekly saving be Rs. 2000?
questions.explanation: The weekly savings 200, 225, 250, ... form an A.P. with a = 200 and d = 25. Put a<sub>n</sub> = 2000: 200 + (n − 1)25 = 2000, so (n − 1)25 = 1800, n − 1 = 72 and n = 73.

questions.question: Find the arithmetic mean between 18 and 26.
Find the arithmetic mean between 10 + 5√3 and 4 − 5√3.
questions.explanation: A.M. = [(10 + 5√3) + (4 − 5√3)]/2 = 14/2 = 7. The irrational parts cancel.

questions.question: Find the arithmetic mean between 3a + 2b and 5a − 6b.
Find the arithmetic mean between 5 + 7√5 i and 8 − 7√5 i.
questions.explanation: A.M. = [(5 + 7√5 i) + (8 − 7√5 i)]/2 = 13/2. The imaginary parts cancel.

questions.question: Find the arithmetic mean between 3a² − 5a + 6 and −a² + 7a − 4.
Find the arithmetic mean between 3a − 5 and 5a + 3.
Insert three arithmetic means between 3 and 11.
questions.explanation: Let the means be A<sub>1</sub>, A<sub>2</sub>, A<sub>3</sub>. Then 3, A<sub>1</sub>, A<sub>2</sub>, A<sub>3</sub>, 11 are 5 terms of an A.P., so d = (11 − 3)/(5 − 1) = 8/4 = 2. Hence the means are 3 + 2 = 5, 7 and 9.

questions.question: Insert four arithmetic means between √2 and 12/√2.
Insert five arithmetic means between √5/2 and 4√5.
Insert six arithmetic means between −30 and 30.
If 5 and 8 are two arithmetic means between c and d, find c and d.
questions.explanation: Since c, 5, 8, d are in A.P. the common difference is 8 − 5 = 3. Hence d = 8 + 3 = 11 and c = 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.question: Find n so that (a<sup>n+5</sup> + b<sup>n+5</sup>)/(a<sup>n+4</sup> + b<sup>n+4</sup>) may be the arithmetic mean between a and b.
questions.explanation: We need (a<sup>n+5</sup> + b<sup>n+5</sup>)/(a<sup>n+4</sup> + b<sup>n+4</sup>) = (a + b)/2. Cross-multiplying: 2a<sup>n+5</sup> + 2b<sup>n+5</sup> = a<sup>n+5</sup> + ab<sup>n+4</sup> + ba<sup>n+4</sup> + b<sup>n+5</sup>, i.e. a<sup>n+5</sup> + b<sup>n+5</sup> = ab<sup>n+4</sup> + ba<sup>n+4</sup>. Rearranging, a<sup>n+4</sup>(a − b) = b<sup>n+4</sup>(a − b), so for a ≠ b we need a<sup>n+4</sup> = b<sup>n+4</sup>, i.e. n + 4 = 0 and n = −4. (Check: n = −4 gives (a + b)/(1 + 1) = (a + b)/2.)

questions.question: Sum the series 3 + 8 + 13 + ... to 16 terms.
Sum the series (−3) + (−1) + 1 + 3 + 5 + ... to 18 terms.
Sum the series 4.57 + 4.87 + 5.17 + ... to 22 terms.
Sum the series 3/√2 + 2√2 + 5/√2 + ... to n terms.
Sum the series 3/√2 + 2√2 + 5/√2 + ... to 15 terms.
Find the number of terms of (−7) + (−5) + (−3) + ... if the sum is 65.
Find the number of terms of −7 + (−4) + (−1) + ... if the sum is 114.
Find the number of terms of −9 + (−6) + (−3) + ... if the sum is 3225.
Find the number of terms of −9 − 6 − 3 + 0 + ... if the sum is 66.
Sum the series 3 + 5 − 7 + 9 + 11 − 13 + 15 + 17 − 19 + ... to 3n terms.
questions.explanation: Group the terms in threes: (3 + 5 − 7) + (9 + 11 − 13) + (15 + 17 − 19) + ... The first terms 3, 9, 15, ... have kth term 6k − 3, the second terms are 6k − 1 and the third are 6k + 1. The kth group is (6k − 3) + (6k − 1) − (6k + 1) = 6k − 5. There are n groups, so S<sub>3n</sub> = Σ(6k − 5) = 6·n(n + 1)/2 − 5n = 3n² + 3n − 5n = 3n² − 2n = n(3n − 2).

questions.question: Sum the series 1 + 4 − 7 + 10 + 13 − 16 + 19 + 22 − 25 + ... to 3n terms.
questions.explanation: Group in threes: (1 + 4 − 7) + (10 + 13 − 16) + (19 + 22 − 25) + ... In the kth group the terms are 9k − 8, 9k − 5 and 9k − 2, so the group sum is (9k − 8) + (9k − 5) − (9k − 2) = 9k − 11. Hence S<sub>3n</sub> = 9·n(n + 1)/2 − 11n = (9n² + 9n − 22n)/2 = (9n² − 13n)/2 = (n/2)(9n − 13).

questions.question: Sum the series 9 + 12 − 15 + 18 + 21 − 24 + 27 + 30 − 33 + ... to 3n terms.
questions.explanation: Group in threes: (9 + 12 − 15) + (18 + 21 − 24) + (27 + 30 − 33) + ... In the kth group the terms are 9k, 9k + 3 and 9k + 6, so the group sum is 9k + 9k + 3 − (9k + 6) = 9k − 3. Hence S<sub>3n</sub> = 9·n(n + 1)/2 − 3n = (9n² + 9n − 6n)/2 = (9n² + 3n)/2 = 3n(3n + 1)/2.

questions.question: If S<sub>n</sub> = n(2n − 1), then find the series.
questions.explanation: The nth term is t<sub>n</sub> = S<sub>n</sub> − S<sub>n−1</sub> = n(2n − 1) − (n − 1)(2n − 3) = 2n² − n − (2n² − 5n + 3) = 4n − 3. Hence the series is 1 + 5 + 9 + 13 + ... (an A.P. with a = 1, d = 4).

questions.question: Find the sum of the first 100 natural numbers which are neither exactly divisible by 3 nor by 7.
If S<sub>2</sub>, S<sub>3</sub>, S<sub>5</sub> are the sums of 2n, 3n and 5n terms of an A.P., show that S<sub>5</sub> = 5(S<sub>3</sub> − S<sub>2</sub>).
questions.explanation: For an A.P. with first term a and common difference d, the sum of kn terms is S<sub>k</sub> = (kn/2)[2a + (kn − 1)d]. Hence S<sub>3</sub> − S<sub>2</sub> = (3n/2)[2a + (3n − 1)d] − (2n/2)[2a + (2n − 1)d] = (n/2)[6a + 3n(3n − 1)d − 4a − 2n(2n − 1)d] = (n/2)[2a + (9n² − 3n − 4n² + 2n)d] = (n/2)[2a + (5n² − n)d] = (n/2)[2a + (5n − 1)d]. Multiplying by 5 gives (5n/2)[2a + (5n − 1)d] = S<sub>5</sub>, as required.

questions.question: The sums of n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio (3n + 2) : (n + 1). Find the ratio of their 8th terms.
questions.explanation: Let the first terms be a, a′ and the common differences d, d′. Then S<sub>n</sub>/S′<sub>n</sub> = [2a + (n − 1)d]/[2a′ + (n − 1)d′] = (3n + 2)/(n + 1). The ratio of the 8th terms is [a + 7d]/[a′ + 7d′], which equals S<sub>n</sub>/S′<sub>n</sub> when (n − 1)/2 = 7, i.e. n = 15. Hence the ratio is (3·15 + 2)/(15 + 1) = 47/16.

questions.question: The sum of three numbers in A.P. is 27 and their product is 405. Find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a − d, a, a + d. Their sum is 3a = 27, so a = 9. Their product is (9 − d)(9)(9 + d) = 405, i.e. 9(81 − d²) = 405, 81 − d² = 45, d² = 36, d = ±6. For d = 6 the numbers are 3, 9, 15; for d = −6 they are 15, 9, 3.

questions.question: Find five numbers in A.P. whose sum is 25 and the sum of whose squares is 135.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a − 2d, a − d, a, a + d, a + 2d. Their sum is 5a = 25, so a = 5. The sum of squares is (25 − 20d + 4d²) + (25 − 10d + d²) + 25 + (25 + 10d + d²) + (25 + 20d + 4d²) = 125 + 10d² = 135, so d² = 1 and d = ±1. The numbers are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (or 7, 6, 5, 4, 3).

questions.question: The sum of Rs. 42,000 is distributed among five persons so that each person after the first receives Rs. 80 less than the preceding person. How much does each person receive?
questions.explanation: Let the shares be a, a − 80, a − 160, a − 240, a − 320 (an A.P. with d = −80). Their sum is 5a − 800 = 42000, so 5a = 42800 and a = 8560. The shares are Rs. 8560, Rs. 8480, Rs. 8400, Rs. 8320 and Rs. 8240.

questions.question: A well digging company charges Rs. 1,250 for the first metre, Rs. 1,500 for the second metre and Rs. 1,750 for the third metre and so on. What is the depth of a well that costs Rs. 50,000?
A man borrows Rs. 25,000 and agrees to repay with a total profit of Rs. 10,000 in 10 installments, each installment being less than the preceding by Rs. 200. What should be his first installment?
questions.explanation: The total repayment is 25000 + 10000 = 35000 in 10 installments forming an A.P. with d = −200. S<sub>10</sub> = (10/2)[2a + 9(−200)] = 5(2a − 1800) = 35000, so 2a − 1800 = 7000 and a = 4400. The first installment is Rs. 4,400.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the G.P. 3, 6, 12, ... ; find the 5th term.
Find the indicated term of the G.P. 32, 16, 8, ... ; find the 9th term.
Find the indicated term of the G.P. 4, 2√2, 2, ... ; find the 12th term.
Find the indicated term of the G.P. i, 1, −i, ... ; find the 16th term.
questions.explanation: a = i and r = 1/i = −i. Then a<sub>16</sub> = i(−i)<sup>15</sup>. Now (−i)<sup>15</sup> = ((−i)²)⁷(−i) = (−1)⁷(−i) = i, so a<sub>16</sub> = i·i = −1.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the G.P. b² − c², b + c, (b + c)/(b − c), ... ; find the 9th term.
questions.explanation: r = (b + c)/(b² − c²) = 1/(b − c). Hence a<sub>9</sub> = (b² − c²)[1/(b − c)]⁸ = (b² − c²)/(b − c)⁸ = (b + c)/(b − c)⁷.

questions.question: In a G.P., a<sub>1</sub> = 5/9 and a<sub>6</sub> = 15625/9. Find its nth term.
questions.explanation: a<sub>6</sub>/a<sub>1</sub> = r⁵ = (15625/9)/(5/9) = 3125 = 5⁵, so r = 5. Then a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>1</sub>r<sup>n−1</sup> = (5/9)5<sup>n−1</sup> = 5<sup>n</sup>/9.

questions.question: Find the nth term of the geometric sequence if a<sub>5</sub>/a<sub>3</sub> = 4/9 and a<sub>2</sub> = 4/9.
questions.explanation: a<sub>5</sub>/a<sub>3</sub> = r² = 4/9, so r = ±2/3. Since a<sub>2</sub> = a<sub>1</sub>r = 4/9, a<sub>1</sub> = (4/9)/r. For r = 2/3, a<sub>1</sub> = 2/3 and a<sub>n</sub> = (2/3)(2/3)<sup>n−1</sup> = (2/3)<sup>n</sup>; for r = −2/3, a<sub>1</sub> = −2/3 and a<sub>n</sub> = (−2/3)(−2/3)<sup>n−1</sup> = (−2/3)<sup>n</sup>. The printed key gives (−1)<sup>n</sup>(2/3)<sup>n</sup> or (−2/3)<sup>n</sup>, but these are the same sequence, so the key omits the equally valid positive ratio r = 2/3, which gives a<sub>n</sub> = (2/3)<sup>n</sup>.

questions.question: Show that the reciprocals of the terms of the G.P. a<sub>1</sub>, a<sub>1</sub>r², a<sub>1</sub>r⁴, ... form another G.P.
questions.answer: The reciprocals 1/a<sub>1</sub>, 1/(a<sub>1</sub>r²), 1/(a<sub>1</sub>r⁴), ... form a G.P. with common ratio 1/r².
questions.explanation: The given terms have the constant ratio a<sub>1</sub>r²/a<sub>1</sub> = r², so they form a G.P. The reciprocals are 1/a<sub>1</sub>, 1/(a<sub>1</sub>r²), 1/(a<sub>1</sub>r⁴), ... and the ratio of any term to the previous one is [1/(a<sub>1</sub>r²)]/[1/a<sub>1</sub>] = 1/r², which is constant. Hence the reciprocals form a G.P. with common ratio 1/r².

questions.question: How many terms are there in the G.P. 1/3, 1/12, 1/48, ..., 1/196608?
Find three consecutive numbers in G.P. whose sum is 39 and whose product is 729.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a/r, a, ar. Their product is a³ = 729, so a = 9. Their sum is 9(1/r + 1 + r) = 39, i.e. 9r² − 30r + 9 = 0, or 3r² − 10r + 3 = 0, giving r = 3 or r = 1/3. The numbers are 3, 9, 27 (or 27, 9, 3).

questions.question: The number of bacteria in a culture increased in G.P. from 515,000 to 15,45,000 in 7 days. Find the daily rate of increase, assuming the rate of increase to be constant.
questions.explanation: Let a<sub>1</sub> = 515000 and a<sub>8</sub> = 1545000 (7 days later). Then a<sub>8</sub> = a<sub>1</sub>r⁷ gives r⁷ = 1545000/515000 = 3, so r = 3<sup>1/7</sup> ≈ 1.1699. The number increases by a factor of about 1.17 each day, i.e. the daily rate of increase is about 17%.

questions.question: Find the profit on Rs. 1000 for 5 years at 4% per annum compound profit.
Find the geometric mean between −2 and −8.
Find the geometric mean between 3 and 1/3.
Find the geometric mean between 8√2 and 9√2.
Find the geometric mean between −2i and 8i.
Find the geometric mean between 7 + i and 7 − i.
Find the geometric mean between 16/9 and 9/25.
Insert two geometric means between 3 and 81.
questions.explanation: The four terms 3, G<sub>1</sub>, G<sub>2</sub>, 81 form a G.P., so 81 = 3r³, r³ = 27, r = 3. Hence G<sub>1</sub> = 3(3) = 9 and G<sub>2</sub> = 9(3) = 27.

questions.question: Insert three geometric means between 2 and 1/2.
Insert four geometric means between 3 and 96.
questions.explanation: There are 6 terms, so 96 = 3r⁵, r⁵ = 32, r = 2. The means are 3(2) = 6, 12, 24 and 48.

questions.question: Insert five geometric means between 16 and 1024.
questions.explanation: There are 7 terms, so 1024 = 16r⁶, r⁶ = 64, r = 2. The means are 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512.

questions.question: The arithmetic mean between two numbers is 29 and the geometric mean is 21; find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b. Then (a + b)/2 = 29, so a + b = 58; and √(ab) = 21, so ab = 441. The numbers are the roots of t² − 58t + 441 = 0, i.e. t = [58 ± √(3364 − 1764)]/2 = (58 ± 40)/2. Hence the numbers are 49 and 9.

questions.question: For what value of n is (a<sup>n−2</sup> + b<sup>n−2</sup>)/(a<sup>n−3</sup> + b<sup>n−3</sup>) the geometric mean between a and b?
questions.explanation: We need (a<sup>n−2</sup> + b<sup>n−2</sup>)/(a<sup>n−3</sup> + b<sup>n−3</sup>) = √(ab) = a<sup>1/2</sup>b<sup>1/2</sup>. With n = 5/2 the expression becomes (a<sup>1/2</sup> + b<sup>1/2</sup>)/(a<sup>−1/2</sup> + b<sup>−1/2</sup>). Now a<sup>−1/2</sup> + b<sup>−1/2</sup> = 1/√a + 1/√b = (√a + √b)/√(ab), so the quotient is (√a + √b) · √(ab)/(√a + √b) = √(ab). Hence n = 5/2.

questions.question: Show that the nth root of the product of n geometric means between x and y is the geometric mean between x and y.
questions.answer: The nth root of the product is √(xy), the G.M. of x and y.
questions.explanation: Let the n geometric means be G<sub>1</sub>, G<sub>2</sub>, ..., G<sub>n</sub>, so that x, G<sub>1</sub>, ..., G<sub>n</sub>, y is a G.P. with ratio r = (y/x)<sup>1/(n+1)</sup> and G<sub>k</sub> = xr<sup>k</sup>. Their product is G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>...G<sub>n</sub> = x<sup>n</sup>r<sup>1+2+...+n</sup> = x<sup>n</sup>r<sup>n(n+1)/2</sup> = x<sup>n</sup>[(y/x)<sup>1/(n+1)</sup>]<sup>n(n+1)/2</sup> = x<sup>n</sup>(y/x)<sup>n/2</sup> = (xy)<sup>n/2</sup>. Taking the nth root gives (xy)<sup>1/2</sup> = √(xy), which is the geometric mean of x and y.

questions.question: The arithmetic mean of two positive integral numbers exceeds their (positive) geometric mean by 2 and their sum is 20. Find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b, with a + b = 20 and (a + b)/2 − √(ab) = 2. Then 10 − √(ab) = 2, so √(ab) = 8 and ab = 64. The numbers are the roots of t² − 20t + 64 = 0, i.e. (t − 16)(t − 4) = 0, giving 16 and 4.

questions.question: The arithmetic mean between two numbers is 5 and their (positive) geometric mean is 4. Find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b. Then a + b = 10 and ab = 4² = 16. They are the roots of t² − 10t + 16 = 0, i.e. (t − 8)(t − 2) = 0, giving 8 and 2.

questions.question: Find the sum: 2⁶ + 2⁷ + 2⁸ + ... + 2¹³.
Find the sum: 1/x + 1/x² + 1/x³ + ... + 1/x⁸.
Find the sum: 0.9 + 0.99 + 0.999 + ... to n terms.
Find the sum: 7 + 77 + 777 + ... to n terms.
Find the sum: 0.2 + 0.22 + 0.222 + ... to n terms.
Find the sum: 3 + 33 + 333 + ... to n terms.
Find the sum to n terms of the series 1 + (a + b) + (a² + ab + b²) + (a³ + a²b + ab² + b³) + ..., where a > 1, b > 1 and a > b.
questions.explanation: The kth term is a<sup>k−1</sup> + a<sup>k−2</sup>b + ... + b<sup>k−1</sup> = (a<sup>k</sup> − b<sup>k</sup>)/(a − b). Hence S<sub>n</sub> = (1/(a − b))Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup>(a<sup>k</sup> − b<sup>k</sup>) = (1/(a − b)){a(a<sup>n</sup> − 1)/(a − 1) − b(b<sup>n</sup> − 1)/(b − 1)}.

questions.question: Find the sum to n terms of the series r + (1 + k)r² + (1 + k + k²)r³ + ..., where k and r are proper fractions.
questions.answer: S<sub>n</sub> = (r/(1 − k)){(1 − r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − r) − k(1 − k<sup>n</sup>r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − kr)}
questions.explanation: The nth term is r<sup>n</sup>(1 + k + ... + k<sup>n−1</sup>) = r<sup>n</sup>(1 − k<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − k) = [r<sup>n</sup> − (kr)<sup>n</sup>]/(1 − k). Hence S<sub>n</sub> = (1/(1 − k))[Σr<sup>n</sup> − Σ(kr)<sup>n</sup>] = (1/(1 − k))[r(1 − r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − r) − kr(1 − k<sup>n</sup>r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − kr)] = (r/(1 − k))[(1 − r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − r) − k(1 − k<sup>n</sup>r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − kr)].

questions.question: If a<sub>n</sub> = (1/4)<sup>n</sup>, then find the sum of the sequence up to n terms.

If a = b/2 + b²/4 + b³/8 + ... where 0 < b < 2, then prove that b = 2a/(1 + a).
questions.explanation: The right side is an infinite G.P. with first term b/2 and common ratio b/2, and 0 < b < 2 gives |b/2| < 1. Hence a = (b/2)/(1 − b/2) = b/(2 − b). Then a(2 − b) = b, i.e. 2a − ab = b, so 2a = b(1 + a) and b = 2a/(1 + a).

questions.question: The sum of an infinite geometric series is half the sum of the squares of its terms. If the sum of its first two terms is 4 1/2, find the series.
questions.explanation: Let the first term be a and the ratio r. Then S = a/(1 − r) and the sum of the squares is a²/(1 − r²). The condition a/(1 − r) = (1/2)a²/(1 − r²) gives 2(1 − r²) = a(1 − r), i.e. 2(1 − r)(1 + r) = a(1 − r), so a = 2(1 + r). Also a + ar = 9/2, i.e. a(1 + r) = 9/2, so 2(1 + r)² = 9/2, (1 + r)² = 9/4 and 1 + r = 3/2. Hence r = 1/2 and a = 3. The series is 3 + 3/2 + 3/4 + 3/8 + ...

questions.question: Joining the midpoints of the sides of an equilateral triangle, an equilateral triangle having half the perimeter of the original triangle is obtained. We form a sequence of nested equilateral triangles in this manner with the original triangle having perimeter 5/2. What will be the total perimeter of all the triangles formed in this way?
questions.explanation: The perimeters are 5/2, 5/4, 5/8, ... — an infinite G.P. with a = 5/2 and r = 1/2. Their total is S<sub>∞</sub> = (5/2)/(1 − 1/2) = (5/2)/(1/2) = 5.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the harmonic progression 1/3, 1/7, 1/11, ... ; find the 9th term.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 3, 7, 11, ... form an A.P. with a = 3 and d = 4. Its 9th term is 3 + 8(4) = 35. Hence the 9th term of the H.P. is the reciprocal, 1/35.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the harmonic progression 1/3, 1/5, 1/7, ... ; find the 12th term.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 3, 5, 7, ... form an A.P. with a = 3 and d = 2. Its 12th term is 3 + 11(2) = 25, so the 12th term of the H.P. is 1/25.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the harmonic progression 9/5, 9/13, 9/21, ... ; find the 8th term.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 5/9, 13/9, 21/9, ... form an A.P. with a = 5/9 and d = 8/9. Its 8th term is 5/9 + 7(8/9) = 61/9. Hence the 8th term of the H.P. is 9/61.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the harmonic progression −1/5, −1/3, −1, ... ; find the 15th term.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals −5, −3, −1, ... form an A.P. with a = −5 and d = 2. Its 15th term is −5 + 14(2) = 23, so the 15th term of the H.P. is 1/23.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the harmonic progression 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... ; find the 8th term.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 2, 5, 8, ... form an A.P. with a = 2 and d = 3. Its 8th term is 2 + 7(3) = 23, so the 8th term of the H.P. is 1/23.

questions.question: Find the indicated term of the harmonic progression 1/3, 1/8, 1/13, ... ; find the 11th term.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 3, 8, 13, ... form an A.P. with a = 3 and d = 5. Its 11th term is 3 + 10(5) = 53, so the 11th term of the H.P. is 1/53.

questions.question: If the 7th and 10th terms of an H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21 respectively, find its 14th and 20th terms.
questions.explanation: The corresponding A.P. of reciprocals has 7th term 3 and 10th term 21/5. Hence 3d = 21/5 − 3 = 6/5, so d = 2/5 and a = 3 − 6(2/5) = 3/5. Then a<sub>14</sub> = 3/5 + 13(2/5) = 29/5, so T<sub>14</sub> = 5/29; and a<sub>20</sub> = 3/5 + 19(2/5) = 41/5, so T<sub>20</sub> = 5/41.

questions.question: If the sum of the first and sixth terms of an H.P. is 31/116, find the harmonic sequence if the first term is 1/4.
questions.explanation: The corresponding A.P. has first term 4. Let its sixth term be x. Then 1/4 + 1/x = 31/116, so 1/x = 31/116 − 29/116 = 2/116 = 1/58, i.e. x = 58. Hence 4 + 5d = 58, d = 54/5, and the A.P. is 4, 74/5, 128/5, ... . Taking reciprocals, the H.P. is 1/4, 5/74, 5/128, ...

questions.question: The first term of an H.P. is −1/3 and the fifth term is 1/5. Find its 9th term.
questions.explanation: The corresponding A.P. has first term −3 and fifth term 5, so 4d = 5 − (−3) = 8 and d = 2. Its 9th term is −3 + 8(2) = 13, so the 9th term of the H.P. is 1/13.

questions.question: If the pth term of an H.P. is q and the qth term is p, prove that the (p + q)th term is pq/(p + q).
questions.explanation: For the corresponding A.P., the pth term is 1/q and the qth term is 1/p. Hence (p − q)d = 1/q − 1/p = (p − q)/(pq), so d = 1/(pq). Then A<sub>1</sub> = 1/q − (p − 1)d = 1/q − (p − 1)/(pq) = (p − p + 1)/(pq) = 1/(pq). Therefore A<sub>p+q</sub> = 1/(pq) + (p + q − 1)/(pq) = (p + q)/(pq), and the (p + q)th term of the H.P. is its reciprocal, pq/(p + q).

questions.question: Insert the harmonic mean between 1/64 and 1/81.
Insert the harmonic mean between 1/5 and 1/17.
Insert the harmonic mean between 3 + √2 and 3 − √2.
Insert the harmonic mean between 2 + 3i and 2 − 3i.
Insert the harmonic mean between 1/7 and 1/11.
Insert the harmonic mean between 3 and 7.
Insert four harmonic means between 4 and 20.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 1/4 and 1/20 must be the first and sixth terms of an A.P., so d = (1/20 − 1/4)/5 = (−4/20)/5 = −1/25. The A.P. is 1/4, 21/100, 17/100, 13/100, 9/100, 1/20, and taking reciprocals of the four middle terms gives 100/21, 100/17, 100/13, 100/9.

questions.question: Insert four harmonic means between 1/9 and 1/81.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 9 and 81 are the first and sixth terms of an A.P., so d = (81 − 9)/5 = 72/5. The A.P. is 9, 117/5, 189/5, 261/5, 333/5, 81, and the harmonic means are 5/117, 5/189, 5/261, 5/333.

questions.question: Insert five harmonic means between 1/4 and 1/24.
questions.explanation: The reciprocals 4 and 24 are the first and seventh terms of an A.P., so d = (24 − 4)/6 = 10/3. The A.P. is 4, 22/3, 32/3, 14, 52/3, 62/3, 24, and the harmonic means are 3/22, 3/32, 1/14, 3/52, 3/62.

questions.question: Prove that the square of the geometric mean of two numbers equals the product of the arithmetic mean and the harmonic mean of the two numbers.
questions.explanation: For two numbers a and b: G = √(ab), A = (a + b)/2 and H = 2ab/(a + b). Then A·H = [(a + b)/2]·[2ab/(a + b)] = ab = G², as required.

questions.question: Find n so that (x<sup>n−5</sup> + y<sup>n−5</sup>)/(x<sup>n−6</sup> + y<sup>n−6</sup>) may be the harmonic mean between x and y.
questions.explanation: We need (x<sup>n−5</sup> + y<sup>n−5</sup>)/(x<sup>n−6</sup> + y<sup>n−6</sup>) = 2xy/(x + y). Cross-multiplying: (x + y)(x<sup>n−5</sup> + y<sup>n−5</sup>) = 2xy(x<sup>n−6</sup> + y<sup>n−6</sup>), i.e. x<sup>n−4</sup> + xy<sup>n−5</sup> + yx<sup>n−5</sup> + y<sup>n−4</sup> = 2x<sup>n−5</sup>y + 2xy<sup>n−5</sup>. Hence x<sup>n−4</sup> + y<sup>n−4</sup> = x<sup>n−5</sup>y + xy<sup>n−5</sup>, i.e. x<sup>n−5</sup>(x − y) = y<sup>n−5</sup>(x − y), so for x ≠ y x<sup>n−5</sup> = y<sup>n−5</sup> and n − 5 = 0, giving n = 5.

questions.question: If 5 is the harmonic mean between 2 and b, find b.
Find the arithmetic, harmonic and geometric means between 1 and 9. Also verify that AH = G².
The arithmetic mean of two numbers is 8 and the harmonic mean is 6. Find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b. Then (a + b)/2 = 8, so a + b = 16, and 2ab/(a + b) = 6 gives 2ab/16 = 6, i.e. ab = 48. The numbers are the roots of t² − 16t + 48 = 0, i.e. (t − 12)(t − 4) = 0, giving 12 and 4.

questions.question: The harmonic mean of two numbers is 24/5 and the geometric mean is 6. Find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b. Then ab = 6² = 36 and 2ab/(a + b) = 24/5 gives 72/(a + b) = 24/5, so a + b = 15. The numbers are the roots of t² − 15t + 36 = 0, i.e. (t − 12)(t − 3) = 0, giving 12 and 3.

questions.question: A sequence is a function whose domain is set of:
questions.explanation: A sequence is a function whose domain is the set of natural numbers (or a subset of it), i.e. it is a list indexed by 1, 2, 3, ...
questions.optionsRaw: a) integers  b) rational numbers  c) natural numbers  d) real numbers

questions.question: If H is the harmonic mean between x and y then H is:
questions.explanation: The harmonic mean of x and y is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals: H = 2/(1/x + 1/y) = 2xy/(x + y).
questions.optionsRaw: a) 2(x + y)/(xy)  b) (x + y)/(2xy)  c) 2xy/(x + y)  d) xy/(x + y)

questions.question: If a<sub>n</sub> − a<sub>n−1</sub> = n + 1 and a<sub>4</sub> = 14 then a<sub>5</sub> = ----------:
questions.explanation: Put n = 5: a<sub>5</sub> − a<sub>4</sub> = 5 + 1 = 6, so a<sub>5</sub> = 14 + 6 = 20.

questions.question: A sequence {a<sub>n</sub>} in which a<sub>n+1</sub> − a<sub>n</sub> is the same number for all n ∈ ℕ is called:
questions.explanation: A constant difference between consecutive terms is the defining property of an arithmetic progression (A.P.).
questions.optionsRaw: a) A.P  b) G.P  c) H.P  d) None of these

questions.question: If a<sub>n−1</sub>, a<sub>n</sub>, a<sub>n+1</sub> are in A.P, then a<sub>n</sub> is called:
questions.explanation: In an A.P. the middle term is the arithmetic mean of the two neighbouring terms: a<sub>n</sub> = (a<sub>n−1</sub> + a<sub>n+1</sub>)/2.
questions.optionsRaw: a) A.M  b) G.M  c) H.M  d) Mid-point

questions.question: Arithmetic mean between c and d is:
questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean of two numbers is half their sum: (c + d)/2.

questions.question: The harmonic mean between √2 and 3√2 is:
questions.optionsRaw: a) 4√2  b) 4/√2  c) (3/2)√2  d) None of these

questions.question: For any G.P the common ratio r is equal to:
questions.explanation: In a G.P. each term is r times the previous one, so r = a<sub>n</sub>/a<sub>n−1</sub>. Option (a) gives 1/r and (d) is the difference of consecutive terms, not a ratio.

options.text: a<sub>n+1</sub> − a<sub>n</sub> for n ∈ ℕ, n > 1

questions.optionsRaw: a) a<sub>n</sub>/a<sub>n+1</sub>  b) a<sub>n−1</sub>/a<sub>n</sub>  c) a<sub>n</sub>/a<sub>n−1</sub>  d) a<sub>n+1</sub> − a<sub>n</sub> for n ∈ ℕ, n > 1

questions.question: No term of a G.P is:
questions.explanation: If a term of a G.P. were 0, every later term (being a fixed multiple of it) would also be 0 and the common ratio would be undefined. Hence no term of a G.P. is zero (terms may be 1, negative or imaginary).
questions.optionsRaw: a) 0  b) 1  c) Negative  d) Imaginary number

questions.question: The sum of infinite geometric series is a finite number if:
questions.explanation: S<sub>∞</sub> = a/(1 − r) exists as a finite number only when |r| < 1, because then r<sup>n</sup> → 0.

questions.question: If the reciprocals of the terms of a sequence form an A.P, then it is:
questions.explanation: A sequence whose reciprocals form an A.P. is, by definition, a harmonic sequence (harmonic progression).
questions.optionsRaw: a) Harmonic sequence  b) Arithmetic sequence  c) Reciprocal sequence  d) Series

questions.question: If (a<sup>n+1</sup> + b<sup>n+1</sup>)/(a<sup>n</sup> + b<sup>n</sup>) is A.M between a and b, then n is equal to:
questions.explanation: The A.M. of a and b is (a + b)/2. For n = 0 the expression becomes (a + b)/(1 + 1) = (a + b)/2, so n = 0. (n = 1 gives a² + b² over a + b, which is not the A.M.)

questions.question: If 1, x − 1, 3 are in A.P., then x = ----------:
questions.explanation: For an A.P. the middle term is the average of the extremes: 2(x − 1) = 1 + 3 = 4, so x − 1 = 2 and x = 3.

questions.question: G.M between −2 and 8 is:
questions.explanation: G = ±√[(−2)(8)] = ±√(−16) = ±4i. (Options (b) and (c) ignore that the product is negative.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) 4i or −4i  b) 4 or −4  c) 16 or −16  d) 3 or −5

questions.question: General term of a sequence is (−1)<sup>n</sup>n². Its 4th term is:
If |r| > 1 then infinite geometric series is ----------:
questions.explanation: When |r| > 1 the terms grow without bound (r<sup>n</sup> → ±∞) and the partial sums do not approach a finite limit, so the series diverges.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Convergent  b) Divergent  c) Undefined  d) both a and b

questions.question: The harmonic mean of 1/3 and 2/5 is:
If (a − b)/(b − c) = a/b, then a, b and c are in:
questions.explanation: Cross-multiplying: b(a − b) = a(b − c), i.e. ab − b² = ab − ac, so b² = ac. This means b is the geometric mean of a and c, hence a, b, c are in G.P.
questions.optionsRaw: a) A.P  b) G.P  c) H.P  d) None of these

questions.question: The 5th term of an arithmetic sequence is 60 and the 8th term is 90. Find the 12th term.
questions.explanation: a<sub>5</sub> = a + 4d = 60 and a<sub>8</sub> = a + 7d = 90. Subtracting, 3d = 30, so d = 10 and a = 60 − 40 = 20. Hence a<sub>12</sub> = 20 + 11(10) = 130.

questions.question: There are n arithmetic means between 8 and 32 such that the ratio of the third and 7th means is 3 : 5. Find the value of n.
questions.explanation: The common difference is d = (32 − 8)/(n + 1) = 24/(n + 1). The third mean is 8 + 3d and the seventh is 8 + 7d, so (8 + 3d)/(8 + 7d) = 3/5. Cross-multiplying: 40 + 15d = 24 + 21d, i.e. 6d = 16 and d = 8/3. Then 24/(n + 1) = 8/3 gives n + 1 = 9, so n = 8.

questions.question: Find the sum of all the integers between 280 and 350 which are exactly divisible by 9.
How many terms are there in a G.P. if a = 8, a<sub>n</sub> = 1/512 and r = 1/2?
questions.explanation: a<sub>n</sub> = ar<sup>n−1</sup> gives 8(1/2)<sup>n−1</sup> = 1/512. As 8 = 2³ and 1/512 = 2<sup>−9</sup>, we get 3 − (n − 1) = −9, so n − 1 = 12 and n = 13. (Check: a<sub>13</sub> = 8(1/2)¹² = 2³·2<sup>−12</sup> = 2<sup>−9</sup> = 1/512.) The printed key gives 12 terms, which is incorrect since a<sub>12</sub> = 1/256, not 1/512.

questions.question: The yearly depreciation of a certain machine is 20% of the value at the beginning of the year. If the original cost of the machine is Rs. 50,000, find the value after 5 years.
questions.explanation: Each year the value is multiplied by 1 − 20/100 = 0.8, so after 5 years it is 50000(0.8)⁵. Now (0.8)⁵ = 0.32768, hence the value is 50000 × 0.32768 = Rs. 16,384.

questions.question: Find r, if S<sub>10</sub> = 244 S<sub>5</sub> in a G.P.
questions.explanation: For a G.P., S<sub>10</sub>/S<sub>5</sub> = [a(1 − r<sup>10</sup>)/(1 − r)]/[a(1 − r<sup>5</sup>)/(1 − r)] = (1 − r<sup>10</sup>)/(1 − r<sup>5</sup>) = 1 + r⁵. Hence 1 + r⁵ = 244, r⁵ = 243 = 3⁵ and r = 3.

questions.question: If the A.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 5 and 4 1/5 respectively, find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b. Then (a + b)/2 = 5 gives a + b = 10, and 2ab/(a + b) = 21/5 gives 2ab/10 = 21/5, i.e. ab = 21. The numbers are the roots of t² − 10t + 21 = 0, i.e. (t − 7)(t − 3) = 0, giving 7 and 3.

questions.question: If the G.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 15 and 5 10/13 respectively, find the numbers.
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be a and b. Then ab = 15² = 225 and 2ab/(a + b) = 75/13 gives 450/(a + b) = 75/13, so a + b = 78. The numbers are the roots of t² − 78t + 225 = 0, i.e. (t − 75)(t − 3) = 0, giving 75 and 3.

questions.question: The second term of an H.P. is 1/2 and the fifth term is −1/4. Find the 12th term.
questions.explanation: For the corresponding A.P. the 2nd term is 2 and the 5th term is −4, so 3d = −6 and d = −2, giving a = 2 − (−2) = 4. Then a<sub>12</sub> = 4 + 11(−2) = −18, so the 12th term of the H.P. is −1/18. (The printed key labels this answer 11 instead of 10.)

questions.question: Sum the series up to the indicated terms: 1<sup>2</sup> + 2<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup> + … + 10<sup>2</sup>.
Sum the series up to the indicated terms: 1<sup>3</sup> + 2<sup>3</sup> + 3<sup>3</sup> + … + 15<sup>3</sup>.
questions.explanation: Use Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> k<sup>3</sup> = [n(n + 1)/2]<sup>2</sup> with n = 15: S = [15·16/2]<sup>2</sup> = 120<sup>2</sup> = 14400.

questions.question: Sum the series up to n terms: 1<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup> + 5<sup>2</sup> + …
Sum the series up to n terms: 2<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup> + 8<sup>2</sup> + …
questions.explanation: The rth term is (2r)<sup>2</sup> = 4r<sup>2</sup>. Hence S = 4Σr<sup>2</sup> = 4n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = 2n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/3.

questions.question: Sum the series up to n terms: 1<sup>3</sup> + 3<sup>3</sup> + 5<sup>3</sup> + …
Sum the series up to n terms: 2 × 1<sup>2</sup> + 5 × 2<sup>2</sup> + 8 × 3<sup>2</sup> + …
Sum the series up to n terms: 1 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2 + 3) + …
Sum the series up to n terms: 2 + (2 + 5) + (2 + 5 + 8) + …
questions.explanation: The rth bracket is the sum of r terms of the A.P. 2, 5, 8, …: r/2[2·2 + (r − 1)3] = r(3r + 1)/2. So S = ½(3Σr<sup>2</sup> + Σr) = ½[n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/2 + n(n + 1)/2] = n(n + 1)(2n + 2)/4 = n(n + 1)<sup>2</sup>/2.

questions.question: Find the sum of n terms of the series whose nth term is 3n<sup>2</sup> + n + 1.
Find the sum of n terms of the series whose nth term is n<sup>2</sup> + 4n + 1.
Find the sum of n terms of the series whose nth term is n<sup>3</sup> + 3n<sup>2</sup> + 2n + 1.
Find the sum of the first forty six natural numbers starting from 10.
questions.explanation: Read literally, the series has 46 terms: 10 + 11 + … + 55. S = 46/2·(10 + 55) = 23 × 65 = 1495. The printed key gives 1036, which is 10 + 11 + … + 46 (37 terms); that treats 46 as the last term rather than the number of terms. The literal reading gives 1495.

questions.question: Find the sum of the last 12 terms of the series: 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 39.
Find the sum of the 9th to 21st terms of the series of squares of the first n natural numbers.
Find the sum of the last 12 terms of the series of cubes of the first 30 natural numbers.
Sum the series up to the indicated terms: 1·2 + 2·2<sup>2</sup> + 3·2<sup>3</sup> + 4·2<sup>4</sup> + … to 50 terms.
questions.explanation: Let S = Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>50</sup> k·2<sup>k</sup>. Then 2S = Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>50</sup> k·2<sup>k+1</sup>. Subtracting, 2S − S = 50·2<sup>51</sup> − (2 + 2<sup>2</sup> + … + 2<sup>50</sup>) = 50·2<sup>51</sup> − 2(2<sup>50</sup> − 1) = 50·2<sup>51</sup> − 2<sup>51</sup> + 2 = 49·2<sup>51</sup> + 2 = 98·2<sup>50</sup> + 2.

questions.question: Sum the series up to the indicated terms: 1 + 2·5 + 3·5<sup>2</sup> + 4·5<sup>3</sup> + … to 30 terms.
questions.explanation: Here the dot denotes multiplication, so r = 5 and S = 1 + 2·5 + 3·5<sup>2</sup> + … + 30·5<sup>29</sup>. Then 5S = 5 + 2·5<sup>2</sup> + … + 29·5<sup>29</sup> + 30·5<sup>30</sup>. Subtracting: −4S = 1 + 5 + 5<sup>2</sup> + … + 5<sup>29</sup> − 30·5<sup>30</sup> = (5<sup>30</sup> − 1)/4 − 30·5<sup>30</sup>. Thus 4S = 30·5<sup>30</sup> − (5<sup>30</sup> − 1)/4 = (119·5<sup>30</sup> + 1)/4 and S = (119·5<sup>30</sup> + 1)/16 = 1/16 + (119/16)·5<sup>30</sup>.

questions.question: Sum the series up to the indicated terms: 1 + 3/2 + 5/2<sup>2</sup> + 7/2<sup>3</sup> + … to 25 terms.
questions.explanation: The rth term is (2r − 1)/2<sup>r−1</sup> with r = 1, …, 25. Let S be the sum; then S/2 = 1/2 + 3/2<sup>2</sup> + … + 47/2<sup>24</sup> + 49/2<sup>25</sup>. Subtracting: S/2 = 1 + (1 + 1/2 + … + 1/2<sup>23</sup>) − 49/2<sup>25</sup> = 3 − 2/2<sup>24</sup> − 49/2<sup>25</sup> = 3 − 53/2<sup>25</sup>. Hence S = 6 − 53/2<sup>24</sup>.

questions.question: Sum the series up to n terms: 1 + 8/5 + 15/5<sup>2</sup> + 22/5<sup>3</sup> + …
Find the sum to infinity of the series: 1 + 4/3 + 9/3<sup>2</sup> + 14/3<sup>3</sup> + 19/3<sup>4</sup> + …
questions.explanation: Take the first term separately: S = 1 + T, where T = 4/3 + 9/3<sup>2</sup> + 14/3<sup>3</sup> + … is an A.G. series with first term a = 4/3, ratio r = 1/3 and numerator difference 5, i.e. d = 5/3. Sum to infinity of T is a/(1 − r) + dr/(1 − r)<sup>2</sup> = (4/3)/(2/3) + (5/3)(1/3)/(4/9) = 2 + 5/4 = 13/4. Hence S = 1 + 13/4 = 17/4.

questions.question: Find the sum to infinity of the series: 1 + 9a + 17a<sup>2</sup> + 25a<sup>3</sup> + … where |a| < 1.
questions.explanation: Here a<sub>1</sub> = 1, d = 8 and r = a with |a| < 1. Sum to infinity = a<sub>1</sub>/(1 − r) + dr/(1 − r)<sup>2</sup> = 1/(1 − a) + 8a/(1 − a)<sup>2</sup> = (1 − a + 8a)/(1 − a)<sup>2</sup> = (1 + 7a)/(1 − a)<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the sum to infinity of the series: 1 + 4b + 7b<sup>2</sup> + 10b<sup>3</sup> + … where |b| < 1.
questions.explanation: Here a<sub>1</sub> = 1, d = 3 and r = b with |b| < 1. Sum to infinity = 1/(1 − b) + 3b/(1 − b)<sup>2</sup> = (1 − b + 3b)/(1 − b)<sup>2</sup> = (1 + 2b)/(1 − b)<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the sum to infinity of the series: 1 + 4/4 + 7/4<sup>2</sup> + 10/4<sup>3</sup> + …
Find the sum to infinity of the series: 1 + 5/3 + 9/3<sup>2</sup> + 13/3<sup>3</sup> + …
Find the sum to infinity of the series: 1 + 5a + 9a<sup>2</sup> + 13a<sup>3</sup> + … where |a| < 1.
questions.explanation: Here a<sub>1</sub> = 1, d = 4 and r = a with |a| < 1. Sum to infinity = 1/(1 − a) + 4a/(1 − a)<sup>2</sup> = (1 − a + 4a)/(1 − a)<sup>2</sup> = (1 + 3a)/(1 − a)<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: 3 + 6 + 12 + 21 + 33 + … to n terms.
questions.explanation: Differences of consecutive terms are 3, 6, 9, 12, … an A.P. with first term 3 and common difference 3. So a<sub>n</sub> = 3 + Σ<sub>r=1</sub><sup>n−1</sup> 3r = 3 + 3n(n − 1)/2 = (3n<sup>2</sup> − 3n + 6)/2. Then S<sub>n</sub> = (3/2)Σn<sup>2</sup> − (3/2)Σn + 3n = 3n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/12 − 3n(n + 1)/4 + 3n = n[(n + 1)(2n + 1) − 3(n + 1) + 12]/4 = n(2n<sup>2</sup> + 10)/4 = n(n<sup>2</sup> + 5)/2.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: 5 + 10 + 17 + 26 + 37 + … to n terms.
questions.explanation: Differences are 5, 7, 9, 11, … an A.P. with first term 5 and common difference 2. So a<sub>n</sub> = 5 + (n − 1)/2·[2·5 + (n − 2)2] = 5 + (n − 1)(n + 3) = n<sup>2</sup> + 2n + 2. Then S<sub>n</sub> = Σn<sup>2</sup> + 2Σn + 2n = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 + n(n + 1) + 2n = n[(n + 1)(2n + 1) + 6(n + 1) + 12]/6 = n(2n<sup>2</sup> + 9n + 19)/6.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: 7 + 14 + 26 + 43 + 65 + … to n terms.
Find the sum of the series: 3 + 6 + 15 + 42 + 123 + … to n terms.
questions.explanation: Differences are 3, 9, 27, 81, … a G.P. with first term 3 and ratio 3. So a<sub>n</sub> = 3 + 3(3<sup>n−1</sup> − 1)/(3 − 1) = 3 + (3<sup>n</sup> − 3)/2 = (3<sup>n</sup> + 3)/2. Then S<sub>n</sub> = ½Σ3<sup>n</sup> + (3/2)n = ½·3(3<sup>n</sup> − 1)/2 + 3n/2 = [3(3<sup>n</sup> − 1) + 6n]/4 = [6n + 3(3<sup>n</sup> − 1)]/4.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: 7 + 14 + 45 + 100 + 179 + … to n terms.
questions.explanation: Differences are 7, 31, 55, 79, … an A.P. with first term 7 and common difference 24. So a<sub>n</sub> = 7 + (n − 1)/2·[2·7 + (n − 2)24] = 7 + (n − 1)(12n − 17) = 12n<sup>2</sup> − 29n + 24. Then S<sub>n</sub> = 12Σn<sup>2</sup> − 29Σn + 24n = 2n(n + 1)(2n + 1) − (29/2)n(n + 1) + 24n = n[4(n + 1)(2n + 1) − 29(n + 1) + 48]/2 = n(8n<sup>2</sup> − 17n + 23)/2.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: 3 + 6 + 21 + 96 + 471 + … to n terms.
questions.explanation: Differences are 3, 15, 75, 375, … a G.P. with first term 3 and ratio 5. So a<sub>n</sub> = 3 + 3(5<sup>n−1</sup> − 1)/(5 − 1) = 3 + 3(5<sup>n−1</sup> − 1)/4 = (9 + 3·5<sup>n−1</sup>)/4. Then S<sub>n</sub> = (9/4)n + (3/4)·(5<sup>n</sup> − 1)/4 = [36n + 3(5<sup>n</sup> − 1)]/16. The printed key reads 3(5<sup>n</sup> − 15), which gives 6/16 = 3/8 for n = 1 instead of the first term 3; this is a key typo for 3(5<sup>n</sup> − 1).

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: 1/(1·3) + 1/(3·5) + 1/(5·7) + … to n terms.
Find the sum of the series: 1/(1·5) + 1/(5·9) + 1/(9·13) + … to n terms.
Find the sum of the series: 1/(1·5·9) + 1/(5·9·13) + 1/(9·13·17) + … to infinity.
Find the sum of the series: 1/(1·4·7) + 1/(4·7·10) + 1/(7·10·13) + … to infinity.
Find the sum of the series: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> 1/(4k<sup>2</sup> − 1).
questions.explanation: 4k<sup>2</sup> − 1 = (2k − 1)(2k + 1), so the kth term is ½[1/(2k − 1) − 1/(2k + 1)]. Hence the partial sum to n terms is ½[1 − 1/(2n + 1)], and as n → ∞ the sum is ½·1 = 1/2.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> 1/(9k<sup>2</sup> + 3k − 2).
questions.explanation: 9k<sup>2</sup> + 3k − 2 = (3k − 1)(3k + 2), so the kth term is ⅓[1/(3k − 1) − 1/(3k + 2)]. Hence S<sub>n</sub> = ⅓[(1/2 − 1/5) + (1/5 − 1/8) + … + (1/(3n − 1) − 1/(3n + 2))] = ⅓[1/2 − 1/(3n + 2)] = ⅓·3n/[2(3n + 2)] = n/[2(3n + 2)]. For n = 1 this is 1/10, the actual first term. The printed key gives n/[6(3n + 2)] (which would give 1/30 for n = 1), so the 6 is a key typo for 2.

questions.question: Find the sum of the series: Σ<sub>k=2</sub><sup>∞</sup> 1/(k<sup>2</sup> − 1).
Find the sum of the series: Σ<sub>k=2</sub><sup>n</sup> 1/(k<sup>2</sup> − k).
If a<sub>n</sub> = 5 − 3n + 2n<sup>2</sup>, then a<sub>2n</sub> = ______.
questions.explanation: Replace n by 2n: a<sub>2n</sub> = 5 − 3(2n) + 2(2n)<sup>2</sup> = 5 − 6n + 8n<sup>2</sup>.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 5 − 6n + 2n<sup>2</sup>  b) 5 − 6n + 4n<sup>2</sup>  c) 5 + 6n + 4n<sup>2</sup>  d) 5 − 6n + 8n<sup>2</sup>

questions.question: If a<sub>n−2</sub> = 3n − 11, then a<sub>n</sub> = ______.
questions.explanation: Put n = m + 2: a<sub>m</sub> = 3(m + 2) − 11 = 3m − 5, so a<sub>n</sub> = 3n − 5.

questions.question: Σ<sub>1</sub><sup>50</sup> n = ______.
1/[n(n + 1)] = ______.
questions.explanation: Partial fractions: 1/[n(n + 1)] = 1/n − 1/(n + 1), since 1/n − 1/(n + 1) = 1/[n(n + 1)].

questions.question: The nth term of 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, … is:
questions.explanation: The denominators 2, 5, 8, … form an A.P. with first term 2 and common difference 3, so the nth denominator is 3n − 1 and the nth term is 1/(3n − 1).

questions.question: Σn is equal to:
questions.explanation: The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2.
questions.optionsRaw: a) n(n + 1)/2  b) n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6  c) n<sup>2</sup>(n + 1)<sup>2</sup>/2  d) n<sup>2</sup>

questions.question: Σn<sup>2</sup> is equal to:
questions.explanation: The sum of the squares of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
questions.optionsRaw: a) n(n + 1)/2  b) n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6  c) n<sup>2</sup>(n + 1)<sup>2</sup>/2  d) n<sup>2</sup>

questions.question: Σn<sup>3</sup> is equal to:
questions.explanation: Σn<sup>3</sup> = [n(n + 1)/2]<sup>2</sup> = n<sup>2</sup>(n + 1)<sup>2</sup>/4.

questions.question: If S<sub>n</sub> = (n + 1)<sup>2</sup>, then S<sub>2n</sub> is equal to:
questions.explanation: Replace n by 2n: S<sub>2n</sub> = (2n + 1)<sup>2</sup> = 4n<sup>2</sup> + 4n + 1.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 2n + 1  b) 4n<sup>2</sup> + 4n + 1  c) (2n − 1)<sup>2</sup>  d) Cannot be determined

questions.question: Σ<sub>n=3</sub><sup>20</sup> n<sup>0</sup> = ______.
questions.explanation: n<sup>0</sup> = 1 for every n, and n runs from 3 to 20, i.e. 20 − 3 + 1 = 18 terms. So the sum is 18 × 1 = 18.

questions.question: Sum the following series up to n terms: 2 × 1<sup>2</sup> + 4 × 2<sup>2</sup> + 6 × 3<sup>2</sup> + …
questions.explanation: The rth term is (2r)r<sup>2</sup> = 2r<sup>3</sup>. Hence S<sub>n</sub> = 2Σr<sup>3</sup> = 2[n(n + 1)/2]<sup>2</sup> = n<sup>2</sup>(n + 1)<sup>2</sup>/2.

questions.question: Sum the series 1/(1·4) + 1/(4·7) + 1/(7·10) + … to infinity.
questions.explanation: The kth term is 1/[(3k − 2)(3k + 1)] = ⅓[1/(3k − 2) − 1/(3k + 1)]. The sum to n terms is ⅓[1 − 1/(3n + 1)], so as n → ∞ the sum is ⅓·1 = 1/3.

questions.question: Evaluate: 4!
Evaluate: 6!
Evaluate: 8! / 5!
Evaluate: 10! / 7!
Evaluate: 5! × 7! × 3!
Evaluate: 10! ÷ 8! + 5!
Evaluate: 16! / (8! 12!)
Evaluate: (9!)² / ((5!)³ × 7!)
Write in factorial form: 6 · 5 · 4
Write in factorial form: 12 · 11 · 10
Write in factorial form: n(n + 1)(n + 2)/(6 · 5)
Write in factorial form: 20 · 19 · 18 · 17
Express as a single fraction: (n + 1)!/(r + 1)! + n!/r!
Express as a single fraction: (n + 1)!/r! + n!/(r + 1)!
Evaluate: <sup>20</sup>P<sub>3</sub>
Evaluate: <sup>16</sup>P<sub>4</sub>
Evaluate: <sup>12</sup>P<sub>5</sub>
Evaluate the coefficient (8; 3, 2) = 8!/(3! × 2!).
questions.explanation: This coefficient counts the arrangements of 8 objects when 3 are alike of one kind and 2 are alike of another: 8!/(3! 2!) = 40,320/(6 × 2) = 40,320/12 = 3360.

questions.question: Evaluate the coefficient (9; 2, 3, 4) = 9!/(2! × 3! × 4!).
Find the value of n: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>2</sub> = 30
questions.explanation: n(n − 1) = 30, i.e. n² − n − 30 = 0, so (n − 6)(n + 5) = 0. Since n must be positive, n = 6 (6 × 5 = 30).

questions.question: Find the value of n: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = 60
Find the value of n: <sup>8</sup>P<sub>n</sub> = 8 · 7 · 6
Find the value of n: <sup>11</sup>P<sub>n</sub> = 11 · 10 · 9
Find the value of n: <sup>n+2</sup>P<sub>4</sub> : <sup>n+1</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = 5 : 1
questions.explanation: <sup>n+2</sup>P<sub>4</sub> = (n + 2)!/(n − 2)! and <sup>n+1</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = (n + 1)!/(n − 2)!. Their ratio is (n + 2)!/(n + 1)! = n + 2 = 5, so n = 3.

questions.question: Find the value of n: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>4</sub> : <sup>n−1</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = 9 : 1
questions.explanation: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>4</sub> = n!/(n − 4)! and <sup>n−1</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = (n − 1)!/(n − 4)!. Their ratio is n!/(n − 1)! = n = 9, so n = 9.

questions.question: In how many ways are different batting orders possible for a cricket team consisting of 11 players?
questions.explanation: A batting order uses all 11 players in a definite order: 11! = 11 × 10 × 9 × ... × 2 × 1 = 39,916,800.

questions.question: In how many ways can two English books, three Chemistry books and four Physics books be arranged on a shelf so that all the books of the same subject are together?
questions.explanation: Treat the three subjects as three blocks: they can be placed on the shelf in 3! = 6 ways. Within the blocks the books can be arranged in 2! = 2, 3! = 6 and 4! = 24 ways. Total = 3! × 2! × 3! × 4! = 6 × 2 × 6 × 24 = 1728.

questions.question: How many different arrangements can be formed of the word "MATRIX" using all its letters? Also find the number of arrangements if each of them starts with "R".
questions.answer: 720 arrangements in all; 120 of them start with R.
questions.explanation: MATRIX has 6 distinct letters, so the number of arrangements is 6! = 720. If the word must begin with R, the remaining 5 letters (M, A, T, I, X) are arranged in 5! = 120 ways.

questions.question: How many signals can be given by 8 flags of different colours when 5 of them are used at a time?
questions.explanation: A signal is fixed by choosing and ordering 5 of the 8 flags: <sup>8</sup>P<sub>5</sub> = 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 6720.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three times. How many outcomes are possible? Find by the fundamental principle and illustrate using a tree diagram.
questions.answer: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.
questions.explanation: By the fundamental principle each toss has 2 possible results, so the three tosses together have 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 ordered outcomes. Tree diagram: the first toss gives the branches H and T; from each of these the second toss again gives H and T; from each of those the third toss gives H and T once more. The 8 end branches, read from top to bottom, are HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.

questions.question: How many 5-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 without repeating any digit?
questions.explanation: All five digits are used once each: 5! = 120 (none of the digits is 0, so every arrangement is a genuine 5-digit number).

questions.question: How many 5-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 without repeating any digit?
questions.explanation: Choose and order 5 of the 6 digits: <sup>6</sup>P<sub>5</sub> = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 720.

questions.question: How many 5-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 2, 4, 6, 8, 0 without repeating any digit?
questions.explanation: The first digit cannot be 0, so it has 4 choices (2, 4, 6, 8). The remaining four places take the other four digits in 4! = 24 ways. Total = 4 × 24 = 96.

questions.question: Prove that: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>r</sub> = <sup>n−1</sup>P<sub>r</sub> + r · <sup>n−1</sup>P<sub>r−1</sub>
questions.explanation:
Take the right-hand side with n−1Pr = (n − 1)!/(n − r − 1)! and n−1Pr−1 = (n − 1)!/(n − r)!. Then
RHS = (n − 1)!/(n − r − 1)! + r(n − 1)!/(n − r)!
= (n − 1)![(n − r) + r]/(n − r)! (common denominator (n − r)!)
= n(n − 1)!/(n − r)! = n!/(n − r)! = nPr = LHS.

questions.question: Prove that: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>r</sub> = n · <sup>n−1</sup>P<sub>r−1</sub>
How many arrangements can be formed using all the letters of the word STATISTICS?
questions.explanation: STATISTICS has 10 letters with S three times, T three times, I twice and A, C once each. Number of arrangements = 10!/(3! 3! 2!) = 3,628,800/72 = 50,400.

questions.question: How many arrangements can be formed using all the letters of the word PLANE?
questions.explanation: PLANE has 5 different letters, so 5! = 120 arrangements.

questions.question: How many arrangements can be formed using all the letters of the word OBJECT?
questions.explanation: OBJECT has 6 different letters, so 6! = 720 arrangements.

questions.question: How many arrangements can be formed using all the letters of the word FASTENS?
questions.explanation: FASTENS has 7 letters in which S occurs twice: 7!/2! = 5040/2 = 2520.

questions.question: How many arrangements can be formed using all the letters of the word MATHEMATICS?
questions.explanation: MATHEMATICS has 11 letters with M, A and T each occurring twice: 11!/(2! 2! 2!) = 39,916,800/8 = 4,989,600.

questions.question: How many arrangements can be formed using all the letters of the word ASSISTANCE?
questions.explanation: ASSISTANCE has 10 letters with A twice and S three times: 10!/(2! 3!) = 3,628,800/12 = 302,400.

questions.question: How many 8-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6? How many among these are greater than 60,000,000?
questions.explanation: The 8 digits contain 2 three times and 3 three times, so the count is 8!/(3! 3!) = 40,320/36 = 1120. For a number greater than 60,000,000 the first digit must be 6 (the only digit not smaller than 6); the remaining 7 places hold 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5, giving 7!/(3! 3!) = 5040/36 = 140 numbers.

questions.question: How many distinct permutations of the letters of the word "ESSENTIAL" are possible?
questions.explanation: ESSENTIAL has 9 letters with E twice and S twice: 9!/(2! 2!) = 362,880/4 = 90,720.

questions.question: How many distinct permutations of the letters of the word "ESSENTIAL" have the two S's together?
questions.explanation: Tie the two S's into one block SS. The 8 objects (SS, E, E, N, T, I, A, L) contain E twice, so they can be arranged in 8!/2! = 40,320/2 = 20,160 ways.

questions.question: How many distinct permutations of the letters of the word "ESSENTIAL" have the two S's separate?
questions.explanation: Separate = all permutations − permutations with the S's together = 90,720 − 20,160 = 70,560.

questions.question: In how many ways can 8 persons be seated around a round table?
questions.explanation: Around a circle only the relative order matters, so fix one person and arrange the other 7: (8 − 1)! = 7! = 5040.

questions.question: In how many ways can 7 keys be arranged in a circular key ring?
questions.explanation: 7 keys in a circle can be arranged in (7 − 1)! = 6! = 720 ways, but a key ring can be turned over, so clockwise and anticlockwise orders are the same: 720/2 = 360.

questions.question: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed by using each one of the digits 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 only once?
questions.explanation: Choose and order 3 of the 5 digits: <sup>5</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

questions.question: How many numbers greater than 23,000 can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 if digits may repeat?
questions.explanation: Only 5-digit numbers are meant. (a) First digit 3, 5 or 6: 3 × 5⁴ = 1875 numbers. (b) First digit 2 and second digit 5 or 6: 2 × 5³ = 250 numbers. (c) First digit 2 and second digit 3: the last three places are free, 5³ = 125 numbers (all exceed 23,000 because 0 is not available). Total = 1875 + 250 + 125 = 2250. Note: the printed key gives 1500, which does not match any consistent count for this question.

questions.question: Find the number of 5-digit numbers that can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 (no digit repeated) in which the digits 2 and 8 are next to each other.
questions.explanation: Tie 2 and 8 into one block: the block and the other three digits give 4! = 24 arrangements, and the block itself can be written 28 or 82 (2 ways). Total = 24 × 2 = 48.

questions.question: Find the number of 5-digit numbers that can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 (no digit repeated) in which the digits 2 and 8 are not next to each other.
questions.explanation: All 5-digit numbers = 5! = 120; those with 2 and 8 together = 48. Hence 120 − 48 = 72.

questions.question: How many 6-digit numbers can be formed without repeating any digit from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5? In how many of them will 0 be at the tens place?
questions.explanation: The first (lakh) digit cannot be 0: 5 choices; the remaining five places take the other five digits in 5! = 120 ways, so 5 × 120 = 600. With 0 fixed at the tens place the first digit again has 5 choices and the other four places are filled by the remaining four digits in 4! = 24 ways: 5 × 24 = 120.

questions.question: How many 5-digit multiples of 5 can be formed from the digits 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 when digits may repeat?
questions.explanation: A multiple of 5 must end in 5 (the only digit of the set divisible by 5). With 5 fixed in the units place, each of the other four places can be any of the five digits, and repetition is allowed, so the count is 5⁴ = 625. The printed key gives 256 = 4⁴, which incorrectly forbids using 5 again in the other four places even though the question says digits may repeat.

questions.question: Evaluate: <sup>12</sup>C<sub>10</sub>
Evaluate: <sup>12</sup>C<sub>3</sub>
Evaluate: <sup>20</sup>C<sub>17</sub>
Evaluate the binomial coefficient "7 over 4", i.e. <sup>7</sup>C<sub>4</sub>.
Find the value of n when: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>2</sub> = 21
Find the value of n when: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>3</sub> = 4
Find the value of n when: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>12</sub> = <sup>n</sup>C<sub>6</sub>
questions.explanation: nCr = nCs with r ≠ s implies r + s = n. Hence n = 12 + 6 = 18.

questions.question: Find the value of n when: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>15</sub> = (17 × 16)/2!
Find the value of n when: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>5</sub> = <sup>n</sup>C<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: nC5 = nC4 gives 5 + 4 = n, i.e. n = 9.

questions.question: Find the value of n when: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>10</sub> = (12 × 11)/2!
questions.explanation: (12 × 11)/2! = 66 = <sup>12</sup>C<sub>10</sub> = <sup>12</sup>C<sub>2</sub>, hence n = 12.

questions.question: Find n and r when <sup>n</sup>P<sub>r</sub> = 210 and <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> = 35.
questions.explanation: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>r</sub>/<sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> = r!, so r! = 210/35 = 6 and r = 3. Then <sup>n</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = n(n − 1)(n − 2) = 210 = 7 × 6 × 5, giving n = 7.

questions.question: Find n and r when <sup>n−1</sup>C<sub>r−1</sub> : <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> : <sup>n+1</sup>C<sub>r+1</sub> = 3 : 6 : 11.
questions.explanation:
n−1Cr−1/nCr = r/n = 3/6 = 1/2, so n = 2r.
nCr/n+1Cr+1 = (r + 1)/(n + 1) = 6/11, so 11(r + 1) = 6(n + 1).
Substituting n = 2r: 11r + 11 = 12r + 6 → r = 5, hence n = 10.

questions.question: If <sup>12</sup>C<sub>r</sub> = <sup>12</sup>C<sub>r+4</sub>, find <sup>6</sup>C<sub>r</sub>.
questions.explanation: From nCr = nCs with r ≠ s we get r + (r + 4) = 12, so 2r = 8 and r = 4. Then 6C4 = 6!/(4! 2!) = (6 × 5)/2 = 15.

questions.question: If <sup>n</sup>C<sub>12</sub> = <sup>n</sup>C<sub>10</sub>, find <sup>25</sup>C<sub>n</sub>.
The members of a club are 12 boys and 8 girls. In how many ways can a committee of 5 members be formed?
questions.explanation: There are 20 members in all; choose any 5: 20C5 = 20!/(5! 15!) = 15,504.

questions.question: The members of a club are 12 boys and 8 girls. In how many ways can a committee of 4 boys and 3 girls be formed?
questions.explanation: Choose 4 of the 12 boys and 3 of the 8 girls: 12C4 × 8C3 = 495 × 56 = 27,720.

questions.question: A box contains 7 red balls and 6 black balls. In how many ways can 5 balls be selected such that exactly 3 are red?
questions.explanation: Choose 3 of the 7 red balls and the remaining 2 from the 6 black balls: 7C3 × 6C2 = 35 × 15 = 525.

questions.question: How many (a) diagonals and (b) triangles can be drawn in a plane by joining the vertices of a polygon having 6 sides?
questions.explanation: A hexagon has 6 vertices. Every pair of vertices gives a segment: 6C2 = 15, of which 6 are sides and the rest diagonals, so diagonals = 15 − 6 = 9. Every set of 3 vertices gives one triangle: 6C3 = 20.

questions.question: How many (a) diagonals and (b) triangles can be drawn in a plane by joining the vertices of a polygon having 8 sides?
questions.explanation: An octagon has 8 vertices. Diagonals = 8C2 − 8 = 28 − 8 = 20. Triangles = 8C3 = 8!/(3! 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/6 = 56.

questions.question: How many (a) diagonals and (b) triangles can be drawn in a plane by joining the vertices of a polygon having 10 sides?
questions.explanation: A decagon has 10 vertices. Diagonals = 10C2 − 10 = 45 − 10 = 35. Triangles = 10C3 = (10 × 9 × 8)/6 = 120.

questions.question: Show that: <sup>9</sup>C<sub>6</sub> + <sup>9</sup>C<sub>5</sub> = <sup>10</sup>C<sub>6</sub>.
questions.explanation: 9C6 = 9!/(6! 3!) = 84, 9C5 = 9!/(5! 4!) = 126 and 84 + 126 = 210. Also 10C6 = 10!/(6! 4!) = 210. The result is the Pascal identity nCr + nCr−1 = n+1Cr with n = 9, r = 6.

questions.question: There are 11 men and 9 women members of a club. How many committees of 8 members can be formed, having exactly five men?
questions.explanation: Choose 5 of the 11 men and 3 of the 9 women: 11C5 × 9C3 = 462 × 84 = 38,808.

questions.question: There are 11 men and 9 women members of a club. How many committees of 8 members can be formed, having at most five women?
There are 11 men and 9 women members of a club. How many committees of 8 members can be formed, having at least five women?
Find the number of combinations of the letters of the word "Question" taken 5 at a time.
questions.explanation: The word Question has 8 different letters, so the number of 5-letter combinations is 8C5 = 8!/(5! 3!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/6 = 56.

questions.question: How many words can be formed by 3 vowels and 4 consonants out of 5 vowels and 7 consonants?
questions.explanation: Choose 3 of the 5 vowels and 4 of the 7 consonants, then arrange the 7 chosen letters: 5C3 × 7C4 × 7! = 10 × 35 × 5040 = 1,764,000.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting same faces.
questions.explanation: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, n(S) = 4. Same faces: HH and TT, so 2 favourable outcomes and P = 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting all heads.
questions.explanation: Only HH is favourable among the 4 outcomes: P = 1/4.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting at most one head.
questions.explanation: At most one head means 0 or 1 head: TT, HT, TH give 3 favourable outcomes, so P = 3/4. (The printed key gives 1/2, which is P(exactly one head) = 2/4.)

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting at least two tails.
questions.explanation: With two coins, at least two tails means both tails: TT only, so P = 1/4 = 0.25.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting at least one tail.
questions.explanation: At least one tail: HT, TH, TT (all except HH) → P = 3/4.

questions.question: Two dice, one red and the other green, are rolled simultaneously. The numbers of dots on the tops are added. Find the probability of getting a sum of 8.
Two dice, one red and the other green, are rolled simultaneously. The numbers of dots on the tops are added. Find the probability of getting a sum of 10.
Two dice, one red and the other green, are rolled simultaneously. The numbers of dots on the tops are added. Find the probability of getting a sum of 12.
questions.explanation: Sum 12 is possible only as (6,6), so P = 1/36.

questions.question: A bag contains 40 balls out of which 5 are green, 15 are red and the remaining are black. A ball is drawn out of the bag. Find the probability that the ball is green.
questions.explanation: n(S) = 40 and there are 5 green balls, so P(green) = 5/40 = 1/8.

questions.question: A bag contains 40 balls out of which 5 are green, 15 are red and the remaining are black. A ball is drawn out of the bag. Find the probability that the ball is black.
questions.explanation: Black balls = 40 − 5 − 15 = 20, so P(black) = 20/40 = 1/2.

questions.question: A bag contains 40 balls out of which 5 are green, 15 are red and the remaining are black. A ball is drawn out of the bag. Find the probability that the ball is not green.
questions.explanation: Non-green balls = 40 − 5 = 35, so P(not green) = 35/40 = 7/8 (= 1 − 1/8).

questions.question: A card is drawn from a well shuffled deck of cards. Find the probability of getting a King.
questions.explanation: A deck has 52 cards and 4 Kings, so P(King) = 4/52 = 1/13.

questions.question: A card is drawn from a well shuffled deck of cards. Find the probability of getting a club.
questions.explanation: There are 13 clubs, so P(club) = 13/52 = 1/4.

questions.question: A card is drawn from a well shuffled deck of cards. Find the probability of getting a face card.
questions.explanation: Face cards are J, Q, K in four suits: 12 cards, so P(face card) = 12/52 = 3/13.

questions.question: A die is rolled. Using a Venn diagram, find the probability of getting an even number.
questions.explanation: S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Let A = {2,4,6} (even) and B = {5,6} (greater than 4). The Venn diagram shows A ∩ B = {6}, A ∪ B = {2,4,5,6} and 1, 3 outside. P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.question: A die is rolled. Using a Venn diagram, find the probability of getting a number greater than 4.
questions.explanation: With A = {2,4,6} and B = {5,6} in S = {1,...,6}, B has 2 outcomes, so P(B) = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.question: A die is rolled. Using a Venn diagram, find the probability of getting a number which is even and greater than 4.
questions.explanation: The overlapping part of the two sets is A ∩ B = {6}, a single outcome, so P = 1/6.

questions.question: In a three child family, by using a tree diagram, find the probability of having three boys.
questions.explanation: Each child is B or G, so the tree has 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equally likely branches: BBB, BBG, BGB, BGG, GBB, GBG, GGB, GGG. Three boys is the single branch BBB, so P = 1/8.

questions.question: In a three child family, by using a tree diagram, find the probability of having exactly two boys.
questions.explanation: Exactly two boys occurs for BBG, BGB, GBB — 3 of the 8 branches, so P = 3/8.

questions.question: In a three child family, by using a tree diagram, find the probability of having at least one girl.
