questions.explanation: All branches except BBB contain a girl: 7 out of 8, so P = 7/8.

questions.question: In a single throw of two fair dice, find the probability that the product of the numbers on the dice is between 2 and 10 (both inclusive).
In a single throw of two fair dice, find the probability that the product of the numbers on the dice is divisible by 5.
questions.explanation: Products divisible by 5: 5 (2 ways), 10 (2), 15 (2), 20 (2), 25 (1), 30 (2) — 11 ways in all, so P = 11/36.

questions.question: A marble is drawn at random from a box containing 20 red, 10 white, 25 orange and 15 blue marbles. Find the probability that it is orange or red.
A marble is drawn at random from a box containing 20 red, 10 white, 25 orange and 15 blue marbles. Find the probability that it is not blue or red.
questions.explanation: Not blue and not red = white + orange = 10 + 25 = 35, so P = 35/70 = 1/2.

questions.question: A marble is drawn at random from a box containing 20 red, 10 white, 25 orange and 15 blue marbles. Find the probability that it is red, white or blue.
The king, queen and jack of clubs are removed from a deck of 52 playing cards and then shuffled. A card is drawn from the remaining cards. Find the probability of getting a heart.
questions.explanation: Remaining cards = 52 − 3 = 49. All 13 hearts are still there, so P(heart) = 13/49.

questions.question: The king, queen and jack of clubs are removed from a deck of 52 playing cards and then shuffled. A card is drawn from the remaining cards. Find the probability of getting a queen.
questions.explanation: The queen of clubs is gone, so 3 queens remain among 49 cards: P = 3/49.

questions.question: The king, queen and jack of clubs are removed from a deck of 52 playing cards and then shuffled. A card is drawn from the remaining cards. Find the probability of getting a club.
questions.explanation: Clubs left = 13 − 3 = 10, so P(club) = 10/49.

questions.question: The king, queen and jack of clubs are removed from a deck of 52 playing cards and then shuffled. A card is drawn from the remaining cards. Find the probability of getting a "9" of red colour.
questions.explanation: There are two red 9s (hearts and diamonds), both still in the pack: P = 2/49.

questions.question: A pair of fair dice is thrown. If the two numbers appearing are different, find the probability that the sum is 10.
questions.explanation: Of the 36 ordered outcomes, 6 are doubles, so 30 outcomes have different numbers — this is the reduced sample space. Sum 10 with different numbers: (4,6) and (6,4), so P = 2/30 = 1/15. (The printed key gives 1/18 = 2/36, which is P(sum 10 and different) without conditioning on the 30 outcomes.)

questions.question: A pair of fair dice is thrown. If the two numbers appearing are different, find the probability that the sum is six or less.
questions.explanation: Among the 30 outcomes with different numbers, sums 2 to 6 occur 15 times, 3 of which are doubles ((1,1), (2,2), (3,3)), leaving 12. Hence P = 12/30 = 2/5. (The printed key gives 1/3 = 12/36, the unconditional probability.)

questions.question: Given that P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.7, P(A ∩ B) = 0.21, find P(A/B).
Given that P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.7, P(A ∩ B) = 0.21, find P(B/A).
If one card is selected at random from a deck of 52 playing cards, what is the probability that the card is a club or a face or both?
questions.explanation: P(club) = 13/52, P(face) = 12/52 and P(club ∩ face) = 3/52. By the addition rule P = 13/52 + 12/52 − 3/52 = 22/52 = 11/26.

questions.question: From two events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.2, P(A ∪ B) = 0.4. Find P(A ∩ B).
A natural number is chosen out of the first 35 natural numbers. What is the probability that the chosen number is divisible by 8 or 9?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 8 up to 35: 8, 16, 24, 32 (4 numbers). Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27 (3 numbers). No number is a multiple of both (72 > 35), so 7 favourable numbers among 35: P = 7/35 = 1/5.

questions.question: A bag contains 15 black, 25 red and 10 white balls. A ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is either red or white.
questions.explanation: Total = 50, red or white = 25 + 10 = 35, so P = 35/50 = 7/10.

questions.question: Two events A and B are such that P(A) = 1/4, P(A/B) = 1/2, P(B/A) = 2/3. Find P(A ∩ B) and P(B).
A fair die is thrown twice. Find the probability that an even number of dots appears in the first throw and the number of dots in the second throw is less than 4.
questions.explanation: The throws are independent: P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 and P(less than 4) = 3/6 = 1/2. Required probability = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.question: Three missiles are fired at a target. If the probabilities of hitting the target are 0.5, 0.3 and 0.6 respectively, and the missiles are fired independently, what is the probability that all the missiles hit the target?
questions.explanation: For independent events multiply the probabilities: 0.5 × 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.09.

questions.question: If n = 0, then (n + 1)!/n! = ______.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 0  b) 1  c) n  d) ∞

questions.question: Probability of getting 7 in throwing a dice is:
questions.explanation: A die shows only 1 to 6, so getting 7 is an impossible event and P = 0/6 = 0.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 0  b) 1  c) −1  d) Not defined

questions.question: The factorial form of 12 · 11 · 10 is:
If two independent events A and B occur in p and q ways respectively, then the number of ways that both events can occur is:
questions.explanation: By the fundamental (product) principle the two operations together can be performed in p × q ways.
questions.optionsRaw: a) p + q ways  b) p·q ways  c) (pq)ʳ ways  d) rp + qr ways

questions.question: An arrangement of n objects according to some definite order is called:
questions.explanation: A permutation is an arrangement in which order matters.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Combination  b) Permutation  c) Factorial  d) none of these

questions.question: An arrangement of n objects without any order is called:
questions.explanation: A combination is a selection in which the order of the objects is not considered.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Combination  b) Permutation  c) Factorial  d) none of these

questions.question: The number of permutations of the letters of the word COMMITTEE is:
questions.explanation: COMMITTEE has 9 letters in which M, T and E each occur twice, so the number is 9!/(2! 2! 2!), i.e. the coefficient (9; 2, 2, 2) = 45,360.

questions.question: 8 · 7 · 6 is equal to:
questions.explanation: <sup>8</sup>P<sub>3</sub> = 8!/(8 − 3)! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336, whereas <sup>8</sup>C<sub>3</sub> = 56.
questions.optionsRaw: a) <sup>8</sup>P<sub>3</sub>  b) <sup>8</sup>C<sub>3</sub>  c) <sup>8</sup>P<sub>5</sub>  d) <sup>8</sup>C<sub>5</sub>

questions.question: If r = n, then <sup>n</sup>P<sub>r</sub> is equal to:
questions.explanation: <sup>n</sup>P<sub>n</sub> = n!/(n − n)! = n!/0! = n! = r!. The printed key gives (c) 1, which is the value of <sup>n</sup>C<sub>n</sub>, not of <sup>n</sup>P<sub>n</sub>.

questions.question: The number of ways that a necklace of n beads of different colours be made is:
questions.explanation: n beads in a circle give (n − 1)! arrangements; a necklace may be turned over, so clockwise and anticlockwise orders coincide and the count is (n − 1)!/2.

questions.question: Any subset of a sample space is called:
questions.explanation: An event is defined as any subset of the sample space S.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Sample space  b) an event  c) a Trial  d) Random variable

questions.question: For two events A and B, if A ∩ B = ∅, then events A and B are called:
questions.explanation: A ∩ B = ∅ means the events have no outcome in common, i.e. they are mutually exclusive.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Mutually exclusive  b) Not mutually exclusive  c) Overlapping  d) Dependent events

questions.question: When a dice is rolled and a coin is tossed, all possible outcomes are:
questions.explanation: By the fundamental principle: 6 × 2 = 12 outcomes.

questions.question: If two events A and B have equal chance of occurrence, then the events are:
questions.explanation: Events that have the same probability of occurrence are called equally likely events.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Equally likely  b) Not equally likely  c) Dependent  d) Not mutually exclusive

questions.question: If E be an event of a sample space S, then:
questions.explanation: Probability always lies between 0 and 1 inclusive. Option (a) has the ratio inverted and (c) excludes the impossible and certain events, so neither is generally true.
questions.optionsRaw: a) P(E) = n(S)/n(E)  b) 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1  c) 0 < P(E) < 1  d) all of these

questions.question: The probability of getting the tail in a single toss of a coin is:
questions.explanation: S = {H, T}; one favourable outcome out of two gives P(T) = 1/2.

questions.question: Three dice are rolled simultaneously, then n(S) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Each die has 6 outcomes, so n(S) = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216.

questions.question: Two teams A and B are playing a match, the probability that team A does not lose is:
questions.explanation: A match between two teams has two possible results, A wins or B wins. "A does not lose" means A wins, so the probability is 1/2.

questions.question: If <sup>n</sup>C<sub>6</sub> = <sup>n</sup>C<sub>12</sub>, then n equals:
questions.explanation: nCr = nCs with r ≠ s gives r + s = n, so n = 6 + 12 = 18.

questions.question: Evaluate: (<sup>6</sup>C<sub>3</sub> × <sup>4</sup>C<sub>3</sub>) / <sup>10</sup>C<sub>4</sub>
Evaluate: (<sup>6</sup>P<sub>3</sub> × <sup>4</sup>P<sub>3</sub>) / <sup>10</sup>P<sub>4</sub>
Evaluate: ∑<sub>r=1</sub><sup>3</sup> <sup>3</sup>C<sub>r</sub>
questions.explanation: <sup>3</sup>C<sub>1</sub> + <sup>3</sup>C<sub>2</sub> + <sup>3</sup>C<sub>3</sub> = 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.

questions.question: There are seven seats available in a compartment. In how many ways can seven persons be seated?
questions.explanation: The 7 persons occupy the 7 seats in order: 7! = 5040.

questions.question: A room has 3 lamps. From a collection of 10 light bulbs of which 6 are no good, a person selects 3 at random and puts them in the sockets. What is the probability that he will have light?
questions.explanation: Only 4 bulbs are good. The room stays dark when all 3 chosen bulbs are from the 6 bad ones: 6C3/10C3 = 20/120 = 1/6. Hence P(light) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6.

questions.question: If two dice are thrown simultaneously, what is the probability of obtaining a sum of 7 or a sum of 11?
questions.explanation: n(S) = 36. Sum 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) = 6 outcomes; sum 11: (5,6), (6,5) = 2 outcomes. The events are mutually exclusive, so P = 6/36 + 2/36 = 8/36 = 2/9.

questions.question: A bag contains 8 white, 10 black and 12 red balls. 3 balls are drawn from the bag. What is the probability that the first ball is white, the second ball is black and the third ball is red, when every time the ball is replaced?
questions.explanation: Total = 30 and the ball is replaced each time, so the draws are independent: (8/30) × (10/30) × (12/30) = 960/27,000 = 8/225.

questions.question: In how many ways can a football team of 11 players be selected out of 15 players? How many of them will include a particular player?
questions.explanation: C(15, 11) = C(15, 4) = 1365. If a particular player must be included, the remaining 10 are chosen from the other 14: C(14, 10) = C(14, 4) = 1001.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n².
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1 and RHS = 1² = 1, so P(1) is true. Induction hypothesis: assume P(k): 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2k − 1) = k². Induction step: the next term is 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1, so the sum for n = k + 1 is k² + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)², which is exactly P(k + 1). Conclusion: P(1) is true and P(k) implies P(k + 1), so by the principle of mathematical induction P(n) is true for all n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 3 + 6 + 9 + … + 3n = (3/2)n(n + 1).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 3 and RHS = (3/2)(1)(2) = 3, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 3 + 6 + … + 3k = (3/2)k(k + 1). Step: adding the next term 3(k + 1) gives (3/2)k(k + 1) + 3(k + 1) = (3/2)(k + 1)(k + 2) = (3/2)(k + 1)((k + 1) + 1), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: by induction the statement holds for every positive integer n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1 + 4 + 7 + … + (3n − 2) = n(3n − 1)/2.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1, RHS = 1(3 − 1)/2 = 1, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 1 + 4 + … + (3k − 2) = k(3k − 1)/2. Step: add 3(k + 1) − 2 = 3k + 1: k(3k − 1)/2 + (3k + 1) = (3k² − k + 6k + 2)/2 = (3k² + 5k + 2)/2 = (k + 1)(3k + 2)/2 = (k + 1)(3(k + 1) − 1)/2, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: P(n) is true for all positive integers n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … + 1/2<sup>n−1</sup> = 2(1 − 1/2<sup>n</sup>).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1 and RHS = 2(1 − 1/2) = 1, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/2k−1 = 2(1 − 2−k). Step: add the next term 1/2k: 2(1 − 2−k) + 2−k = 2 − 2·2−k + 2−k = 2 − 2−k = 2(1 − 2−(k+1)), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: the formula holds for all n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 2 + 6 + 18 + … + 2·3<sup>n−1</sup> = 3<sup>n</sup> − 1.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 2 and RHS = 31 − 1 = 2, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 2 + 6 + … + 2·3k−1 = 3k − 1. Step: the next term is 2·3k, so the sum becomes 3k − 1 + 2·3k = 3·3k − 1 = 3k+1 − 1, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: by induction P(n) is true for every positive integer n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 2 + 6 + 12 + … + n(n + 1) = (1/3)n(n + 1)(n + 2).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1·2 = 2 and RHS = (1/3)(1)(2)(3) = 2, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 2 + 6 + … + k(k + 1) = (1/3)k(k + 1)(k + 2). Step: add (k + 1)(k + 2): (1/3)k(k + 1)(k + 2) + (k + 1)(k + 2) = (k + 1)(k + 2)(k/3 + 1) = (1/3)(k + 1)(k + 2)(k + 3), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: the statement is true for all positive integers n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 2² + 4² + 6² + … + (2n)² = (2/3)n(n + 1)(2n + 1).
Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1·3 + 2·4 + 3·5 + … + n(n + 2) = (1/6)n(n + 1)(2n + 7).
Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1/(1·2) + 1/(2·3) + 1/(3·4) + … + 1/(n(n + 1)) = n/(n + 1).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1/2 and RHS = 1/2, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 1/(1·2) + … + 1/(k(k + 1)) = k/(k + 1). Step: add 1/((k + 1)(k + 2)): k/(k + 1) + 1/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = [k(k + 2) + 1]/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = (k² + 2k + 1)/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = (k + 1)²/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = (k + 1)/(k + 2), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: the identity holds for all n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: 1·2 + 2·2² + 3·2³ + 4·2⁴ + … + n·2<sup>n</sup> = (n − 1)2<sup>n+1</sup> + 2, n a positive integer. (The book misprints the third and fourth terms as 3·2² and 4·2²; the general term n·2<sup>n</sup> and the stated sum require 3·2³ and 4·2⁴.)
questions.explanation: The sum is Σr=1n r·2r. Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1·2 = 2 and RHS = (1 − 1)2² + 2 = 2, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: Σr=1k r·2r = (k − 1)2k+1 + 2. Step: add (k + 1)2k+1: (k − 1)2k+1 + 2 + (k + 1)2k+1 = 2k·2k+1 + 2 = k·2k+2 + 2 = ((k + 1) − 1)2(k+1)+1 + 2, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: by induction the formula is true for all positive integers n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1!·1 + 2!·2 + 3!·3 + … + n!·n = (n + 1)! − 1.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1!·1 = 1 and RHS = 2! − 1 = 1, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 1!·1 + 2!·2 + … + k!·k = (k + 1)! − 1. Step: add (k + 1)!·(k + 1): (k + 1)! − 1 + (k + 1)(k + 1)! = (k + 1)!(1 + k + 1) − 1 = (k + 1)!(k + 2) − 1 = (k + 2)! − 1, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: the statement holds for every positive integer n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: 1/(a(a + 1)) + 1/((a + 1)(a + 2)) + … + 1/((a + n − 1)(a + n)) = n/(a(a + n)), n a positive integer.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1/(a(a + 1)) and RHS = 1/(a(a + 1)), so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: the sum up to the term 1/((a + k − 1)(a + k)) equals k/(a(a + k)). Step: add 1/((a + k)(a + k + 1)): k/(a(a + k)) + 1/((a + k)(a + k + 1)) = [k(a + k + 1) + a]/[a(a + k)(a + k + 1)] = (k² + ak + k + a)/[a(a + k)(a + k + 1)] = (k + 1)(k + a)/[a(a + k)(a + k + 1)] = (k + 1)/(a(a + k + 1)), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: by induction the identity holds for all positive integers n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction for every positive integer n: 1²/(1·3) + 2²/(3·5) + … + n²/((2n − 1)(2n + 1)) = n(n + 1)/(2(2n + 1)).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1/3 and RHS = (1)(2)/(2·3) = 1/3, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: the sum up to the k-th term equals k(k + 1)/(2(2k + 1)). Step: add (k + 1)²/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)). With common denominator 2(2k + 1)(2k + 3), the numerator is k(k + 1)(2k + 3) + 2(k + 1)² = (k + 1)[k(2k + 3) + 2(k + 1)] = (k + 1)(2k² + 5k + 2) = (k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 1). Hence the sum is (k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 1)/[2(2k + 1)(2k + 3)] = (k + 1)(k + 2)/(2(2k + 3)), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: P(n) is true for all n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: a + ar + ar² + … + ar<sup>n−1</sup> = a(1 − r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − r), r ≠ 1, n a positive integer. (The book prints a(a − r<sup>n</sup>)/(1 − r); the repeated a is a misprint.)
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = a and RHS = a(1 − r)/(1 − r) = a (since r ≠ 1), so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: a + ar + … + ark−1 = a(1 − rk)/(1 − r). Step: add the next term ark: a(1 − rk)/(1 − r) + ark = [a(1 − rk) + ark(1 − r)]/(1 − r) = [a − ark + ark − ark+1]/(1 − r) = a(1 − rk+1)/(1 − r), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: the geometric-sum formula holds for every positive integer n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>0</sub> + <sup>n</sup>C<sub>1</sub> + <sup>n</sup>C<sub>2</sub> + … + <sup>n</sup>C<sub>n</sub> = 2<sup>n</sup>, n a positive integer.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): 1C0 + 1C1 = 1 + 1 = 2 = 21, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: Σr=0k kCr = 2k. Step: using Pascal's rule k+1Cr = kCr−1 + kCr for 1 ≤ r ≤ k, Σr=0k+1 k+1Cr = 1 + 1 + Σr=1k(kCr−1 + kCr) = 2 + (2k − 1) + (2k − 1) = 2k+1, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: by induction the sum of all binomial coefficients is 2n.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r−1</sub> + <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> = <sup>n+1</sup>C<sub>r</sub> for n ≥ r (Pascal's rule).
questions.explanation: Work by induction on n with r fixed. Basis (n = r): rCr−1 + rCr = r + 1 = r+1Cr, so P(r) is true. Hypothesis: kCr−1 + kCr = k+1Cr for some k ≥ r. Step: for n = k + 1, k+1Cr−1 + k+1Cr = (k + 1)!/[(r − 1)!(k − r + 2)!] + (k + 1)!/[r!(k − r + 1)!] = (k + 1)![r + (k − r + 2)]/[r!(k − r + 2)!] = (k + 1)!(k + 2)/[r!(k − r + 2)!] = (k + 2)!/[r!(k + 2 − r)!] = k+2Cr, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: Pascal's rule holds for all n ≥ r.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: 2<sup>3n+2</sup> − 28n − 4 is divisible by 49 for all n ∈ ℕ.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): 25 − 28 − 4 = 32 − 32 = 0 = 49·0, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 23k+2 − 28k − 4 = 49m for some integer m, i.e. 23k+2 = 49m + 28k + 4. Step: 23(k+1)+2 − 28(k + 1) − 4 = 8·23k+2 − 28k − 32 = 8(49m + 28k + 4) − 28k − 32 = 392m + 224k + 32 − 28k − 32 = 392m + 196k = 49(8m + 4k), which is divisible by 49, so P(k + 1) is true. Conclusion: by induction the expression is divisible by 49 for every n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: 3<sup>2n+2</sup> − 8n − 9 is divisible by 64 for all n ∈ ℕ.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): 34 − 8 − 9 = 81 − 17 = 64 = 64·1, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 32k+2 − 8k − 9 = 64m, i.e. 32k+2 = 64m + 8k + 9. Step: 32(k+1)+2 − 8(k + 1) − 9 = 9·32k+2 − 8k − 17 = 9(64m + 8k + 9) − 8k − 17 = 576m + 72k + 81 − 8k − 17 = 576m + 64k + 64 = 64(9m + k + 1), which is divisible by 64, so P(k + 1) is true. Conclusion: the statement holds for every n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: 7<sup>n</sup> − 4<sup>n</sup> is divisible by 3 (for all n ∈ ℕ).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): 7 − 4 = 3 = 3·1, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 7k − 4k = 3m, i.e. 7k = 4k + 3m. Step: 7k+1 − 4k+1 = 7·7k − 4·4k = 7(4k + 3m) − 4·4k = 3·4k + 21m = 3(4k + 7m), which is divisible by 3, so P(k + 1) is true. Conclusion: by induction 7n − 4n is divisible by 3 for all n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by induction: 2<sup>n+1</sup> > 2n + 3 for all integral values of n ≥ 2.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 2): 23 = 8 > 2(2) + 3 = 7, so P(2) is true. Hypothesis: 2k+1 > 2k + 3 for some k ≥ 2. Step: 2k+2 = 2·2k+1 > 2(2k + 3) = 4k + 6 > 2k + 5 = 2(k + 1) + 3, because 4k + 6 − (2k + 5) = 2k + 1 > 0. Hence P(k + 1) is true. Conclusion: by induction the inequality holds for every integer n ≥ 2.

questions.question: Prove by induction: 3<sup>n−1</sup> > 2<sup>n</sup> for all integral values of n ≥ 3.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 3): 3² = 9 > 2³ = 8, so P(3) is true. Hypothesis: 3k−1 > 2k for some k ≥ 3. Step: 3k = 3·3k−1 > 3·2k > 2·2k = 2k+1, so P(k + 1) is true. Conclusion: 3n−1 > 2n for every integer n ≥ 3.

questions.question: Prove by induction: n! > 3<sup>n−1</sup> for all integral values of n ≥ 5.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 5): 5! = 120 > 34 = 81, so P(5) is true. Hypothesis: k! > 3k−1 for some k ≥ 5. Step: (k + 1)! = (k + 1)·k! > (k + 1)·3k−1. Since k + 1 ≥ 6 > 3, (k + 1)·3k−1 > 3·3k−1 = 3k, so (k + 1)! > 3k, which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: by induction n! > 3n−1 for every integer n ≥ 5.

questions.question: Expand by means of the binomial theorem: (a + b)<sup>8</sup>.
questions.explanation: (a + b)<sup>8</sup> = Σ<sub>r=0</sub><sup>8</sup> <sup>8</sup>C<sub>r</sub> a<sup>8−r</sup>b<sup>r</sup>. The coefficients are row 8 of Pascal's triangle: 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1, giving a<sup>8</sup> + 8a<sup>7</sup>b + 28a<sup>6</sup>b<sup>2</sup> + 56a<sup>5</sup>b<sup>3</sup> + 70a<sup>4</sup>b<sup>4</sup> + 56a<sup>3</sup>b<sup>5</sup> + 28a<sup>2</sup>b<sup>6</sup> + 8ab<sup>7</sup> + b<sup>8</sup>.

questions.question: Expand by means of the binomial theorem: (2x − 3y)<sup>4</sup>.
questions.explanation: <sup>4</sup>C<sub>0</sub>(2x)<sup>4</sup> − <sup>4</sup>C<sub>1</sub>(2x)<sup>3</sup>(3y) + <sup>4</sup>C<sub>2</sub>(2x)<sup>2</sup>(3y)<sup>2</sup> − <sup>4</sup>C<sub>3</sub>(2x)(3y)<sup>3</sup> + <sup>4</sup>C<sub>4</sub>(3y)<sup>4</sup> = 16x<sup>4</sup> − 4·8x<sup>3</sup>·3y + 6·4x<sup>2</sup>·9y<sup>2</sup> − 4·2x·27y<sup>3</sup> + 81y<sup>4</sup> = 16x<sup>4</sup> − 96x<sup>3</sup>y + 216x<sup>2</sup>y<sup>2</sup> − 216xy<sup>3</sup> + 81y<sup>4</sup>.

questions.question: Expand by means of the binomial theorem: (√(x/y) − √(y/x))<sup>4</sup>.
questions.explanation: Let p = √(x/y) and q = √(y/x), so pq = 1, p² = x/y and q² = y/x. Then p<sup>4</sup> = x<sup>2</sup>/y<sup>2</sup>, p<sup>3</sup>q = p² = x/y, p<sup>2</sup>q<sup>2</sup> = 1, pq<sup>3</sup> = q² = y/x and q<sup>4</sup> = y<sup>2</sup>/x<sup>2</sup>. Hence (p − q)<sup>4</sup> = p<sup>4</sup> − 4p<sup>3</sup>q + 6p<sup>2</sup>q<sup>2</sup> − 4pq<sup>3</sup> + q<sup>4</sup> = x<sup>2</sup>/y<sup>2</sup> − 4x/y + 6 − 4y/x + y<sup>2</sup>/x<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Expand by means of the binomial theorem: (x<sup>2</sup>/2 − 2/x)<sup>6</sup>.
questions.explanation: (x<sup>2</sup>/2 − 2/x)<sup>6</sup> = <sup>6</sup>C<sub>0</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>/2)<sup>6</sup> − <sup>6</sup>C<sub>1</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>/2)<sup>5</sup>(2/x) + <sup>6</sup>C<sub>2</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>/2)<sup>4</sup>(2/x)<sup>2</sup> − <sup>6</sup>C<sub>3</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>/2)<sup>3</sup>(2/x)<sup>3</sup> + <sup>6</sup>C<sub>4</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>/2)<sup>2</sup>(2/x)<sup>4</sup> − <sup>6</sup>C<sub>5</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>/2)(2/x)<sup>5</sup> + <sup>6</sup>C<sub>6</sub>(2/x)<sup>6</sup> = x<sup>12</sup>/64 − 6(x<sup>10</sup>/32)(2/x) + 15(x<sup>8</sup>/16)(4/x<sup>2</sup>) − 20(x<sup>6</sup>/8)(8/x<sup>3</sup>) + 15(x<sup>4</sup>/4)(16/x<sup>4</sup>) − 6(x<sup>2</sup>/2)(32/x<sup>5</sup>) + 64/x<sup>6</sup> = x<sup>12</sup>/64 − 3x<sup>9</sup>/8 + 15x<sup>6</sup>/4 − 20x<sup>3</sup> + 60 − 96/x<sup>3</sup> + 64/x<sup>6</sup>.

questions.question: Expand by means of the binomial theorem: (3x<sup>2</sup> − 2y<sup>3</sup>)<sup>5</sup>.
questions.explanation: (3x<sup>2</sup> − 2y<sup>3</sup>)<sup>5</sup> = (3x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>5</sup> − 5(3x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>4</sup>(2y<sup>3</sup>) + 10(3x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>3</sup>(2y<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> − 10(3x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>(2y<sup>3</sup>)<sup>3</sup> + 5(3x<sup>2</sup>)(2y<sup>3</sup>)<sup>4</sup> − (2y<sup>3</sup>)<sup>5</sup> = 243x<sup>10</sup> − 5·81x<sup>8</sup>·2y<sup>3</sup> + 10·27x<sup>6</sup>·4y<sup>6</sup> − 10·9x<sup>4</sup>·8y<sup>9</sup> + 5·3x<sup>2</sup>·16y<sup>12</sup> − 32y<sup>15</sup> = 243x<sup>10</sup> − 810x<sup>8</sup>y<sup>3</sup> + 1080x<sup>6</sup>y<sup>6</sup> − 720x<sup>4</sup>y<sup>9</sup> + 240x<sup>2</sup>y<sup>12</sup> − 32y<sup>15</sup>.

questions.question: Use the binomial theorem to find the value of: (11)<sup>5</sup>.
Use the binomial theorem to find the value of: (19)<sup>6</sup>.
Use the binomial theorem to find the value of: (99)<sup>4</sup>.
Use the binomial theorem to compute (1.01)<sup>6</sup> correct to four places of decimal.
Use the binomial theorem to compute (1.02)<sup>7</sup> correct to four places of decimal.
Use the binomial theorem to compute (2.03)<sup>5</sup> correct to four places of decimal.
Evaluate: (1 + 2√a)<sup>4</sup> − (1 − 2√a)<sup>4</sup>.
questions.explanation: For u = 2√a, (1 + u)<sup>4</sup> − (1 − u)<sup>4</sup> = 2[<sup>4</sup>C<sub>1</sub>u + <sup>4</sup>C<sub>3</sub>u<sup>3</sup>] = 2(4u + 4u<sup>3</sup>) = 8u + 8u<sup>3</sup>. Substituting u = 2√a gives 16√a + 8(8a√a) = 16√a + 64a√a.

questions.question: Evaluate: (2 − √(1 − a))<sup>5</sup> + (2 + √(1 − a))<sup>5</sup>.
Evaluate: (2 + √3)<sup>5</sup> − (2 − √3)<sup>5</sup>.
Find the indicated term in the expansion of (2x/3 − 3/2)<sup>10</sup>: the 8<sup>th</sup> term.
questions.explanation: The general term is T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>10</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(2x/3)<sup>10−r</sup>(−3/2)<sup>r</sup>. For the 8<sup>th</sup> term r = 7: T<sub>8</sub> = <sup>10</sup>C<sub>7</sub>(2x/3)<sup>3</sup>(−3/2)<sup>7</sup> = 120·(8x<sup>3</sup>/27)·(−2187/128) = −(120·8·2187)/(27·128)x<sup>3</sup> = −(960·81)/128 x<sup>3</sup> = −(1215/2)x<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: Find the indicated term in the expansion of (a/b − b/a)<sup>8</sup>: the 7<sup>th</sup> term.
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>8</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(a/b)<sup>8−r</sup>(−b/a)<sup>r</sup>. For the 7<sup>th</sup> term r = 6: T<sub>7</sub> = <sup>8</sup>C<sub>6</sub>(a/b)<sup>2</sup>(−b/a)<sup>6</sup> = 28·(a<sup>2</sup>/b<sup>2</sup>)(b<sup>6</sup>/a<sup>6</sup>) = 28b<sup>4</sup>/a<sup>4</sup>.

questions.question: Find the indicated term in the expansion of (2x − 1/y)<sup>10</sup>: the last term.
questions.explanation: The last term corresponds to r = 10: T<sub>11</sub> = <sup>10</sup>C<sub>10</sub>(2x)<sup>0</sup>(−1/y)<sup>10</sup> = (−1)<sup>10</sup>/y<sup>10</sup> = 1/y<sup>10</sup>.

questions.question: Find the middle term in the expansion of (b − 2c/3)<sup>10</sup>.
questions.explanation: Here n = 10 is even, so there is one middle term, the (10/2 + 1) = 6<sup>th</sup> term. T<sub>6</sub> = <sup>10</sup>C<sub>5</sub>b<sup>5</sup>(−2c/3)<sup>5</sup> = 252·(−32/243)b<sup>5</sup>c<sup>5</sup> = −8064/243 b<sup>5</sup>c<sup>5</sup> = −(896/27)b<sup>5</sup>c<sup>5</sup>.

questions.question: Find the middle term in the expansion of (1 − (1/2)a<sup>2</sup>)<sup>14</sup>.
questions.explanation: n = 14 is even, so the middle term is the (14/2 + 1) = 8<sup>th</sup> term. T<sub>8</sub> = <sup>14</sup>C<sub>7</sub>(−a<sup>2</sup>/2)<sup>7</sup> = 3432·(−1/128)a<sup>14</sup> = −(3432/128)a<sup>14</sup> = −(429/16)a<sup>14</sup>.

questions.question: Find the middle term in the expansion of (a/b − b/a)<sup>18</sup>.
questions.explanation: n = 18 is even, so the middle term is the 10<sup>th</sup> term. T<sub>10</sub> = <sup>18</sup>C<sub>9</sub>(a/b)<sup>9</sup>(−b/a)<sup>9</sup> = 48620·(a<sup>9</sup>/b<sup>9</sup>)(−b<sup>9</sup>/a<sup>9</sup>) = −48620.

questions.question: Find the middle term in the expansion of (a − 1/a)<sup>2n</sup>.
questions.explanation: The index 2n is even, so the middle term is the (n + 1)<sup>th</sup> term. T<sub>n+1</sub> = <sup>2n</sup>C<sub>n</sub>a<sup>n</sup>(−1/a)<sup>n</sup> = <sup>2n</sup>C<sub>n</sub>(−1)<sup>n</sup> = (−1)<sup>n</sup>(2n)!/(n!)<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the two middle terms of (x<sup>3</sup> + 1/x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>7</sup>.
questions.explanation: n = 7 is odd, so the middle terms are the (7 + 1)/2 = 4<sup>th</sup> and (7 + 3)/2 = 5<sup>th</sup> terms. T<sub>4</sub> = <sup>7</sup>C<sub>3</sub>(x<sup>3</sup>)<sup>4</sup>(x<sup>−2</sup>)<sup>3</sup> = 35x<sup>12</sup>·x<sup>−6</sup> = 35x<sup>6</sup>; T<sub>5</sub> = <sup>7</sup>C<sub>4</sub>(x<sup>3</sup>)<sup>3</sup>(x<sup>−2</sup>)<sup>4</sup> = 35x<sup>9</sup>·x<sup>−8</sup> = 35x.

questions.question: Find the two middle terms of (2b − b<sup>2</sup>/4)<sup>9</sup>.
questions.explanation: n = 9 is odd, so the middle terms are the 5<sup>th</sup> and 6<sup>th</sup> terms. T<sub>5</sub> = <sup>9</sup>C<sub>4</sub>(2b)<sup>5</sup>(−b<sup>2</sup>/4)<sup>4</sup> = 126·32b<sup>5</sup>·b<sup>8</sup>/256 = (126·32/256)b<sup>13</sup> = (63/4)b<sup>13</sup>; T<sub>6</sub> = <sup>9</sup>C<sub>5</sub>(2b)<sup>4</sup>(−b<sup>2</sup>/4)<sup>5</sup> = 126·16b<sup>4</sup>·(−b<sup>10</sup>/1024) = −(2016/1024)b<sup>14</sup> = −(63/32)b<sup>14</sup>.

questions.question: Write, in simplified form, the term independent of x in (2x + 1/x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>9</sup>.
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>9</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(2x)<sup>9−r</sup>(1/x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>r</sup> = <sup>9</sup>C<sub>r</sub>2<sup>9−r</sup>x<sup>9−3r</sup>. For the term independent of x, 9 − 3r = 0, so r = 3. Hence T<sub>4</sub> = <sup>9</sup>C<sub>3</sub>2<sup>6</sup> = 84·64 = 5376.

questions.question: Write, in simplified form, the term independent of x in (2x + 5/x)<sup>6</sup>.
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>6</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(2x)<sup>6−r</sup>(5/x)<sup>r</sup> = <sup>6</sup>C<sub>r</sub>2<sup>6−r</sup>5<sup>r</sup>x<sup>6−2r</sup>. Independence of x requires 6 − 2r = 0, so r = 3. Hence T<sub>4</sub> = <sup>6</sup>C<sub>3</sub>2<sup>3</sup>5<sup>3</sup> = 20·8·125 = 20000.

questions.question: Obtain in simplified form the term involving x<sup>6</sup> in the expansion of (2x<sup>3</sup> − 1/x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>7</sup>.
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>7</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(2x<sup>3</sup>)<sup>7−r</sup>(−1/x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>r</sup> = <sup>7</sup>C<sub>r</sub>2<sup>7−r</sup>(−1)<sup>r</sup>x<sup>21−5r</sup>. For x<sup>6</sup>, 21 − 5r = 6, so r = 3. Then T<sub>4</sub> = <sup>7</sup>C<sub>3</sub>2<sup>4</sup>(−1)<sup>3</sup>x<sup>6</sup> = 35·16·(−1)x<sup>6</sup> = −560x<sup>6</sup>.

questions.question: Obtain in simplified form the term involving a<sup>8</sup> in the expansion of (a<sup>2</sup> − 1/a<sup>2</sup>)<sup>12</sup>.
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>12</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(a<sup>2</sup>)<sup>12−r</sup>(−1/a<sup>2</sup>)<sup>r</sup> = <sup>12</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(−1)<sup>r</sup>a<sup>24−4r</sup>. For a<sup>8</sup>, 24 − 4r = 8, so r = 4. Then T<sub>5</sub> = <sup>12</sup>C<sub>4</sub>(−1)<sup>4</sup>a<sup>8</sup> = 495a<sup>8</sup>.

questions.question: Obtain in simplified form the coefficient of x in the expansion of (x<sup>2</sup> + a<sup>2</sup>/x)<sup>5</sup>.
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>5</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(x<sup>2</sup>)<sup>5−r</sup>(a<sup>2</sup>/x)<sup>r</sup> = <sup>5</sup>C<sub>r</sub>a<sup>2r</sup>x<sup>10−3r</sup>. For x<sup>1</sup>, 10 − 3r = 1, so r = 3. The coefficient is <sup>5</sup>C<sub>3</sub>a<sup>6</sup> = 10a<sup>6</sup>.

questions.question: Does the expansion of (3a/2 − 1/(3a<sup>3</sup>))<sup>9</sup> contain a term independent of a?
questions.explanation: T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>9</sup>C<sub>r</sub>(3a/2)<sup>9−r</sup>(−1/(3a<sup>3</sup>))<sup>r</sup>, whose power of a is a<sup>9−r−3r</sup> = a<sup>9−4r</sup>. Independence of a would require 9 − 4r = 0, i.e. r = 9/4, which is not a non-negative integer. Hence no such term exists.

questions.question: Does the expansion of (3a/2 − 1/(3a<sup>3</sup>))<sup>9</sup> contain a term involving a<sup>10</sup>?
questions.explanation: The general term has power a<sup>9−4r</sup>. A term in a<sup>10</sup> would require 9 − 4r = 10, i.e. r = −1/4, which is impossible for r = 0, 1, …, 9. Hence the expansion has no term involving a<sup>10</sup>.

questions.question: The coefficients of the fifth, sixth and seventh terms of the expansion of (1 + x)<sup>n</sup> form an A.P. Find n.
questions.explanation: The coefficients are <sup>n</sup>C<sub>4</sub>, <sup>n</sup>C<sub>5</sub>, <sup>n</sup>C<sub>6</sub>. Since they are in A.P., 2<sup>n</sup>C<sub>5</sub> = <sup>n</sup>C<sub>4</sub> + <sup>n</sup>C<sub>6</sub>. Dividing by <sup>n</sup>C<sub>4</sub>: 2(n − 4)/5 = 1 + (n − 4)(n − 5)/30. Put m = n − 4: 12m = 30 + m(m − 1), so m<sup>2</sup> − 13m + 30 = 0, (m − 3)(m − 10) = 0. Thus m = 3 or 10 and n = 7 or 14.

questions.question: Find the first four terms in the expansion of ∛(8 − 16x).
questions.explanation: ∛(8 − 16x) = 8<sup>1/3</sup>(1 − 2x)<sup>1/3</sup> = 2(1 − 2x)<sup>1/3</sup>. Using (1 + u)<sup>1/3</sup> = 1 + u/3 − u<sup>2</sup>/9 + 5u<sup>3</sup>/81 − … with u = −2x gives (1 − 2x)<sup>1/3</sup> = 1 − 2x/3 − 4x<sup>2</sup>/9 − 40x<sup>3</sup>/81 − …, so the expansion is 2(1 − 2x/3 − 4x<sup>2</sup>/9 − 40x<sup>3</sup>/81 − …).

questions.question: Find the first four terms in the expansion of 3/(3 + x).
questions.explanation: 3/(3 + x) = 1/(1 + x/3) = (1 + x/3)<sup>−1</sup>. Using (1 + u)<sup>−1</sup> = 1 − u + u<sup>2</sup> − u<sup>3</sup> + … with u = x/3 gives 1 − x/3 + x<sup>2</sup>/9 − x<sup>3</sup>/27 + ….

questions.question: Find the first four terms in the expansion of (1 + 3x)<sup>−1/3</sup>.
Find the first four terms in the expansion of √(1 + 2x)/(1 − x).
questions.explanation: (1 + 2x)<sup>1/2</sup> = 1 + x − x<sup>2</sup>/2 + x<sup>3</sup>/2 − … and (1 − x)<sup>−1</sup> = 1 + x + x<sup>2</sup> + x<sup>3</sup> + …. Multiplying and collecting terms up to x<sup>3</sup>: constant 1; x: 1 + 1 = 2; x<sup>2</sup>: 1 + 1 − 1/2 = 3/2; x<sup>3</sup>: 1 + 1 − 1/2 + 1/2 = 2. Hence 1 + 2x + (3/2)x<sup>2</sup> + 2x<sup>3</sup> + …. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1 and |x| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/2.

questions.question: Find the first negative term in the expansion of (1 + y)<sup>4/3</sup>.
questions.explanation: (1 + y)<sup>4/3</sup> = 1 + (4/3)y + [(4/3)(1/3)/2]y<sup>2</sup> + [(4/3)(1/3)(−2/3)/6]y<sup>3</sup> + … = 1 + (4/3)y + (2/9)y<sup>2</sup> − (4/81)y<sup>3</sup> + …. The coefficients are positive until the term in y<sup>3</sup>, whose coefficient 4·1·(−2)/(3·3·3·6) = −4/81 is the first negative one. Hence the first negative term is −(4/81)y<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: Find the first negative term in the expansion of (1 + 2x)<sup>5/2</sup>.
If x is so small that its square and higher powers may be neglected, show that √(1 + (1/4)x) ≈ 1 + (1/8)x.
If x is so small that its square and higher powers may be neglected, show that ∜(1 + 8x) ≈ 1 + 2x.
questions.explanation: (1 + 8x)<sup>1/4</sup> = 1 + (1/4)(8x) + [(1/4)(−3/4)/2](8x)<sup>2</sup> + … = 1 + 2x − 6x<sup>2</sup> + …. Neglecting x<sup>2</sup> and higher powers leaves 1 + 2x.

questions.question: Using the binomial series, find √24 up to three places of decimals.
questions.answer: ≈ 4.899. (The printed key gives 4.898, which is a truncation of 4.89898.)

questions.question: Using the binomial series, find ∛28 up to three places of decimals.
questions.answer: ≈ 3.037. (The printed key gives 3.036, which is a truncation of 3.03659.)

questions.question: Using the binomial series, find <sup>5</sup>√241 up to three places of decimals.
Using the binomial series, find (1280)<sup>1/4</sup> up to three places of decimals.
Using the binomial series, find 1/<sup>5</sup>√252 up to three places of decimals.
Identify the series 1 + 3/4 + (3·5)/(4·8) + (3·5·7)/(4·8·12) + … as a binomial expansion and find its sum.
Identify the series 1 + (1/2)(1/5) − (1/(2!·4))(1/5)<sup>2</sup> + … as a binomial expansion and find its sum.
questions.explanation: This is (1 + x)<sup>n</sup> with x = 1/5. Comparing the first two terms gives nx = 1/10 and n(n − 1)x<sup>2</sup>/2 = −1/200. Dividing the second relation by the first gives (n − 1)x/2 = −1/20, so (n − 1)x = −1/10. With x = 1/(10n) this becomes (n − 1)/(10n) = −1/10, hence n − 1 = −n and n = 1/2, x = 1/5. The coefficient −1/8 = −1/(2!·4) agrees with n(n − 1)/2. Therefore the series is (1 + 1/5)<sup>1/2</sup> = √(6/5).

questions.question: Identify the series 1 − (1/2)(1/4) + (1·3)/(2!·4)(1/4)<sup>2</sup> − (1·3·5)/(3!·8)(1/4)<sup>3</sup> + … as a binomial expansion and find its sum.
Identify the series 1 − (1/2)(1/2) + (1·3)/(2·4)(1/2)<sup>2</sup> − (1·3·5)/(2·4·6)(1/2)<sup>3</sup> + … as a binomial expansion and find its sum.
questions.explanation: The series is (1 + x)<sup>−1/2</sup> = 1 − x/2 + (1·3)/(2·4)x<sup>2</sup> − (1·3·5)/(2·4·6)x<sup>3</sup> + … evaluated at x = 1/2. Hence the sum is (1 + 1/2)<sup>−1/2</sup> = (3/2)<sup>−1/2</sup> = √(2/3).

questions.question: Identify the series 1 − (1/2)(1/3) + (1·3)/(2·4)(1/3)<sup>2</sup> − (1·3·5)/(2·4·6)(1/3)<sup>3</sup> + … as a binomial expansion and find its sum.
questions.explanation: This is the expansion of (1 + x)<sup>−1/2</sup> with x = 1/3: 1 − x/2 + (1·3)/(2·4)x<sup>2</sup> − (1·3·5)/(2·4·6)x<sup>3</sup> + …. Hence the sum is (1 + 1/3)<sup>−1/2</sup> = (4/3)<sup>−1/2</sup> = √3/2.

questions.question: Use the binomial theorem to show that 1 + 1/4 + (1·3)/(4·8) + (1·3·5)/(4·8·12) + … = √2.
Use the binomial theorem to show that 1 + 1/4 + (1·3)/(4·6) + (1·3·5)/(4·6·8) + … = ∛4.
questions.explanation: Write (1 − x)<sup>−1/3</sup> = 1 + (1/3)x + (2/9)x<sup>2</sup> + (14/81)x<sup>3</sup> + …, where (1/3)(4/3)/2 = 2/9 and (1/3)(4/3)(7/3)/6 = 14/81. At x = 3/4 the first terms are 1 + 1/4 + (2/9)(9/16) + (14/81)(27/64) + … = 1 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 7/96 + …. Thus the series is (1 − 3/4)<sup>−1/3</sup> = (1/4)<sup>−1/3</sup> = 4<sup>1/3</sup> = ∛4. (The printed fourth term (1·3·5)/(4·6·8) = 5/64 is a misprint; the correct value is 7/96, since the first two terms already force n = −1/3 and x = 3/4.)

questions.question: The general term of the binomial expansion (a + x)<sup>n</sup>, where n ∈ ℕ, is:
questions.explanation: In (a + x)<sup>n</sup> the powers of a decrease from n to 0 while those of x increase from 0 to n, so T<sub>r+1</sub> = <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> a<sup>n−r</sup>x<sup>r</sup>.
questions.optionsRaw: a) <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> a<sup>n</sup>x  b) <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> a<sup>n−r</sup>x<sup>r</sup>  c) <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> a<sup>r</sup>x<sup>n−r</sup>  d) <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> (ax)<sup>n−r</sup>

questions.question: The number of terms in the expansion of (a + b)<sup>2n</sup> are:
questions.explanation: The expansion of (a + b)<sup>m</sup> has m + 1 terms. With m = 2n this gives 2n + 1 terms.
questions.optionsRaw: a) n  b) 2n + 1  c) 2<sup>n</sup>  d) 2<sup>n−1</sup>

questions.question: In the expansion (a + x)<sup>n</sup>, the exponent of x:
questions.explanation: The successive terms are a<sup>n</sup>, <sup>n</sup>C<sub>1</sub>a<sup>n−1</sup>x, …, x<sup>n</sup>, so the exponent of x starts at 0 and increases by 1 up to n.
questions.optionsRaw: a) decreases from n to 0  b) increases from 0 to n  c) remains n every where  d) becomes 0 at the end

questions.question: Middle term in the expansion of (a + b)<sup>2n</sup> is:
questions.explanation: (a + b)<sup>2n</sup> has 2n + 1 terms, so the single middle term is the (n + 1)th term.
questions.optionsRaw: a) nth term  b) (n + 1)th term  c) (2n + 1)th term  d) (2n − 1)th term

questions.question: The term independent of x in the expansion of (a + 2x)<sup>n</sup> is:
questions.explanation: The general term <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub>a<sup>n−r</sup>(2x)<sup>r</sup> contains x<sup>r</sup>. It is independent of x only when r = 0, which gives the first term a<sup>n</sup>.
questions.optionsRaw: a) First term  b) Middle term  c) Last term  d) 2<sup>nd</sup> last term

questions.question: The coefficient of the last term in the expansion of (2 − x)<sup>7</sup> is/are:
questions.explanation: The last term is (−x)<sup>7</sup> = −x<sup>7</sup>, whose coefficient is −1.

questions.question: In the expansion (a + 1/2)<sup>7</sup>, the number of middle terms is/are:
questions.explanation: n = 7 is odd, so the expansion has 8 terms and therefore two middle terms, the 4th and the 5th.
questions.optionsRaw: a) one  b) two  c) three  d) four

questions.question: Sum of odd binomial coefficients in the expansion of (a + x)<sup>n</sup> is:
questions.explanation: Adding and subtracting (1 + 1)<sup>n</sup> and (1 − 1)<sup>n</sup> gives the sum of the odd coefficients as 2<sup>n</sup>/2 = 2<sup>n−1</sup>.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 2<sup>n</sup>  b) 2<sup>n−1</sup>  c) 2<sup>n+1</sup>  d) n + 1

questions.question: <sup>n+1</sup>C<sub>0</sub> + <sup>n+1</sup>C<sub>1</sub> + <sup>n+1</sup>C<sub>2</sub> + … + <sup>n+1</sup>C<sub>n+1</sub> is equal to:
questions.explanation: This is the sum of all binomial coefficients of (1 + 1)<sup>n+1</sup>, which equals 2<sup>n+1</sup>.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 2<sup>n</sup>  b) 2<sup>n+1</sup>  c) 2<sup>n−1</sup>  d) Cannot be determined

questions.question: The number of terms in the expansion of (1 + x)<sup>1/3</sup> is ______.
questions.explanation: The index 1/3 is not a positive integer, so the binomial expansion is an infinite series with infinitely many terms.

questions.question: 1 − x + x<sup>2</sup> − x<sup>3</sup> + … is equal to:
questions.explanation: (1 + x)<sup>−1</sup> = 1 − x + x<sup>2</sup> − x<sup>3</sup> + … for |x| < 1, which is exactly the given series.
questions.optionsRaw: a) (1 + x)<sup>−1</sup>  b) (1 − x)<sup>−1</sup>  c) (1 + x)<sup>−2</sup>  d) (1 − x)<sup>−2</sup>

questions.question: The expansion of (1 − 2x)<sup>−2</sup> is valid if:
questions.explanation: The binomial series for (1 + u)<sup>n</sup> converges for |u| < 1. Here u = −2x, so |−2x| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/2.

questions.question: The middle term in the expansion of (a + b)<sup>n</sup> is (n/2 + 1)th term; then n is:
questions.explanation: A single middle term occurs only when the number of terms n + 1 is odd, i.e. n is even. Then the middle term is the (n/2 + 1)th term.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Odd  b) Even  c) Prime  d) None of these

questions.question: In (a + 1/a)<sup>8</sup>, the sum of the binomial coefficients is:
questions.explanation: The sum of the binomial coefficients of (a + b)<sup>n</sup> is 2<sup>n</sup> (put a = b = 1). Here n = 8, so the sum is 2<sup>8</sup> = 256.

questions.question: Prove by the principle of mathematical induction that 8 × 10<sup>n</sup> − 2 is divisible by 6 for all n ∈ ℕ.
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): 8 × 10 − 2 = 78 = 6 × 13, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 8 × 10k − 2 = 6m for some integer m. Step: 8 × 10k+1 − 2 = 10(8 × 10k) − 2 = 10(6m + 2) − 2 = 60m + 18 = 6(10m + 3), which is divisible by 6, so P(k + 1) is true. Conclusion: by induction 8 × 10n − 2 is divisible by 6 for every n ∈ ℕ.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction: 1<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup> + 5<sup>2</sup> + … + (2n − 1)<sup>2</sup> = (1/3)n(2n − 1)(2n + 1).
questions.explanation: Basis (n = 1): LHS = 1 and RHS = (1/3)(1)(1)(3) = 1, so P(1) is true. Hypothesis: 12 + 32 + … + (2k − 1)2 = (1/3)k(2k − 1)(2k + 1). Step: add the next odd square (2k + 1)2: (1/3)k(4k2 − 1) + (2k + 1)2 = (2k + 1)[k(2k − 1)/3 + (2k + 1)] = (2k + 1)(2k2 + 5k + 3)/3 = (2k + 1)(k + 1)(2k + 3)/3 = (1/3)(k + 1)(2(k + 1) − 1)(2(k + 1) + 1), which is P(k + 1). Conclusion: the formula holds for every positive integer n.

questions.question: Given that the coefficient of y<sup>2</sup> in the expansion of 1/(1 + my)<sup>2</sup> is 96, find m.

Given that terms involving m<sup>4</sup> and higher powers may be neglected and that 1/(a + bm)<sup>3</sup> − 1/(1 + 3m)<sup>4</sup> = cm<sup>2</sup> + dm<sup>3</sup>, find the values of a, b, c and d.
questions.explanation: 1/(a + bm)<sup>3</sup> = a<sup>−3</sup>(1 + (b/a)m)<sup>−3</sup> ≈ a<sup>−3</sup>[1 − 3(b/a)m + 6(b/a)<sup>2</sup>m<sup>2</sup> − 10(b/a)<sup>3</sup>m<sup>3</sup>] and 1/(1 + 3m)<sup>4</sup> = (1 + 3m)<sup>−4</sup> ≈ 1 − 12m + 90m<sup>2</sup> − 540m<sup>3</sup>. The difference has no constant term, so a<sup>−3</sup> = 1 and a = 1. The coefficient of m must vanish: −3b + 12 = 0, so b = 4. Then c = 6b<sup>2</sup> − 90 = 96 − 90 = 6 and d = −10b<sup>3</sup> + 540 = −640 + 540 = −100. Check: (1 + 4m)<sup>−3</sup> − (1 + 3m)<sup>−4</sup> = (1 − 12m + 96m<sup>2</sup> − 640m<sup>3</sup>) − (1 − 12m + 90m<sup>2</sup> − 540m<sup>3</sup>) = 6m<sup>2</sup> − 100m<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: Let X = {a, b, c} and Y = {1, 2, 3}. State whether or not the relation shown in figure (i) is a function from X to Y: a → 1, b has no image, c → 2.
questions.explanation: A function must give every element of X exactly one image in Y. The element b has no image, so the relation is not a function from X to Y.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram (i): X = {a, b, c}, Y = {1, 2, 3}; an arrow joins a to 1, another joins c to 2, and b has no arrow.

questions.question: Let X = {a, b, c} and Y = {1, 2, 3}. State whether or not the relation shown in figure (ii) is a function from X to Y: a → 2, b → 1, b → 3, c → 2.
questions.explanation: The element b has two images, 1 and 3, in Y. A function assigns one and only one image to each element of its domain, so this relation is not a function.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram (ii): X = {a, b, c}, Y = {1, 2, 3}; arrows a → 2, b → 1, b → 3 and c → 2.

questions.question: Let X = {a, b, c} and Y = {1, 2, 3}. State whether or not the relation shown in figure (iii) is a function from X to Y: a → 2, b → 3, c → 2.
questions.answer: It is a function (neither injective nor surjective).
questions.explanation: Each of a, b, c has exactly one image, so the relation is a function. It is not one-to-one because a and c both map to 2, and it is not onto because 1 ∈ Y has no pre-image; the range is {2, 3} ≠ Y.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram (iii): X = {a, b, c}, Y = {1, 2, 3}; arrows a → 2, b → 3 and c → 2.

questions.question: Which of the following functions is injective, surjective or bijective? Give reason: f<sub>1</sub> with X = {2, 5, 8}, Y = {1, 2, 9} and 2 → 1, 5 → 2, 8 → 9.
questions.explanation: Distinct elements of X have distinct images (2 → 1, 5 → 2, 8 → 9), so f<sub>1</sub> is injective. Its range {1, 2, 9} equals Y, so it is surjective. Being both, f<sub>1</sub> is bijective.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram f<sub>1</sub>: 2 → 1, 5 → 2, 8 → 9 with X = {2, 5, 8} and Y = {1, 2, 9}.

questions.question: Which of the following functions is injective, surjective or bijective? Give reason: f<sub>2</sub> with X = {2, 5, 8}, Y = {−3, 1, 2, 9} and 2 → −3, 5 → 1, 8 → 2.
questions.explanation: The images −3, 1, 2 are all different, so distinct elements of X have distinct images and f<sub>2</sub> is injective. The range is {−3, 1, 2}, which is a proper subset of Y (9 has no pre-image), so f<sub>2</sub> is not surjective and hence not bijective.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram f<sub>2</sub>: 2 → −3, 5 → 1, 8 → 2 with X = {2, 5, 8} and Y = {−3, 1, 2, 9}.

questions.question: Which of the following functions is injective, surjective or bijective? Give reason: f<sub>3</sub> with X = {1, 2, 3}, Y = {3, 4} and 1 → 3, 2 → 4, 3 → 3.
questions.explanation: The range is {3, 4} = Y, so f<sub>3</sub> is surjective. But f<sub>3</sub>(1) = f<sub>3</sub>(3) = 3, so two elements of X share an image; f<sub>3</sub> is not injective and therefore not bijective.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram f<sub>3</sub>: 1 → 3, 2 → 4, 3 → 3 with X = {1, 2, 3} and Y = {3, 4}.

questions.question: Which of the following functions is injective, surjective or bijective? Give reason: f<sub>4</sub> with X = {2, 4, 5}, Y = {7, 8, 9} and 2 → 7, 4 → 9, 5 → 8.
questions.explanation: The three images 7, 9, 8 are distinct, so f<sub>4</sub> is injective; the range {7, 8, 9} equals Y, so f<sub>4</sub> is surjective. Hence f<sub>4</sub> is one-to-one and onto, i.e. bijective.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram f<sub>4</sub>: 2 → 7, 4 → 9, 5 → 8 with X = {2, 4, 5} and Y = {7, 8, 9}.

questions.question: Which of the following functions is injective, surjective or bijective? Give reason: f<sub>5</sub> with X = {a, b, c}, Y = {1, 2, 3, 4} and a → 2, b → 1, c → 3.
questions.explanation: Distinct elements of X have distinct images (2, 1 and 3), so f<sub>5</sub> is injective. Its range {1, 2, 3} is a proper subset of Y because 4 is never used, so f<sub>5</sub> is not surjective and not bijective.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram f<sub>5</sub>: a → 2, b → 1, c → 3 with X = {a, b, c} and Y = {1, 2, 3, 4}.

questions.question: Which of the following functions is injective, surjective or bijective? Give reason: f<sub>6</sub> with X = {a, b, c, d}, Y = {1, 2, 3} and a → 1, b → 2, c → 3, d → 3.
questions.explanation: The range is {1, 2, 3} = Y, so f<sub>6</sub> is surjective. But c and d both map to 3, so f<sub>6</sub> is not injective and therefore not bijective.
questions.figure: Mapping diagram f<sub>6</sub>: a → 1, b → 2, c → 3, d → 3 with X = {a, b, c, d} and Y = {1, 2, 3}.

questions.question: If f: ℤ → ℝ is defined by f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> + 1, find (if possible) f(0).
questions.explanation: Put x = 0 (an integer, so it lies in the domain ℤ): f(0) = 0<sup>3</sup> + 1 = 1.

questions.question: If f: ℤ → ℝ is defined by f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> + 1, find (if possible) f(5).
If f: ℤ → ℝ is defined by f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> + 1, find (if possible) f(3/4).
questions.explanation: The domain of f is the set of integers ℤ, and 3/4 is not an integer, so f(3/4) is not defined. (Substituting in the formula would give 27/64 + 1 = 91/64, but that value is outside the stated domain.)

questions.question: If f: ℤ → ℝ is defined by f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> + 1, find (if possible) f(−2).
questions.explanation: Put x = −2: f(−2) = (−2)<sup>3</sup> + 1 = −8 + 1 = −7.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(2).
If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(−10).
questions.explanation: f(−10) = (−10)<sup>3</sup> = −1000.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(1/2).
If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(5a).
questions.explanation: f(5a) = (5a)<sup>3</sup> = 5<sup>3</sup>a<sup>3</sup> = 125a<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(a/3).
questions.explanation: f(a/3) = (a/3)<sup>3</sup> = a<sup>3</sup>/3<sup>3</sup> = a<sup>3</sup>/27.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(a + h).
questions.explanation: f(a + h) = (a + h)<sup>3</sup>. Expanding by the binomial theorem: a<sup>3</sup> + 3a<sup>2</sup>h + 3ah<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find [f(a + h) − f(a − h)] / 2h, (h ≠ 0).
questions.explanation: f(a + h) = a<sup>3</sup> + 3a<sup>2</sup>h + 3ah<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>3</sup> and f(a − h) = a<sup>3</sup> − 3a<sup>2</sup>h + 3ah<sup>2</sup> − h<sup>3</sup>. Subtracting: 6a<sup>2</sup>h + 2h<sup>3</sup>. Dividing by 2h (h ≠ 0): 3a<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup>, find f(a + h) − f(a − h).
questions.explanation: f(a + h) − f(a − h) = (a<sup>3</sup> + 3a<sup>2</sup>h + 3ah<sup>2</sup> + h<sup>3</sup>) − (a<sup>3</sup> − 3a<sup>2</sup>h + 3ah<sup>2</sup> − h<sup>3</sup>) = 6a<sup>2</sup>h + 2h<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: Given f: ℝ → ℝ defined by f(x) = x<sup>2</sup>, find [f(5 + h) − f(5)] / h, (h ≠ 0).
questions.explanation: f(5 + h) = (5 + h)<sup>2</sup> = 25 + 10h + h<sup>2</sup> and f(5) = 25. So the quotient is (10h + h<sup>2</sup>)/h = 10 + h (h ≠ 0).

questions.question: Given f: ℝ → ℝ defined by f(x) = x<sup>2</sup>, find [f(a + h) − f(a)] / h, (h ≠ 0).
questions.explanation: f(a + h) = a<sup>2</sup> + 2ah + h<sup>2</sup> and f(a) = a<sup>2</sup>. The quotient is (2ah + h<sup>2</sup>)/h = 2a + h (h ≠ 0).

questions.question: The domain of the function f(x) = 5x + 1 is {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Find its range.
questions.explanation: Evaluate f at each element of the domain: f(0) = 1, f(1) = 6, f(2) = 11, f(3) = 16, f(4) = 21, f(5) = 26. These six distinct values form the range.

questions.question: Find the domain of f(x) = x<sup>2</sup> + 3.
questions.explanation: A polynomial is defined for every real number (no denominator and no even root), so the domain is all of ℝ.

questions.question: Find the domain of f(x) = √(x + 3).
questions.explanation: The radicand must be non-negative: x + 3 ≥ 0, so x ≥ −3.

questions.question: Find the domain of f(x) = 1/x.
questions.explanation: The function is undefined where the denominator vanishes, i.e. at x = 0, so 0 is excluded from ℝ.

questions.question: Find the domain of f(x) = √(x − 5).
questions.explanation: For a real square root we need x − 5 ≥ 0, i.e. x ≥ 5.

questions.question: Find the domain of f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2).
questions.explanation: The denominator x − 2 vanishes at x = 2, where the function is undefined; every other real number is allowed.

questions.question: Find the domain of f(x) = x<sup>2</sup>/(x<sup>2</sup> − 9). (This part is misprinted as (iv) again in the book.)
questions.explanation: Set the denominator equal to zero: x<sup>2</sup> − 9 = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or x = −3. Both values are excluded, so the domain is ℝ − {−3, 3}.

questions.question: The domain of the function f is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Find the range of f(x) = 5x<sup>2</sup> + 3.
questions.explanation: f(1) = 8, f(2) = 23, f(3) = 48, f(4) = 83, f(5) = 128. Since x<sup>2</sup> is strictly increasing on the positive integers, these five values are the whole range.

questions.question: The domain of the function f is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Find the range of f(x) = x/(x + 1).
questions.explanation: f(1) = 1/2, f(2) = 2/3, f(3) = 3/4, f(4) = 4/5, f(5) = 5/6. These five distinct values form the range.

questions.question: Find the range of the function f(x) = √(x<sup>2</sup> + 1).
questions.explanation: Since x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0 for all real x, x<sup>2</sup> + 1 ≥ 1, so √(x<sup>2</sup> + 1) ≥ 1. The least value 1 occurs at x = 0 and the values increase without bound, so the range is [1, ∞). (The printed key gives y ≥ 0, which ignores the minimum value 1.)

questions.question: Find the domain and range of the function f(x) = 1/(1 + x<sup>2</sup>).
questions.explanation: The denominator 1 + x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 1 is never zero, so the domain is all of ℝ. Also 1 + x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 1 gives 0 < 1/(1 + x<sup>2</sup>) ≤ 1, with value 1 at x = 0; as |x| grows the fraction tends to 0 but never reaches it. Hence the range is (0, 1]. (The printed key gives ℝ<sup>+</sup> ∪ {0} = [0, ∞), which is incorrect.)

questions.question: Find the domain and range of f(x) = 1/√(25 − x).
questions.explanation: The expression under the root must be positive (it is in a denominator too): 25 − x > 0 ⇒ x < 25. For such x the denominator takes every positive value, so f takes every positive value, giving range ℝ<sup>+</sup>.

questions.question: A function is defined by f(x) = ax + b. The images of 1 and 5 are −2 and 10 respectively. Find the values of a and b.
questions.explanation: f(1) = −2 gives a + b = −2; f(5) = 10 gives 5a + b = 10. Subtracting: 4a = 12, so a = 3 and then b = −2 − 3 = −5.

questions.question: For f(x) = ax + b with f(1) = −2 and f(5) = 10 (so a = 3, b = −5), the domain of f is {1, 3, 5}. Find the range of f.
questions.explanation: Using f(x) = 3x − 5: f(1) = −2, f(3) = 9 − 5 = 4, f(5) = 15 − 5 = 10. Hence the range is {−2, 4, 10}.

questions.question: If f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> − ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + 1, find the values of a and b, where f(2) = −3 and f(−1) = 0.
questions.explanation: f(2) = 8 − 4a + 2b + 1 = −3 ⇒ −4a + 2b = −12 ⇒ −2a + b = −6. f(−1) = −1 − a − b + 1 = 0 ⇒ a + b = 0 ⇒ b = −a. Then −2a − a = −6 ⇒ a = 2 and b = −2.

questions.question: If f(x) = −5x + 1, find f<sup>−1</sup>(36).
questions.explanation: Write y = −5x + 1 ⇒ 5x = 1 − y ⇒ x = (1 − y)/5, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − x)/5. Then f<sup>−1</sup>(36) = (1 − 36)/5 = −35/5 = −7.

questions.question: If f(x) = −5x + 1, find f<sup>−1</sup>(−14).
questions.explanation: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − x)/5, so f<sup>−1</sup>(−14) = (1 + 14)/5 = 15/5 = 3.

questions.question: If f(x) = −5x + 1, find f<sup>−1</sup>(0).
questions.explanation: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − x)/5, so f<sup>−1</sup>(0) = 1/5 (indeed f(1/5) = −1 + 1 = 0).

questions.question: If f(x) = −5x + 1, find f<sup>−1</sup>(a).
questions.explanation: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − x)/5; replacing x by a gives f<sup>−1</sup>(a) = (1 − a)/5 = 1/5 − a/5.

questions.question: Given g(t) = 1/(t − 5), (t ≠ 5), find g<sup>−1</sup>(1/2).
questions.explanation: Let y = 1/(t − 5) ⇒ t − 5 = 1/y ⇒ t = 5 + 1/y = (5y + 1)/y, so g<sup>−1</sup>(t) = (5t + 1)/t. Then g<sup>−1</sup>(1/2) = (5/2 + 1)/(1/2) = (7/2)/(1/2) = 7.

questions.question: Given g(t) = 1/(t − 5), (t ≠ 5), find g<sup>−1</sup>(2).
Given g(t) = 1/(t − 5), (t ≠ 5), find g<sup>−1</sup>(−1).
questions.explanation: g<sup>−1</sup>(t) = (5t + 1)/t, so g<sup>−1</sup>(−1) = (−5 + 1)/(−1) = 4.

questions.question: Given g(t) = 1/(t − 5), (t ≠ 5), find g<sup>−1</sup>(a).
questions.explanation: g<sup>−1</sup>(t) = (5t + 1)/t; replacing t by a gives g<sup>−1</sup>(a) = (5a + 1)/a = 5 + 1/a.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(x) = 12 − (1/2)x.
questions.explanation: Let y = 12 − x/2. Then x/2 = 12 − y ⇒ x = 24 − 2y, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = 24 − 2x.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(x) = (1/2)(x − 3).
questions.explanation: Let y = (x − 3)/2 ⇒ x − 3 = 2y ⇒ x = 2y + 3, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = 2x + 3.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(x) = (2x + 1)/5.
questions.explanation: Let y = (2x + 1)/5 ⇒ 2x + 1 = 5y ⇒ x = (5y − 1)/2, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (5x − 1)/2 = −1/2 + (5/2)x (the form given in the key).

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(x) = (5/9)(x − 32).
questions.explanation: Let y = (5/9)(x − 32) ⇒ x − 32 = (9/5)y ⇒ x = 32 + (9/5)y, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = 32 + (9/5)x.

questions.question: Find the inverse of g(x) = 180(x − 2).
questions.explanation: Let y = 180(x − 2) ⇒ x − 2 = y/180 ⇒ x = 2 + y/180, so g<sup>−1</sup>(x) = 2 + x/180.

questions.question: Find the inverse of h(x) = 2πx.
questions.explanation: Let y = 2πx ⇒ x = y/(2π), so h<sup>−1</sup>(x) = x/(2π).

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(t) = t<sup>2</sup> + 5, (t ≥ 0).
questions.explanation: Let y = t<sup>2</sup> + 5 ⇒ t<sup>2</sup> = y − 5. Because t ≥ 0 we take the positive root: t = √(y − 5). Hence f<sup>−1</sup>(t) = √(t − 5), defined for t ≥ 5.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(t) = 5√t, (t ≥ 0).
questions.explanation: Let y = 5√t ⇒ √t = y/5 ⇒ t = y<sup>2</sup>/25, so f<sup>−1</sup>(t) = t<sup>2</sup>/25 for t ≥ 0.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(t) = (t − 5)<sup>3</sup>.
questions.explanation: Let y = (t − 5)<sup>3</sup> ⇒ t − 5 = y<sup>1/3</sup> ⇒ t = y<sup>1/3</sup> + 5, so f<sup>−1</sup>(t) = ∛t + 5.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f(t) = ∛(t + 1).
questions.explanation: Let y = ∛(t + 1) ⇒ t + 1 = y<sup>3</sup> ⇒ t = y<sup>3</sup> − 1, so f<sup>−1</sup>(t) = t<sup>3</sup> − 1.

questions.question: Find the inverse of g(x) = 1/(x − 3), (x ≠ 3).
questions.explanation: Let y = 1/(x − 3) ⇒ x − 3 = 1/y ⇒ x = 3 + 1/y = (3y + 1)/y, so g<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (3x + 1)/x.

questions.question: Find the inverse of g(x) = 1/(2x + 1), (x ≠ −1/2).
questions.explanation: Let y = 1/(2x + 1) ⇒ 2x + 1 = 1/y ⇒ 2x = 1/y − 1 = (1 − y)/y ⇒ x = (1 − y)/(2y), so g<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − x)/(2x). (The book prints the restriction as x ≠ 1/2, a misprint: 2x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1/2, and the inverse is undefined at x = 0.)

questions.question: Find the inverse of f and the domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> for f(x) = (x − 1)/(x − 3), x ≠ 3.
questions.answer: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (3x − 1)/(x − 1); Domain = {x | x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ 1}; Range = {y | y ∈ ℝ, y ≠ 3}.
questions.explanation: Let y = (x − 1)/(x − 3) ⇒ y(x − 3) = x − 1 ⇒ xy − x = 3y − 1 ⇒ x(y − 1) = 3y − 1 ⇒ x = (3y − 1)/(y − 1). Thus f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (3x − 1)/(x − 1). It is undefined at x = 1 (so 1 is not in the domain) and no value equals 3 (3 is not in the range); indeed range of f<sup>−1</sup> = domain of f = ℝ − {3}.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f and the domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> for f(x) = 5x + 7.
questions.explanation: Let y = 5x + 7 ⇒ x = (y − 7)/5, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (x − 7)/5. A linear function is defined on all of ℝ and takes all real values, so domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> are both ℝ.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f and the domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> for f(x) = 1/(x + 5), x ≠ −5.
questions.answer: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − 5x)/x = 1/x − 5; Domain = {x | x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ 0}; Range = {y | y ∈ ℝ, y ≠ −5}.
questions.explanation: Let y = 1/(x + 5) ⇒ x + 5 = 1/y ⇒ x = 1/y − 5 = (1 − 5y)/y, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (1 − 5x)/x. It is undefined at x = 0, and its value is never −5; the range is the domain of f, namely ℝ − {−5}.

questions.question: Find the inverse of f and the domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> for f(x) = (x − 5)<sup>2</sup>, x ≥ 5.
questions.answer: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = √x + 5; Domain = {x | x ∈ ℝ, x ≥ 0}; Range = {y | y ∈ ℝ, y ≥ 5}.
questions.explanation: Let y = (x − 5)<sup>2</sup>. Since x ≥ 5, x − 5 ≥ 0, so x − 5 = √y and x = √y + 5; hence f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = √x + 5. The domain of f<sup>−1</sup> is the range of f, [0, ∞), and its range is the domain of f, [5, ∞).

questions.question: Find the inverse of f and the domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> for f(x) = √(x + 7), x ≥ −7.
questions.answer: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = x<sup>2</sup> − 7; Domain = {x | x ∈ ℝ, x ≥ 0}; Range = {y | y ∈ ℝ, y ≥ −7}.
questions.explanation: Let y = √(x + 7) ⇒ y<sup>2</sup> = x + 7 ⇒ x = y<sup>2</sup> − 7, so f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = x<sup>2</sup> − 7. Because f takes only non-negative values, the domain of f<sup>−1</sup> is [0, ∞), and its range is the domain of f, [−7, ∞). (The printed key gives the domain as all of ℝ; for f<sup>−1</sup> to be the inverse function the domain must be restricted to x ≥ 0.)

questions.question: Find the inverse of f and the domain and range of f<sup>−1</sup> for f(x) = (x − 1)/(x − 4), x ≠ 4.
questions.answer: f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (4x − 1)/(x − 1); Domain = {x | x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ 1}; Range = {y | y ∈ ℝ, y ≠ 4}.
questions.explanation: Let y = (x − 1)/(x − 4) ⇒ y(x − 4) = x − 1 ⇒ xy − x = 4y − 1 ⇒ x(y − 1) = 4y − 1 ⇒ x = (4y − 1)/(y − 1). Hence f<sup>−1</sup>(x) = (4x − 1)/(x − 1) with domain ℝ − {1}; its range is the domain of f, ℝ − {4}.

questions.question: Sketch the graph of y = 5x + 2.
questions.answer: Straight line with slope 5, y-intercept 2 and x-intercept −2/5; it passes through (0, 2) and (−0.4, 0). Domain ℝ, range ℝ.
questions.explanation: Take a table of values: x = −2, −1, 0, 1 give y = −8, −3, 2, 7. Plotting these points and joining them with a straight line gives a line rising steeply (slope 5) that cuts the y-axis at (0, 2) and the x-axis at (−2/5, 0).
questions.figure: Graph of y = 5x + 2: a straight line rising from lower left to upper right, cutting the y-axis at (0, 2) and the x-axis at (−2/5, 0), with plotted points (−1, −3) and (1, 7).

questions.question: Sketch the graph of y = x<sup>2</sup> + 5.
questions.answer: Parabola opening upward with vertex (0, 5), axis x = 0, y-intercept 5 and no x-intercepts. Domain ℝ, range [5, ∞).
questions.explanation: Table: x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 give y = 9, 6, 5, 6, 9. The points form a U-shaped parabola with its lowest point at (0, 5); since x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0, y ≥ 5 and the curve never meets the x-axis (x<sup>2</sup> = −5 has no real root).
questions.figure: Graph of y = x<sup>2</sup> + 5: upward parabola, vertex (0, 5), points (±1, 6) and (±2, 9), no x-intercepts.

questions.question: Sketch the graph of y = x<sup>5</sup>.
questions.answer: An increasing curve through the origin, symmetric about the origin (an odd function); it passes through (−1, −1), (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 32). Domain ℝ, range ℝ.
questions.explanation: Table: x = −2, −1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2 give y = −32, −1, −0.031, 0, 0.031, 1, 32. The curve is flat near the origin, rises steeply for |x| > 1 and passes through the origin; f(−x) = −f(x) so the graph has point symmetry about O.
questions.figure: Graph of y = x<sup>5</sup>: curve through (−1, −1), (0, 0), (1, 1), rising steeply on both sides, symmetric about the origin.

questions.question: Sketch the graphs of the square root functions obtained from x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = 25.
questions.answer: y = √(25 − x<sup>2</sup>) and y = −√(25 − x<sup>2</sup>), for −5 ≤ x ≤ 5: the upper and lower semicircles of the circle of radius 5 centred at the origin. Upper: domain [−5, 5], range [0, 5]; lower: domain [−5, 5], range [−5, 0].
questions.explanation: Solving for y: y<sup>2</sup> = 25 − x<sup>2</sup> ⇒ y = ±√(25 − x<sup>2</sup>), with 25 − x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0, i.e. −5 ≤ x ≤ 5. Putting x = 0, ±3, ±4, ±5 gives y = ±5, ±4, ±3, 0. The plus sign gives the upper half of the circle x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = 25 (x-intercepts (±5, 0), y-intercept (0, 5)) and the minus sign gives the lower half (y-intercept (0, −5)). Together the two branches form the complete circle of radius 5 about the origin.
questions.figure: Graph: a circle of radius 5 centred at O split into two semicircles y = √(25 − x<sup>2</sup>) above the x-axis and y = −√(25 − x<sup>2</sup>) below it, meeting the x-axis at (−5, 0) and (5, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 5) and (0, −5).

questions.question: Sketch the graph of the quadratic function y = x<sup>2</sup> − 2x + 1.
questions.answer: y = (x − 1)<sup>2</sup>: parabola opening upward with vertex (1, 0), touching the x-axis at x = 1, y-intercept 1. Domain ℝ, range [0, ∞).
questions.explanation: Complete the square: x<sup>2</sup> − 2x + 1 = (x − 1)<sup>2</sup>. Table: x = −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 give y = 4, 1, 0, 1, 4. The lowest point is the vertex (1, 0), the axis of symmetry is x = 1, and the curve cuts the y-axis at (0, 1).
questions.figure: Graph of y = x<sup>2</sup> − 2x + 1 = (x − 1)<sup>2</sup>: upward parabola with vertex (1, 0), y-intercept (0, 1), points (0, 1) and (2, 1).

questions.question: Sketch the graph of the quadratic function y = −3x<sup>2</sup> + 6x.
questions.answer: y = −3(x − 1)<sup>2</sup> + 3: parabola opening downward with vertex (1, 3), x-intercepts 0 and 2, y-intercept 0. Domain ℝ, range (−∞, 3].
questions.explanation: Factor: y = −3x(x − 2), so y = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2. Completing the square: −3(x<sup>2</sup> − 2x) = −3[(x − 1)<sup>2</sup> − 1] = −3(x − 1)<sup>2</sup> + 3, giving vertex (1, 3). Since a = −3 < 0 the parabola opens downward, with maximum value 3.
questions.figure: Graph of y = −3x<sup>2</sup> + 6x: downward parabola, vertex (1, 3), x-intercepts (0, 0) and (2, 0).

questions.question: Sketch the graph of y = x<sup>2</sup> + 3x + 2 using factors.
questions.answer: y = (x + 1)(x + 2): upward parabola with x-intercepts −1 and −2, y-intercept 2, vertex (−3/2, −1/4). Domain ℝ, range [−1/4, ∞).
questions.explanation: Factorising: y = (x + 1)(x + 2), so the graph cuts the x-axis at (−1, 0) and (−2, 0). At x = 0, y = 2, the y-intercept. The vertex lies midway between the roots, x = −3/2, where y = (1/2)(−1/2) = −1/4. Since a = 1 > 0 the parabola opens upward.
questions.figure: Graph of y = x<sup>2</sup> + 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x + 2): upward parabola with x-intercepts (−2, 0) and (−1, 0), y-intercept (0, 2), vertex (−1.5, −0.25).

questions.question: Sketch the graph of y = −x<sup>2</sup> − 5x using factors.
questions.answer: y = −x(x + 5): downward parabola with x-intercepts 0 and −5, y-intercept 0, vertex (−5/2, 25/4). Domain ℝ, range (−∞, 25/4].
questions.explanation: Factorising: y = −x(x + 5), so y = 0 at x = 0 and x = −5. At x = 0, y = 0, so the y-intercept is the origin. The vertex is at x = −5/2, where y = −(−5/2)(5/2) = 25/4. Since a = −1 < 0 the parabola opens downward, with maximum value 25/4.
questions.figure: Graph of y = −x<sup>2</sup> − 5x = −x(x + 5): downward parabola with x-intercepts (−5, 0) and (0, 0), vertex (−2.5, 6.25).

questions.question: Find the equation of the function of the type y = f(x) = ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c whose graph cuts the x-axis at the points (−4, 0) and (3, 0) and also passes through the point (2, −4).
questions.explanation: The x-intercepts give y = a(x + 4)(x − 3). Substitute (2, −4): −4 = a(2 + 4)(2 − 3) = −6a, so a = 2/3. Hence y = (2/3)(x + 4)(x − 3) = (2/3)(x<sup>2</sup> + x − 12) = (2/3)x<sup>2</sup> + (2/3)x − 8.

questions.question: Find the equation of the graph of the function of the type y = ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c which crosses the x-axis at the points (−8, 0) and (9, 0) and also passes through (5, 10).
questions.explanation: From the intercepts y = a(x + 8)(x − 9). Substitute (5, 10): 10 = a(5 + 8)(5 − 9) = −52a, so a = −5/26. Hence y = (−5/26)(x + 8)(x − 9) = (−5/26)(x<sup>2</sup> − x − 72) = (−5/26)x<sup>2</sup> + (5/26)x + 180/13.

questions.question: Find the equation of the function of the type y = 3x<sup>2</sup> + bx + c of the parabola which cuts the x-axis at the points (−3, 0) and (5, 0).
questions.explanation: With leading coefficient 3 and roots −3 and 5: y = 3(x + 3)(x − 5) = 3(x<sup>2</sup> − 2x − 15) = 3x<sup>2</sup> − 6x − 45. Comparing with 3x<sup>2</sup> + bx + c gives b = −6 and c = −45.

questions.question: Find the equation of the graph of the function of the type y = 2x<sup>2</sup> + bx + c which crosses the x-axis at the points (−4, 0) and (5, 0).
questions.explanation: With leading coefficient 2 and roots −4 and 5: y = 2(x + 4)(x − 5) = 2(x<sup>2</sup> − x − 20) = 2x<sup>2</sup> − 2x − 40. Hence b = −2 and c = −40.

questions.question: Graphically find the points of intersection of the linear function f(x) = x + 7 with the coordinate axes.
questions.answer: P(−7, 0) on the x-axis and Q(0, 7) on the y-axis.
questions.explanation: For the x-intercept put y = 0: x + 7 = 0 ⇒ x = −7. For the y-intercept put x = 0: y = 7. Plotting the line through (−7, 0) and (0, 7) shows it crossing the axes at these two points.

questions.question: Graphically find the points of intersection of the linear function f(x) = −x + 5 with the coordinate axes.
questions.answer: P(5, 0) on the x-axis and Q(0, 5) on the y-axis.
questions.explanation: y = 0 gives −x + 5 = 0 ⇒ x = 5; x = 0 gives y = 5. The line falls with slope −1 and meets the axes at (5, 0) and (0, 5).

questions.question: Graphically find the points of intersection of the linear function f(x) = 3x + 2 with the coordinate axes.
questions.answer: Q(0, 2) on the y-axis and P(−2/3, 0) on the x-axis.
questions.explanation: y = 0 gives 3x + 2 = 0 ⇒ x = −2/3; x = 0 gives y = 2. The line rises with slope 3 and crosses the axes at (−2/3, 0) and (0, 2).

questions.question: Graphically find the points of intersection of the linear function f(x) = −2x + 4 with the coordinate axes.
questions.answer: Q(0, 4) on the y-axis and P(2, 0) on the x-axis.
questions.explanation: y = 0 gives −2x + 4 = 0 ⇒ x = 2; x = 0 gives y = 4. The line falls with slope −2 and crosses the axes at (2, 0) and (0, 4).

questions.question: Find graphically the point of intersection of the functions 2x + y = 5 and x + y = 4 (y a function of x).
questions.explanation: Rewrite as y = 5 − 2x and y = 4 − x. Table for y = 5 − 2x: (0, 5), (1, 3), (2, 1); for y = 4 − x: (0, 4), (1, 3), (2, 2). Plotting both lines, they cross at (1, 3). Check: 2(1) + 3 = 5 and 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.question: Find graphically the point of intersection of the functions 3x − 2y = 4 and x + 4y = 6 (y a function of x).
questions.explanation: Rewrite as y = (3x − 4)/2 and y = (6 − x)/4. Table for y = (3x − 4)/2: (0, −2), (2, 1), (4, 4); for y = (6 − x)/4: (0, 1.5), (2, 1), (6, 0). The two lines meet at (2, 1). Check: 3(2) − 2(1) = 4 and 2 + 4(1) = 6.

questions.question: Find graphically the point of intersection of the functions f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = x<sup>2</sup> − 4x + 6.
questions.answer: The line meets the parabola at (1, 3) and (4, 6).
questions.explanation: Table for y = x + 2: (0, 2), (1, 3), (4, 6); for y = x<sup>2</sup> − 4x + 6: (0, 6), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 6). The parabola opens upward with vertex (2, 2). Plotting both graphs shows intersection points (1, 3) and (4, 6). Algebraically x + 2 = x<sup>2</sup> − 4x + 6 ⇒ x<sup>2</sup> − 5x + 4 = 0 ⇒ x = 1, 4, giving y = 3, 6.
questions.figure: Graph: line y = x + 2 cutting the upward parabola y = x<sup>2</sup> − 4x + 6 (vertex (2, 2)) at (1, 3) and (4, 6).

questions.question: Find graphically the point of intersection of the functions f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = x<sup>2</sup> − 6x + 10.
questions.answer: The line meets the parabola at (1, 5) and (6, 10).
questions.explanation: Table for y = x + 4: (0, 4), (1, 5), (6, 10); for y = x<sup>2</sup> − 6x + 10: (0, 10), (1, 5), (3, 1), (5, 5), (6, 10). The parabola opens upward with vertex (3, 1). The graphs cross at (1, 5) and (6, 10). Algebraically x + 4 = x<sup>2</sup> − 6x + 10 ⇒ x<sup>2</sup> − 7x + 6 = 0 ⇒ x = 1, 6, giving y = 5, 10.
questions.figure: Graph: line y = x + 4 cutting the upward parabola y = x<sup>2</sup> − 6x + 10 (vertex (3, 1)) at (1, 5) and (6, 10).

questions.question: The paths of two aeroplanes A and B in the plane are determined by the straight lines 2x − y = 6 and 3x + y = 4 respectively. Graphically find the point where the two paths cross each other.
questions.explanation: Rewrite as y = 2x − 6 and y = 4 − 3x. Table for y = 2x − 6: (0, −6), (2, −2), (4, 2); for y = 4 − 3x: (0, 4), (2, −2), (3, −5). Plotting both lines, they intersect at (2, −2). Check: 2(2) − (−2) = 6 and 3(2) + (−2) = 4.
questions.figure: Graph: line 2x − y = 6 (y = 2x − 6) and line 3x + y = 4 (y = 4 − 3x) crossing at (2, −2).

questions.question: If the sum of two numbers is 6 and the square of the first number is greater than 6 by the second number, solve graphically and find the numbers.
questions.answer: The numbers are 3 and 3, or −4 and 10.
questions.explanation: Let the first number be x and the second y. Then x + y = 6 and x<sup>2</sup> = y + 6, i.e. y = 6 − x and y = x<sup>2</sup> − 6. Table for y = 6 − x: (0, 6), (3, 3), (6, 0); for y = x<sup>2</sup> − 6: (0, −6), (2, −2), (3, 3), (4, 10). The line and the parabola intersect at (3, 3) and (−4, 10). Check: 3 + 3 = 6 and 3<sup>2</sup> = 3 + 6; also −4 + 10 = 6 and (−4)<sup>2</sup> = 10 + 6.
questions.figure: Graph: line y = 6 − x and upward parabola y = x<sup>2</sup> − 6 (vertex (0, −6)) intersecting at (3, 3) and (−4, 10).

questions.question: If f: A → B is a function, then it is an onto function if:
questions.explanation: A function is onto (surjective) when every element of the co-domain B is an image, i.e. when the range equals B. Range ⊂ B would make it into B but not onto.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Range = B  b) Range ⊂ B  c) Image is not repeated  d) Domain ≠ A

questions.question: The graph of y = x<sup>6</sup> is symmetric to ______.
questions.explanation: x<sup>6</sup> is an even power, so f(−x) = (−x)<sup>6</sup> = x<sup>6</sup> = f(x). The graph is therefore symmetric about the y-axis.
questions.optionsRaw: a) x − axis  b) y − axis  c) origin  d) none

questions.question: An one to one function is also called ______ function:
questions.explanation: A one-to-one (distinct elements have distinct images) function is called injective. Bijective means both injective and surjective.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Injective  b) Surjective  c) Bijective  d) Inverse

questions.question: Inverse of a function exists only if it is:
questions.explanation: f<sup>−1</sup> is a function only when f is one-to-one and onto, i.e. bijective. Injective alone fails to be onto and surjective alone fails to be one-to-one.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Injective  b) Bijective  c) Surjective  d) all of these

questions.question: The function f = {(x, y) | y = mx + c}, m and c are real numbers is:
questions.explanation: y = mx + c has degree 1 in x, so its graph is a straight line; the function is linear.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Linear  b) Quadratic  c) A circle  d) A point

questions.question: The function f = {(x, y) | y = ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c, a ≠ 0} is:
questions.explanation: The highest power of x is 2 with non-zero coefficient a, so the function is quadratic and its graph is a parabola.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Linear  b) Quadratic  c) A circle  d) A point

questions.question: The range of f(x) = x<sup>2</sup> + 3 ∀x ∈ ℝ is ______.
questions.explanation: x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0 for all real x, so x<sup>2</sup> + 3 ≥ 3, with value 3 at x = 0. The range is [3, ∞).
questions.optionsRaw: a) ℝ  b) ℝ<sup>−</sup>  c) (3, ∞)  d) [3, ∞]

questions.question: Graph of y = x<sup>n</sup> is symmetric to ______ if n is an odd integer.
questions.explanation: For odd n, (−x)<sup>n</sup> = −x<sup>n</sup>, i.e. f(−x) = −f(x); the graph has point symmetry about the origin.
questions.optionsRaw: a) x − axis  b) y − axis  c) origin  d) none

questions.question: The graph of linear function is:
questions.explanation: A linear function f(x) = ax + b (a ≠ 0) has a graph of degree 1, which is a straight line.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Circle  b) Straight line  c) Parabola  d) Triangle

questions.question: If f is function from A to B, domain of f is equal to:
questions.explanation: A function f: A → B must assign an image to every element of A, so its domain is the whole set A.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Any subset of A  b) A × B  c) A  d) B

questions.question: Every function is a:
questions.explanation: A function is a special relation in which each element of the domain has exactly one image, so every function is a relation (but not conversely).
questions.optionsRaw: a) Relation  b) Inverse function  c) One to one  d) None of these

questions.question: If f and g are equal where f(x) = 7x − 4 and g(x) = x then x =:
questions.explanation: Set f(x) = g(x): 7x − 4 = x ⇒ 6x = 4 ⇒ x = 2/3.

questions.question: Domain of the function f(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 1) is set of all:
questions.explanation: The denominator x − 1 is zero at x = 1, where f is undefined; every other real number is allowed. Hence the domain is ℝ − {1}.
questions.optionsRaw: a) real numbers  b) rational numbers  c) complex numbers  d) real numbers except 1

questions.question: A function f(x) = |x| − x<sup>2</sup> is:
questions.explanation: f(−x) = |−x| − (−x)<sup>2</sup> = |x| − x<sup>2</sup> = f(x), so the function is even (its graph is symmetric about the y-axis).
questions.optionsRaw: a) odd  b) Linear  c) Even  d) Neither even nor odd

questions.question: Find the domain of the function f(x) = (2x − 1)/(x + 4).
questions.explanation: The denominator vanishes at x = −4, where the function is undefined; all other real numbers are admissible.

questions.question: Find the domain of the function f(x) = √(x + 3).
questions.explanation: The radicand must be non-negative: x + 3 ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≥ −3.

questions.question: Graphically find the point of intersection of the functions f(x) = x and g(x) = x<sup>2</sup> − x.
questions.explanation: Table for y = x: (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2); for y = x<sup>2</sup> − x: (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 2), (−1, 2). The line y = x cuts the upward parabola y = x<sup>2</sup> − x at (0, 0) and (2, 2). Algebraically x = x<sup>2</sup> − x ⇒ x<sup>2</sup> − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 0, 2.
